item.title: Ex-Goldman Sachs MD accused of inhumanity after making new colleagues work 100 hour week
item.description:
Mark Carney was once a managing director in investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> at Goldman Sachs. He has not done this job for 15 years, but as ex-Goldman Sachs associate turned academic Alexandra Michel has shown, </news/2020/05/why-bankers-overwork>banking hours don't stop when you leave banking. Many former bankers continue working at the same pace, and attempt to enforce the ethos on their new colleagues, says Michel after studying them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Carney is now president of an entire country - Canada - rather than an entire investment banking division, but he appears to be well along this path. The Canadian press <https://globalnews.ca/news/12166399/liberals-carney-defend-pace-bill-c-39/> is reporting a furore after a lawmaking committee in Canada's House of Commons spent 100 hours in seven days debating a bill. These included two 15 hour days on Saturday and Sunday.
The hours were "on the line of being inhumane,” said one lawmaker. They were “pretty brutal,” said another. They hours were effectively communicating that, "‘We’re going to fatigue you, we’re going to burn you out," said the first.
Not so, declared Carney, schooled in the ways of Goldman Sachs. The pace was “absolutely not,” excessive, he said, adding that he wanted to "salute" all involved "for the time they put in."
“They didn’t get to spend quality time with their family on the weekend, at various events. Some people came in, missed birthdays and other things, in order to move forward,” Carney observed.
This is a badge of honour. Junior bankers everywhere will sympathise.
Carney is not the first bank to fall foul of the different culture in government jobs. When Morgan Stanley technology banker Michael Grimes </news/michael-grimes>briefly went to work in the Chips Program Office he was said to cause an upset by firing questions like "What’s four to the fourth power?,” in interviews.

item.title: Singapore private banking jobs appear to be a horrible grind
item.description:
Private banking jobs can pay well in Singapore </news/this-is-what-your-private-banking-salary-and-bonus-should-be-in-singapore>, but you will be worked hard for your money.
A new report from Quinlan & Associates, a strategy consulting firm in Hong Kong, suggests the job of a relationship manager in Singapore (and in Hong Kong) is a grind. It is a grind because you will have loads of clients. It is also a grind because you will have loads of admin.
After surveying 62 relationship managers in both Hong Kong and Singapore, Quinlan suggested that clients are assigned to relationship managers in the proportions shown in the chart above. At worst, one person has 400 clients associated with them in the mass affluent premier banking section. At best, they have 30.
Servicing these people is a slog. Quinlan said relationship managers are afflicted with an admin burden that consumes between 3.5-9.5 hours of their time for each client meeting. This follows a report <https://asianprivatebanker.com/private-banking-wealth-management/average-private-banking-book-size-grew-by-us62m-in-2025/>in Asian Private Banker which said assets under management per relationship manager increased 15% in the past year.
As relationship managers attempt to service their many clients with their growing assets, Quinlan found they're wasting hours on "fragmented systems," manual processes and inaccurate data. "We receive many compliance queries every day, and whenever there is a question, we have to take out a lot of emails or data sources to address the questions,” complained one head of desk at a European private bank.
AI could solve all these issues, declares Quinlan, who is coincidentally selling AI solutions. However, this may prove a double-edged sword, particularly among the people with 400 clients each. HSBC, for example, is reportedly cutting up to 70% of its UK financial advisers <https://www.ft.com/content/dd553fc2-532c-4afc-a773-47cd7f786260?syn-25a6b1a6=1>in preparation for the great and automated future yet to come.

item.title: Reports of zero bonuses at the bank that cut 30% of researchers are incorrect
item.description:
It's December, which means some banks are about to pay bonuses. Which means some people are thinking about how large their bonuses might be. Some of those people are at Berenberg.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It's not so long ago now that Berenberg fired 30% of its London equity researchers. </news/berenberg-equity-research-cuts>It's also not so long ago now that head of the European investment bank Laura Janssens </news/2023/05/laura-janssens-berenberg> left the firm. And within living memory, Berenberg bonuses were cut to zero. </news/2022/11/berenberg-bonuses>
It's with this in mind, perhaps, that rumours are circulating in the market that Berenberg will once again shrink bonuses to nothing this year. We understand that there will be bonuses at Berenberg, and that they will be paid in March.
March payments appear to be the norm at Berenberg now, although one insider informs us that the numbers have historically been shared with the business in December.
A spokesperson for Berenberg said: “Any suggestion we do not plan on paying bonuses this year is wholly incorrect. The year-end process will run as normal; bonus payments will made in March, as usual.”

item.title: How to become a technology managing director in a bank
item.description:
The path from analyst to MD </news/career-paths-technology-banking>in an investment banking team is pretty cut and dry; pay your dues in your first few years, build the right connections and prove your worth. For many banks, technology staff </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank>make up a massive portion of headcount; is their path to the top any different?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"As you move up the ladder, EQ becomes much more important," said one managing director at a US bank, speaking to us anonymously. "Some of the junior engineers I've worked with have been extremely smart, high IQ people, but shifting to EQ becomes more important as you grow."
This is because, as you become more senior, you need to speak to many more people outside of engineering to understand which problems need to be solved and how to solve them. The MD said that you must have "empathy towards someone who is not doing the work that a technologist is doing on a day-to-day basis." Another MD working in artificial intelligence told us that "the most important person to bring into the room is the one who deals with the consequences of your decisions." Building connections with those other teams in your formative years will give you a better understanding of what the most high-impact problems are by the time you're eligible for an MD promotion.
Banking as an industry is all about image; much like investment bankers need to be on the highest-value deals, engineers need to work on the most visible technical issues. Projects with quantifiable results are especially valuable; "are you able to show you contributed to the commercial value of the business with your engineering and design?" asks the US bank MD.
The level of technical ability required will differ from role to role. One MD told us in 2024 </news/i-stopped-coding-to-manage-developers-in-a-bank-and-now-i-can-t-find-a-job> that he "stopped coding a decade ago" to focus on managing developers and organizing their workflows. At the time, this made it difficult for the MD to find work outside of banking, though AI coding tools </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> may have changed things. Banks have other ways to show appreciation for their most technical people; Goldman Sachs has tech fellows, </news/goldman-promoted-a-group-of-top-technologists-one-office-got-particularly-lucky> Morgan Stanley has distinguished engineers.
Individual contributors beware: being able to build a team is essential to becoming a tech MD. "Managing" is in the name, after all. The AI MD said that a good question to ask engineers when hiring is "have you ever changed a technical decision because someone close to the problem saw something you missed?" He said this question will tell you "a lot about someone’s engineering judgement, how well they listen and whether they give others credit."
How does the role compare to leadership positions in Big Tech? The AI MD, who also worked for a major technology firm, said that tech firms "start with the experience we wanted someone to have and work backwards into the engineering." Banks focus on this experience too, but place much more focus on "what happens when something goes wrong." The US bank MD said that the culture in Big Tech is "make fast and break fast," but the impact of those breaks is "not as damaging or disrupting to the life of individuals" as it is in finance if anything goes wrong. (Those impacted by Microsoft's recent Outlook outage </news/outlook-outage-banking> might beg to differ.)

item.title: Morning Coffee: 25-year-old hedge fund genius still seeking older soul mate. Citadel Securities and the AI agents
item.description:
Leopold Aschenbrenner, </news/leopold-aschenbrenner-friends> the not entirely modest-seeming 24-year-old hedge fund manager has been humbled by the markets. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/aschenbrenners-situational-awareness-tells-investors-it-lost-65-in-third-quarter-de8e9797>has seen Leopold's letter to his investors and Leopold says his Situational Awareness fund was down 65% in the third quarter, including his cataclysmic 67% meltdown in July.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Despite this, Situational Awareness is still up 88% year-to-date, and so Leopold is still saying such things as, “Our risk scenarios and portfolio construction must respect the volatility of the singularity.” He is also predicting that “a civilization of alien geniuses” will imminently arrive in San Francisco, comprised of AI tools.
Aschenbrenner is an opinionated person and the volatility preceding the singularity has not deprived him of this. Having spent the last three months "focused inward", he's reportedly concluded that Tesla, SpaceX, Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Microsoft and Apple are likely to lose their competitive moats. He's still bullish on Anthropic.
But after being rescued by Citadel in the July meltdown </news/citadel-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness>, Aschenbrenner also wants some wisdom in his room. The WSJ notes that he's still looking for an 'experienced chief risk officer.' Last week, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/1fcbc6ea-1be3-44d2-b564-8ebf91181639?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported that Situational Awareness had increased headcount from eight to 30 people between June and November.
Leopold has already leaned on experience. Citadel told Risk Magazine <https://www.risk.net/awards/7964526/hedge-fund-of-the-year-citadel> that during Situational Awareness's darkest hour, it got in touch through the fund's treasurer, who previously worked for Citadel. This was presumably Sven Khatri </news/2020/08/citadel-hiring-from-goldman-sachs>, who is also a former Goldman Sachs managing director and has circa 20 years' experience. Similarly, Leopold's prime broker relationships have reportedly been worked by David Geffen, a self-described 'advisor to investment managers' whose career began in 1986 and who once worked for collapsed hedge fund Amaranth Advisors.
If you want to be Leopold's chief risk officer, you can possibly still apply. The FT said last week that Situational Awareness still has $10bn in assets under management and that the fund is working with Clear Street's prime broking arm and has been talking to Jefferies about opening a prime brokerage account, too. Before the July rupture, Situational Awareness was reportedly <https://www.ft.com/content/bdec4129-ccac-4149-aa53-90ddd50cb925?syn-25a6b1a6=1> the biggest client for Goldman Sachs' prime broking business. Goldman reportedly earned $200m in fees from the fund in the months before the blow up, but having been burned in July it may be less keen. JPMorgan reportedly <https://www.ft.com/content/916eea1b-d483-49e1-9a70-53b4df8f9870?syn-25a6b1a6=1> cut lending to Situational Awareness after July.
The new chief risk officer would arrive as Leopold leverages up again. One investor who spoke to the FT said: “all they’ve learnt is [that their] risk management needs a little more fine tuning.” That's a big responsibility for someone.
Separately, not only is Citadel </news/citadel-is-hedge-fund-of-the-year-is-ken-griffin-its-secret-sauce>the hedge fund of the year according to Risk Magazine <https://www.risk.net/awards/7964526/hedge-fund-of-the-year-citadel>, but Citadel Securities is the market maker of the year according to the same publication. <https://www.risk.net/awards/7964540/flow-market-maker-of-the-year-citadel-securities>
The accolade has been awarded in part for Citadel Securities' apparently unrivalled ability to provide liquidity in challenging markets, but also for its "differentiated insights."
Some of these insights are the result of AI. Earlier this month, Matt Robinson <https://www.ai-street.co/p/citadel-securities-develops-ai-agents> reported that Citadel Securities has been helping clients develop AI agents. Risk Magazine says the firm is also using AI agents to "play the offense" in terms of identifying, organising and testing data.
Training these agents is like training junior researchers, said Matt Culek, Citadel Securities' chief COO. Using them has enabled Citadel Securities' human researchers to cut the number of hours they spend evaluating new data sets from 40 to two, he added.
This doesn't necessarily sound great for the 300+ PhDs that Citadel Securities' technology COO Jeff Maurone said the firm employs in research at an event <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f26osxg5uy0> recently, but all may be well. Risk says Citadel Securities is simply using the AI agents to add 50% more datasets than last year and is assigning its human researchers to higher value tasks. Compute spending appears to be increasing exponentially, though: it's up 20 times since 2021. This in itself may focus minds on paying heavily for humans. </news/data-centre-spending-is-coming-for-pay-at-hedge-funds-and-electronic-trading-firms>
Meanwhile...
Santander appointed ex-Credit Suisse banker Felipe Portillo as head of corporate and investment banking for Europe, replacing Ignacio Domínguez-Adame, who's been there 32-years. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/santander-shakes-up-investment-bank-with-new-europe-head>
Qube </news/qube-us-market-making-firm> will be absorbing its $2 billion Moebius fund into its Qube strategy in early 2027. It's not clear why but everyone wants to be invested in Qube. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-26/qrt-to-merge-2-billion-hedge-fund-with-flagship-qube-strategy?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>
Stakes in VC funds traded on the secondary market at an average discount of 32% to their net asset value in the first half of 2026. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/0278cbea-a0b6-4a30-80f2-f31ac6657f11?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
The best thing to be now is a crypotographer. “In the coming years, we must expect that some of these methods will fail quickly and with little warning. This reinforces the argument for cryptographic agility . . . which is the major cryptographic challenge of the 21st century.” (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/450920b9-82b8-4a66-960b-5740aa7f94ae?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Hernández de Cos, the new head of the European Central Bank is a quiet fellow who is soft-spoken but knows a lot about everything from privatization in Spain, to stablecoins and fiscal policy. (FT) <https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/europe-has-picked-a-new-central-bank-chief-hes-in-for-a-bumpy-ride-7d6f7fea?mod=WSJ_home_feature_1_pos_4>
The quiet money is in East London. "The best thing I have ever bought came from a woman with no shopfront and no signage, working from a studio above another bike repair place, whom you find through someone who knows someone." (Substack) <https://substack.com/home/post/p-219407854>

item.title: Mizuho has some shiny new MDs in New York from UBS, Santander, and TD
item.description:
Every bank bigger than your local credit union, at some point in the last few years, has declared a rather impressive goal for its investment banking operation. Top five in the USA, top three in Europe, top sixth or seventh globally – take your pick. It’s quite common. What’s rarer is for a bank to still be stacking up bankers </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> and traders </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> years after it has made such a promise.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
The biggest new name at Mizuho in New York this month was Colin Renz, who joined the firm as head of data centers investment banking. Renz was previously at UBS, which he joined in 2021 as a tech banker and MD from Credit Suisse (rather fortuitous, really).
Kevin Dong also joined Mizuho in New York this month, as head of agency CMO trading. He joined the Japanese bank from Santander, where he had the same title. Dong joined Santander by acquisition; he was previously at Amherst Pierpont Securities, a fixed income broker-dealer which Santander acquired in 2022.
Vanessa Simonetti rounded out the trinity. Simonetti joined Mizuho in New York this month to help build out its structured notes business, according to market intelligence firm Structured Retail Products <https://www.structuredretailproducts.com/insights/85387/mizuho-hires-former-td-structured-notes-head-to-build-us-business>. Simonetti joined Mizuho from TD Securities, where she was global head of structured notes and equity derivatives. Simonetti spent almost nine years at TD Securities; she was head of Americas financial intermediaries for Deutsche Bank before that.
Mizuho didn't respond to a request to comment on this article. The bank has had some measure of ambition historically; in 2023, after acquiring boutique investment bank Greenhill, head of Mizuho Securities USA Jerry Rizzieri told the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/03875c28-b3f5-4ca8-aa4d-9551b98e6554> that the bank aimed to be “solidly inside the top 10 corporate investment banks within three years." According to market intelligence provider LSEG, Mizuho is not in the top 10 for Americas investment banking fees in year-to-date 2026. Here’s to a strong December, then.

item.title: Come back Geoff Weber, your Citi colleagues just want to say goodbye
item.description:
As we reported this week, Geoff Weber </news/geoff-weber-citi>has vanished from Citi. No one knows where Geoff has gone. He is not answering his phones. He is not responding to messages.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Weber was Citi's New York-based head of G 10 rates trading. He joined the bank from UBS in 2012 according to his FINRA registration, and he was promoted to run the G10 rates trading business at the bank in 2023.
It is not clear where Weber is going next. Jane Street and Goldman Sachs have been the subject of speculation, but both are understood to be incorrect. Citadel Securities is being suggested, but remains speculation too. Weber is ignoring our messages. Wherever he turns up, it will need to be a very senior role, say headhunters.
Weber could probably afford to retire. In 2016 alone, his desk was said to have made <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-10-27/citigroup-trading-desk-said-to-reap-300-million-on-rate-swaps> $300m. However, he is not thought to be retiring. When Citi traders retire, they are typically clapped off the trading floor and may spend a few weeks travelling between offices and saying goodbye. Zoeb Sachee </news/citi-s-big-euro-rates-trader-left-what-if-he-goes-to-barclays>, who spent 36 years at the US bank is understood to have had this kind of send-off.
Weber, however, appears to have disappeared suddenly. Bloomberg reported that people at Citi only learned of his departure when Deirdre Dunn, the bank’s head of rates, informed them that he was leaving in a call. Until that point, Weber had reportedly been considered as her replacement.
Weber's former colleagues and friends would like to say goodbye to him. We understand that some have texted without success. Maybe he will respond if he turns up at Citadel Securities.

item.title: Ex-girlfriend accuses 6-foot London finance bro of emotional illiteracy in new song
item.description:
Not so long ago, tall men in finance were all the rage on TikTok. <https://www.tiktok.com/@girl_on_couch/video/7364483352545529130?lang=en> But now that these relationships have had time to mature, some of the female participants appear to be having second thoughts.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Among them is a London-based singer called Alis Naya, who has a day job making coffee for "finance bros" at an unnamed investment bank in London. Naya has spent the past month pounding TikTok <https://www.tiktok.com/@whothefuckisalis/video/7712009981150661910> with her new song about dating a unnamed six foot finance bro, who she says was emotionally inarticulate.
The full song is available here on Spotify. <https://open.spotify.com/track/1SFVZExCcnBshttxD1ir8V>Naya's lyrics include lines such as "You preach that you’re so nice/But ignorance isn’t bliss," and, "There’s got to be more to you you’re just afraid to show it/ I want to see your tears, there’s more inside I know it," and, "You’re a man you work in finance and you’re six feet tall so maybe you don’t know what it’s like to be broken at all."
Her chorus accuses the bro of looking away when she cries and concludes, "Emotionally dried up, but I want to make it rain." "You don't have the capacity to handle me emotionally," she adds.
It's not clear who Naya is singing about, but her efforts have been spotted by the London finance community. Hers is the latest in a long history of works about finance boyfriends. TikTok now has an entire area <https://www.tiktok.com/discover/pov-your-boyfriend-work-in-finance> devoted to the genre.
Naya's observations coincide with those of Richard Ptardio, a former trader at Lehman and elsewhere, who says he had three wives from outside of financial services, each of whom extracted all his money.
Three of my wives never worked a day in finance. Couldn't tell you what a derivative was. All three absolutely cleaned me out in the divorce. Quite exceptional traders, in retrospect.
— Richard Z. Ptardio (@RichardPtardio) November 25, 2026 <https://x.com/RichardPtardio/status/2125516482457260279?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw>

item.title: Hedge fund Qube may only hire 10 new people for its new US market making firm. Good luck!
item.description:
As we were first to observe, Qube Research and Technologies (QRT) is up to something. In March, it hired Beat Ammon </news/hedge-fund-qube-research-hired-hudson-river-trading-s-head-of-options-market-making>, the former head of options market making at Hudson River Trading, who has also done time at Morgan Stanley and Citadel.
Someone like Ammon does not come cheaply. There are unconfirmed suggestions that he was subject to a bidding war before joining Qube. Before joining HRT, he spent a brief six months at Point72, suggesting he may have been bid out of there too. In March, another quant hedge fund is thought to have wanted him.
Ammon did not respond to a request to comment when we enquired in July. Qube declined to comment for this article.
Having hired its prize, QRT is unsurprisingly putting him to work. Ammon is head of options research at QRT. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/b519698f-6ace-47e9-9cd5-1e18f8fdd71b?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported yesterday that the London-based fund is setting up a new market making firm with a view to trading options in the US market. It has reportedly applied for a US broker dealer license and plans to launch in the second half of next year.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Ammon is European but has spent much of his career in the US. Qube moved him back to London. Maybe he'll go back to New York soon.
In the meantime, the FT says Qube plans to launch its new US broker dealer with 25 people. That sounds like a reasonable amount of hiring, except we understand that around 15 people are already in place.
H1B Visa data suggests that Qube might pay $230k base salaries to its US quants, <https://h1bgrader.com/h1b-sponsors/qrt-us-services-llc-l0yzgppv2x/salaries/2026> which is less than the $850k+ starting salaries </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street>at some US rivals. The firm is known to have an interesting pay structure </news/qrt-hedge-fund> in which employees have limited visibility of their own P&L and bonuses are entirely discretionary.
It's not clear whether this will apply to the options business, or how popular it will prove in the US market.
Qube's most recently filed ADV form, for the year ending 2025, shows investment staff were distributed between global offices as per the chart below. London isn't included, despite being the largest office and employing circa 822 people in total.
Qube's most recent filing with Companies House, also for 2025, shows it employing 1,336 people at group level, up from 827 the year before. They were paid an average of $868k per head.
One top US trading firm recruiter said getting a job at Qube may be quite easy. "They often employ B players and somehow generate A class returns," he suggested. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/quant-hedge-fund-july-performance-renaissance-technologies-two-sigma-cfm-2026-8> reported that Qube was up 18% in the year through to August 2026.

item.title: Goldman Sachs hired an engineering partner from Microsoft's AI team
item.description:
This thanksgiving, investment banking executives are presumably thankful for all of the costs they've been able to cut with AI, but there is work yet to do. Goldman Sachs, </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> which has historically been more cautious of the technology than other banks, has dialled back usage of its AI tools in recent months, but is still hiring AI specialists to build out its infrastructure.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This month, it hired Bogdan Arsintescu as a managing director. His exact role is unknown but Arsintescu's Linkedin profile suggests the role will involve work on knowledge graphs; systems which give AI tools more context when operating in complex environments. He was most recently a partner director of engineering at Microsoft, working within its CoreAI organization, which manages development for the tech firms full AI stack, including Copilot. Arsintescu also spent six years as a technical lead at Google working on knowledge graphs.
Making sure AI systems operate within a specific context can be especially important for banks, which have more stringent regulatory requirements. At the start of the month, the bank stopped its non-technical staff from using vibe coding tools like Claude Code after front-office staff allegedly created thousands of prototyped tools that could not all be implemented into Goldman's tech stack. For front-office work specificall, Goldman Sachs CIO Marco Argenti said that AI often lacks the "tricks and tribal knowledge" </news/goldman-sachs-ai>to operate as efficiently as a human banker.
Microsoft's systems, meanwhile, have come under fire as a result of the infamous outlook outage earlier this month that left many of Microsoft's services unusable. Microsoft said that this was a technical issue not related to AI <https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/cq5y10ge3dp3t>, and was in fact a months old bug. <https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/16/microsoft-global-outage-cause>

item.title: Morning Coffee: Morgan Stanley’s ex-AI head explains the nightmare underlying banks’ tech systems. Anthropic’s share price causes drama in the research department
item.description:
“These systems are incredibly complicated, they’ve been built in some cases over 30 years… most of the code is old, the businesspeople may have moved on, and now you’re in a situation where you’re sitting on top of a code base that you don’t fully understand”. That’s the basic problem of banking tech <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-25/bank-outages-become-side-effect-of-race-to-fight-ai-cyber-threats?srnd=homepage-uk>, as set out by Jeff McMillan, founder of a consultancy firm called McMillan AI.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It’s also the reason why, if you happen to look at people’s desks in the COO division, you will often see the motto “Never Change Anything” on signs and desk toys. Any time that you make changes to the system, you are taking the risk that the “patch” you installed to fix some bug or vulnerability will interact with some other code in an unpredictable way. Poorly installed patches or poorly documented legacy systems are the biggest causes of outages and data losses.
Unfortunately, one consequence of the AI revolution is that there are a lot more patches to deploy. Frontier models have turned out to be really good at discovering new cybersecurity flaws. This has led to an arms race, in which the tech companies have had to enlist the help of AI coding tools to secure the vulnerabilities. And the poor old IT staff of major banks and other large organisations, many of whom have no real idea what's under the bonnet, have found themselves having to constantly apply hastily-released, vibe coded patches to creaky old systems with bits of COBOL everywhere.
This might be why we’ve seen so many websites and trading systems crashing recently. Speaking last week, Jane Fraser of CEO estimated that “The volume of changes going through the world’s tech stack at the same time is five- to 10-fold what we’ve ever seen before,” and warned that “We should be expecting for a while some more downtime, some more outages in different areas.”
Jeff McMillan might have seen this nightmare coming. He’s got a good track record in being one step ahead of the game in banking IT, ever since he left the US Army </news/2016/11/veterans-journey-from-the-army-to-morgan-stanley-big-data-chief> and worked his way up to being Morgan Stanley’s “chief analytics and data officer” for wealth management, just at the height of the Big Data era. He rapidly grew that team </news/2022/05/morgan-stanley-ai-jobs>, positioning himself very well to shift to being the firmwide AI guy, implementing a system called “AIMS” </news/morgan-stanley-ai> which allowed wirehouse brokers to look up client data and populate forms really quickly. The last time we saw him, he was suggesting </news/ai-replacing-software-developers-gaslighting> that the rise of AI tools would mean that “the demand for deep technical expertise will decline”.
McMillan left Morgan Stanley in February. Presciently, this was just a few months before AI started causing a lot of unanticipated problems for the industry which might otherwise have landed on Jeff McMillan’s desk. His new company <https://mcmillanai.com/> promises to help people “Navigate the AI transformation with clarity” and he might be worth listening to as he seems to have seen a lot of things coming.
Elsewhere, when you come to think of it, it is quite strange that equity research </news/research-job-investment-bank> departments have a “house view”. Research analysts </news/i-spent-30-years-in-equity-research-the-job-only-got-harder> advertise themselves as independent thinkers, who are able to find ideas that the rest of the market has missed. But somehow, they always agree with their colleagues.
Obviously, there are decent organisational reasons for this – professional courtesy, the need to build teams and the fact that it’s difficult enough selling research when the message is clear, let alone when it’s contradictory. But that makes it all the more interesting when two analysts at the same house <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/anthropic-s-stock-sparks-rare-divide-inside-one-wall-street-firm?srnd=homepage-uk> have diametrically opposed views.
Andrew Freedman, of Hedgeye Risk Management, thinks that Anthropic is a good buy at these prices, as the market isn’t giving it credit for the potential upside of becoming the new default application for business. Felix Wang, also of Hedgeye, thinks it’s a short because the difficulty of building data centres is going to hurt its profit margins.
Freedman seems a little bit irked – he is the official coverage analyst, and according to social media <https://x.com/HedgeyeComm/status/2125382731194650864>, he wasn’t consulted by Wang. But it might be good for his career in the long run. If he’s wrong, then he gets a chance to take the credit for his colleague’s call. And if he’s right, then he gets bragging rights over a colleague forever. That’s surely a win-win.
Meanwhile …
Jamie Dimon is a famous Anglophile, but it seems that his loyalty is to London rather than Bournemouth. In response to UK tax changes which affect the banking industry, he’s considering cancelling some investment in the bank’s huge operations centre down by the seaside. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/jamie-dimon-loved-britainuntil-it-raised-taxes-on-jpmorgan-3462d7b6?st=y5Lj29&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink>)
Matthew Sebag-Montefiore has retired from his job as CEO of Rokos Capital Management. Individual decisions like this aren’t usually very informative but it’s worth keeping an eye on the trend, as no matter what their personal circumstances, people tend to feel more like sticking it out a few years when the industry trends are favourable. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/rokos-capital-ceo-sebag-montefiore-retires-from-macro-hedge-fund?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261125&utm_campaign=author_19458291>)
After hiring the head of options trading from Hudson River, Qube Research & Technologies has now added 25 staff to its New York office and applied for a broker-dealer licence, suggesting a serious push to expand. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/b519698f-6ace-47e9-9cd5-1e18f8fdd71b?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
If the Boomer MDs in your office are getting grumpy and moaning about pensions, while the Zoomer VPs are looking happy and talking about starting a family, it’s probably because the price of London flats are in free fall. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-11-25/london-luxury-property-quiet-crash-is-getting-louder>)
Just in case anyone thought that bygones might have been bygones, Bill Ackman has taken a little social media jab at Carl Icahn. The bad blood related to their disagreement over Herbalife is still sour, apparently. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/bill-ackman-carl-icahn-feud-wealth-herbalife-billionaires-investing-short-2026-11>)
Compliance officers have been fretting because the main reporting portal for the money laundering enforcement authority FinCen is down …(FT <https://www.ft.com/content/43aa7321-2a95-463c-8cb9-77fcc7e39291?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
… which means that it’s maybe not a great look for the CIO of the US government department responsible for FinCen to making quite so many public updates to his spare-time project to vibe-code a Civilisation game (404 Media <https://www.404media.co/sam-corcos-legatum-treasury-cio-is-vibe-coding-a-civilization-clone-during-treasury-department-hack/>)

item.title: Data centre spending is coming for pay at hedge funds and electronic trading firms
item.description:
You don't make good money in banks any more. At least this is what traders on some desks will tell you. The money has migrated. It's gone to jobs in hedge funds. It's gone to jobs in electronic trading firms.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It's unfortunate then, that the $800k+ starting salaries </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street> at some of these entities may also prove a flash in the pan. It's becoming increasingly clear that a major new expense has appeared: the cost of data centres.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/hrt-trading-revenue-tops-21-billion-eclipsing-full-year-record>reported today that Hudson River Trading's net income and trading revenues were flat year-on-year in the third quarter, even as the firm increases its spending on trading infrastructure, including data centres and access to compute power. Last month, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-10-22/jane-street-hrt-are-spending-billions-to-win-in-ai-era>also reported that HRT is spending $1bn on AI, including the construction of a data centre inside a mine inside a mountain in Norway. As models get "bigger and better" more compute is needed to power them, said HRT's head of AI Ian Dunning.
It's not just HRT. XTX Markets just opened a data centre staffed by 30 employees in Finland. It is now complaining <https://www.xtxmarkets.com/news/2026-xtx-markets-opens-first-data-centre/> about the government bureaucracy that means it's committing " billions of euros while leaving critical infrastructure decisions in administrative limbo."
Jan Boomers, CEO of Optiver, told Bloomberg he has "billions in capital expenditure planned in the years ahead”. Data centre spending is unlike anything else, said Boomers. “Our capex is fundamentally different versus a few years ago. This is a 10-year-plus investment cycle.”
There are some suggestions that this new and long investment cycle has the potential to cause problems with multistrategy hedge funds' pod model. Although many funds charge investors for technology investments through the pass-through model </news/hedge-fund-pass-throughs>, pods are typically also charged for the resources they use. The cost of those resources is increasing dramatically.
"The pod model is becoming stressed," says one senior infrastructure engineer, who asked not to be named. "If you're a large fund with multiple pods and you want to secure your future by building a data centre, how do you charge the forward cost of that to the individual pods?" It's easier where there's a central fund and the cost can be recouped in aggregate, he claimed.
Some quant hedge funds are finding solutions. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-03/how-hedge-fund-d-e-shaw-plans-to-stay-king-of-quant?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>reported earlier this month that DE Shaw has told clients that it will add a 0.12% technology surcharge to the 3% management fee, 35% profit cut and 0.23% fee for other expenses at its Composite Fund.
Speaking earlier this month, Bobby Jain </news/bobby-jain-jain-global>, founder of hedge fund Jain Global, said accessing Millennium's enormous AI resources and compute power was a major factor in his decision to return external investors' money and to manage money exclusively for Millennium. It takes years to build out AI infrastructure, said Jain. There's increasing competition for compute power from the likes of Anthropic, he added. "The biggest providers will want to go to their biggest clients."
Jain didn't say so, but this is why the infrastructure engineer says more and more funds and trading houses are reaching the conclusion that they need data centres of their own to secure their futures. "Financial services firms are bidding for GPUs and cloud space against the likes of Anthropic," he told us. "They're being crowded out. The competition has completely changed."
Data centres are needed and they don't come cheap. For the moment, many funds are renting cloud infrastructure from the likes of AWS, Google and CoreWeave, but this is not a long term solution, said Boomaars at Optiver. “It’s much more expensive and you’re not in charge of your own destiny… We have to be in charge of our own compute infrastructure,” he explained.

item.title: Frontier AI models are struggling to do even the most junior bankers’ work
item.description:
It’s easy to doom and gloom about AI if you work in finance. AI will destroy this </news/ai-in-compliance-finance>; AI will destroy that </news/ai-in-operations>. You might secretly have prompted Claude to do some aspect of your work and been unpleasantly surprised. But just how good is AI at doing your job, if you’re a front-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> banker?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Truth is, nowhere near as good as you think. A recent research paper <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22085> published by AI training firm Handshake AI found that putting AI in the shoes of bankers is simply not a good idea at all. It devised this perhaps obvious conclusion with an amusing series of tests.
Each AI agent plays the role of a fictional analyst at a fictional bank. It has fictional Outlook, Slack, Google Drive, Google Calendar, and OneNote apps. It has an average of over 1,300 fictional emails to trawl through and identify its target brief, build a real model, and send it to a fictional recipient before a set deadline.
The paper even trolls the AI agent somewhat, passing on realistic on-task corrections, such as telling it to “disregard the 44.50 and use 48.00” in a certain column. It did not note sending this email at 2am after a 16-hour workday.
So which AI agent is best? There are three: Opus 5, Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra. These are more than twice as good as anything else tested at the first attempt. The rest are broadly comparable in capability: Grok 4.6, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and so on. Some other models, such as Gemini 3.1 Pro, performed significantly worse. Given the cadence at which frontier labs release new models, however, it’s worth taking that current lineup with a pinch of salt.
The best definitions of success, either way, show that the models are broadly unsuccessful – or, at the very least, need substantial oversight. Opus 5 gets around 11% of its tasks done to a passable standard. On partial credit, the top three score around 70%, meaning that they have generally the right idea, but rarely do it all correctly.
That is where flesh-and-blood analysts come into it. Ironically, however, many of the mistakes that the AI made were small, typical mistakes made by tired individuals: applying 2.5% to the wrong figure (contract price vs build cost), forgetting to attach a workbook, or sending it in the wrong email.
The paper was written by a rather motley crew. Jonas Mueller, the last-named author, was a senior scientist at AWS before joining Handshake’s research team. Others, such as Amir Bouzidi and Collin Schweiker, are former analysts at Rothschild and JPMorgan, respectively.
“Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete,” the paper says, and were developed by bankers of “up to” VP level from Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, UBS, and Rothschild. The paper also credits professionals from Moelis for their contribution.
Amusingly, both Rothschild and Moelis are listed as clients <https://rogo.com/customers> of Rogo and its main product, Felix. Rogo </news/the-new-team-of-ai-bankers-with-a-cool-name-some-of-the-most-profitable-traders-in-the-world-don-t-know-how-much-they-ve-made>’s Felix is an AI agent that senior bankers can email like any junior analyst, and it does menial work: deal screening, buyer outreach, that sort of thing. Rogo does not have its own LLM, but rather uses frontier models such as the ones tested above.
Felix’s value is that it contains a degree of the establishment in it; Rogo was founded by ex-Lazard and JPM analysts, among others, meaning it is taught by these people how to do things. Email Felix and you get a JPM-tier draft of something, hypothetically. It's perhaps an easy way to outsource smaller jobs than the complicated tasks in Handshake's experiment.

item.title: The apparent departure of Citi's UK chief risk officer may say something about risky risk jobs
item.description:
Where is Manjira Sen-Gosain, UK chief risk officer at Citi? No longer in her UK role, it seems. Maybe no longer at Citi at all. Citi isn't commenting and Sen-Gosain herself didn't respond to a request to comment, but Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/citis-uk-chief-risk-officer-stands-down-regulator-website-shows-2026-11-25/> notes that the FCA Register shows her leaving Citi's UK entities on November 3rd.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Sen-Gosain spent four years in her senior London risk job at Citi. She joined from HSBC in 2022 after 22 fruitful years at the British bank, where she ended up as head of enterprise risk and global banking and markets CRO.
At Citi, Sen-Gosain was designated the 'SMF4 Chief Risk' person for Citibank UK Ltd, for Citigroup Global Markets Ltd. and for Citibank Europe Plc. This is the kind of job which allows you to "clip coupons" </news/career-advice-banking> in terms of pay. It is also the kind of job where you're in a senior management function and can be held personally liable for regulatory breaches. If rules are breached, significant individual fines can be levied.
There are no suggestions that Sen-Gosain has breached any rules. However, Reuters notes that her apparent departure comes after Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/business/citi-incorrectly-booked-trades-underestimated-risky-assets-by-35-billion-sources-2026-11-19/> also reported that Citi had underestimated the risk weighted assets in its European trading unit by $35bn after apparently using an internal Citi risk model instead of a standardised model with regulatory approval. This was reportedly <https://financefeeds.com/citigroups-35-billion-risk-asset-error-threatens-progress-on-u-s-regulatory-exit/> equivalent to 23% of the total risk weighted assets at Citigroup Global Markets at the end of 2025.
Banks in the UK can only use internal models to calculate risk-weighted assets once the PRA has approved them for the relevant business. Otherwise they must use the standardised approach. Gontran de Quillacq, a New York-based former derivatives trader who now runs Navesink International, an expert witness network, said the mistake seemed peculiar and must have affected a core model. "$35bn is very large. What could generate such a miscalculation? Besides counterparty risk or market risk, it's hard to imagine what could cause this," he told us.
Citi's issues with declarations concerning its UK risk weighted assets preceded Sen Gosain's arrival. In 2019, the bank was fined £44m <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/news/2019/november/pra-fines-citigroups-uk-operations-44-million-for-failings>for understating its risk weighted assets by a cumulative $15.4bn between 2014 and 2018.
In 2019, it was noted that while the UK finance function at Citi was responsible for submitting regulatory returns they worked with teams in Mumbai and Budapest. The PRA noted <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/news/2019/november/pra-decision-notice-citigroup.pdf> that preparing and checking was a manual process hampered by high staff turnover and that, "a high degree of reliance was placed on a single member of the Budapest team."
Citi told Reuters last week that it "completed remedial actions and injected capital to immediately restore the subsidiary's buffers." It added: "The subsidiary remained fully compliant with regulatory minimums throughout, with no impact on the holding company or main operating bank."

item.title: The industry’s favourite private capital firms are (mostly) who you'd imagine
item.description:
From time to time, we ask our readership who they want to work for. We’ve asked almost a hundred thousand professionals this exact question since 2023, and they sometimes for a private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> or private credit </news/private-credit> firm. This year, the 19,000 voters in our Ideal Employer report cast their votes again.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
For the fourth year in a row, the Ideal Employer in Private Equity & Credit was Blackstone. Blackstone captured a huge percentage of interest in the private capital industry – around a quarter of votes cast, and as many votes as second-place Apollo and third-place Bain Capital combined.
Blackstone was a very aspirational employer. Just 15% of people who selected it as their Ideal Employer had experience at the firm – less than (almost) all category winners, including BlackRock, JPMorgan and Deloitte. Apollo, which came second in our ranking, had 24% of its votes from insiders, and Bain Capital 26%.
Blackstone performed excellently on qualitative rankings. It performed notably above average on all metrics, especially ones related to pay and prestige and belonging – people who chose Blackstone said that it was a place for “people like [them]” more than other firms.
Blackstone is “huge, powerful, efficient, and rich,” said one UK-based director working for a rival who worked in sales. “In France, this is the most prestigious fund to work for,” added a JPMorgan risk analyst, indeed working in France.
For the second year in a row, Apollo Global Management was the runner-up for voters. The firm did not perform as strongly on qualitative metrics as Blackstone did, but it did score above average for its innovation and leadership. “A company without micromanaging,” is how one UK-based associate described it.
Bain Capital came third. The firm scored above average for its flexible work offering, and was also perceived as a place of integrity. “Remote work is the main driver for me now,” said one operations professional in London who chose Bain as his ideal employer.

item.title: Citadel is hedge fund of the year, again. Is Ken Griffin himself the secret sauce?
item.description:
It's happened again. For at least the fourth time, Citadel has been declared hedge fund of the year by Risk Magazine. <https://www.risk.net/awards/7964526/hedge-fund-of-the-year-citadel>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Various reasons are given for the repeated triumph. Acquiring the public equities portfolio of hedge fund Situational Awareness, reducing the risk by 80% and completing nearly 100 block trades worth more than $4bn in a three week period, helped. So did Citadel's reputation in the market: “A broker knows that if they’re doing business with Citadel and Citadel says, ‘We’ve got $500 million of this to go’, when we sell $500 million, we are done. They’re not going to have to tell their client the next day: ‘That block you just traded, they’ve got more to sell," Citadel CEO and founder Ken Griffin </news/ken-griffin-citadel-culture>told Risk.
Performance helped too. In the year through to the end of October, Citadel returned 15.3% after fees </news/hedge-fund-performance-2026>, versus 5.7% at arch rival Millennium. Some of this seems to have been driven by the equities and quant businesses and the Situational Awareness halo, but Citadel is also a major risk taker across commodities and fixed income. It's thought to be outperforming rivals there, too.
Citadel is having a good year. So, particularly, is Perry Vais, the head of equity quantitative research, his co-CIO Pablo Salame, COO Gerald Beeson and head of Legal Shawn Fagan, all of whom Risk says worked on the Situational Awareness transaction with Griffin. But Griffin is having the best year of the lot.
Senior portfolio managers familiar with the firm say it's Griffin himself who sets Citadel's performance paradigm. Speaking to Morgan Stanley last month, Citadel's head of global equities, Justin Lubell said Griffin “does not care about the authorship of any great idea. He wants the best ideas. It doesn’t matter where they come from.” Griffin takes “no pride of ownership,” explained Lubell. If you've been driving 1,000 miles an hour in one direction and there's a better idea, he has no hesitation about driving 1,000 miles an hour in reverse.
Griffin can be a bit intense </news/ken-griffin-citadel-culture>. Sometimes he dresses as a velociraptor at Citadel's annual Halloween parties, but if you like him, it seems you like him a lot.
"Ken is the beginning of a new league for a professional," one former senior Citadel portfolio manager tells us, speaking off the record. Griffin is "genial", he explains. He's not rigid. He allows people to "express themselves in risk limits that reflect his judgement of the exact situation the market is living." Ken is in the "trading weeds," says another senior portfolio manager with knowledge of the firm. "With Ken, a portfolio manager can really mature as a professional," says the first.
Citadel declined to comment for this article. Griffin is far from micromanaging his investment empire. Investment decisions are made by Citadel's portfolio managers, its business heads, its head of risk and her team, </news/citadel-head-of-risk>and by co-chief investment officer Salame. Griffin is part of the mix, but insiders say he has a major influence on the flavour.
58-year-old Griffin played a central role when Citadel bought and traded out of the circa $16bn Situational Awareness portfolio in late July. He was awake 40 hours, says Risk. Citadel first heard that Situational Awareness was in trouble on the 28th. There was a call on the evening of the 29th. By 1am on Thursday the 30th, Citadel was ready to purchase the book. An agreement was signed at 8.50am.
Millennium and Jane Street were also interested, says Risk. This wasn't the first time Citadel stepped in to rescue a flailing fund. It purchased Amaranth's gas book in 2006 and Sowood Asset Management in 2007.
Multiple portfolio managers tell us it's much easier to take big directional risks at Citadel than other major funds. Griffin sets the tone. In March 2025, for example, he reportedly instructed his team to "play offense" during the equities sell-off early in the month.
This approach makes a difference in challenging markets. If PMs have a significant drawdown, they are not necessarily cut. If Citadel portfolio managers have a strong record and the firm has conviction in their strategy, it may keep them on. Sometimes they leave anyway </news/dave-brodsky-balyasny-citadel>, but over 50% of the firm's fundamental equities portfolio managers were internally promoted, suggesting more longevity than at some rivals.
Speaking to Risk, Beeson said Citadel is a "crisis capital provider." Griffin said the issue with Situational Awareness was how to "manage the exposure to the AI factor writ large.” This was achieved using liquid assets like index products and large mega cap stocks to "immunise macro risk" and then exiting "individual idiosyncratic risks" over time, he told Risk.
At the end of October, S&P Global upgraded Citadel's credit rating to BBB. In doing so, it cited the Situational Awareness transaction and Citadel's "ability to seize investment opportunities" and "take on additional risk at times but manage it effectively." The correlation between Citadel's strategies was low throughout the first nine months of 2026, said S&P. Over the past three years, the firm has maintained a 40%+ liquidity buffer. No other multistrategy hedge fund has an investment grade rating.
Significantly, Citadel also has red carpet treatment from the largest prime brokers. S&P said it has six-month margin agreements, meaning the method for computing margin calls cannot be changed for 180 days. When Citadel began offloading the Situational Awareness positions, Situational Awareness's own prime brokers trusted the house of Griffin enough not to take action against the client on the morning of July 30th, Risk says.
One senior portfolio manager tells us Citadel is akin to a Ferrari, and describes a rival fund as like a Ford by comparison. "Citadel is a way better firm, way more prestigious," he insists.
Griffin himself doesn't suffer fools gladly. A New Yorker <https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/06/22/ken-griffins-billions-and-billions>profile earlier this year said he's averse to people who like the sound of their own voice and to those who "gild the lily." He has unsettlingly blue eyes. He is attuned to the sublime. </news/ken-griffin-s-message-to-young-people-coming-age-in-a-complicated-world>
Griffin told the New Yorker his mother changed the mobile over his crib every week when he was a baby. Maybe this is why he can respond quickly to change and take big, well managed risks where others fear to tread.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Traders who got $2m in 2025 are doing even better in 2026. JPMorgan banker who earned $700k a month in London is back for a new job
item.description:
It is an ill wind that doesn’t blow somebody a bit of good, as the proverb goes. So far, 2026 has been pretty miserable <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/quant-funds-are-having-a-hard-time-keeping-up-with-this-market?srnd=homepage-uk> for the quant </news/quant-jobs-finance> funds, as it’s apparently difficult to find an algorithm which can guess whether Jensen Huang has been forgiven or not. But it’s been absolutely fantastic for Citadel Securities <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/citadel-securities-trading-revenue-already-tops-full-year-record>; they have already equalled the full year revenue from 2025 (which was itself a record year at the time), and they are tracking up 29% for 2026.
Get Morning Coffee </myefc/preferences/subscribe?newsletter=network_newsletter>☕ in your inbox. Sign up here. </myefc/preferences/subscribe?newsletter=network_newsletter>
The good news for Citadel Securities reads through to Hudson River Trading <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-25/hrt-trading-revenue-tops-21-billion-eclipsing-full-year-record>, whose revenues were up an even more impressive 74% in the first nine months of this year. It's also likely to be good news for Jane Street and other trading firms. </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms>
How can this be? It seems the reason that they’ve done so well is that it’s been a year of “the right kind of volatility”. Trading desks suffer greatly when there’s a lack of market moving news, because there’s no volume to trade and nothing to take advantage of. They also tend to have a tough time when there are big directional moves, because they end up taking the other side of the trades which make up the flow of money.
But in a market which goes broadly sideways, in a rough and choppy way, market makers tend to find themselves structurally buying the dips and selling the rallies. It doesn’t necessarily matter so much that overall market volumes haven’t been particularly high; just that the traders have been handsomely rewarded for providing liquidity to a group of investors who have constantly been changing their minds.
Which means that there might be a few awkward parties this holiday season. There is a lot of crossover between the kind of people who go to work at electronic trading companies like Citadel Securities, and the kind of people who get jobs at quant hedge funds. Both industries are big employers of mathematics, physics and computer science PhDs. Citadel Securities paid its staff incredibly well last year (an average of over $2m a head </news/citadel-securities-pay-2m>, meaning that front office engineers might be getting quite a bit more than that). Although there’s no direct link between revenue and compensation, the market for electronic trading engineers is competitive enough that you’d have to guess that the benchmark for 2026 will be around 20-30% higher.
This will be happening in a year in which the quant funds are more likely to be telling people that “your bonus this year is that you can keep your job”. Is this a trend that’s going to continue, or will things return to normality, with hedge funds paying better than intermediaries? Ironically, that’s the kind of forecasting problem that physics PhDs in finance love to have opinions on.
Elsewhere, Dan Pinto is back in London <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/former-jp-morgan-executive-appointed-bank-england-committee-2026-11-24/>. The former COO and President of JP Morgan left the bank last year, after spending a long time as Jamie Dimon’s right hand man. Now he’s been appointed to the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee (subject to approval by MPs), advising on market conditions, systemic risks and the best regulatory responses to changing conditions. He replaces Jonathan Hall a former Goldman banker and portfolio manager at Eisler Capital.
It’s not clear from the press release whether Pinto will be returning to live in London from New York. Admittedly that’s probably because it’s none of our business, but he did give an interview in 2019 </news/daniel-pinto-jpmorgan> saying that after living in London for 23 years, he regarded it as his family’s home. And he probably has fond memories of the way in which his compensation package interacted with the UK’s regulations on bonuses to mean that he was getting a really big cash component </news/finance/daniel-pinto-jpmorgan-pay> relative to performance-related stock units. Decisions on how bankers ought to be compensated will be among the things that he’s likely to be asked to have an opinion on, too.
Meanwhile …
One of the least pleasant things about trying to trade out of a large position is that in the process, everyone on the Street gets to have look at how you put it together in the first place. Hamza Lemssouguer’s Arini Capital is reducing its leverage, and consequently it is having to give up information on the big trade that it’s trying to reduce. This appears to be a correlation trade of sorts – a “principal only credit index tranche” which pays off if defaults on European high yield don’t go too high, loses money if everything goes bad together, but hangs around for quite a few years before it can be definitively called good or bad. It’s the kind of investment that you only make if you’re very confident in your ability to see it out to maturity. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/lemssouguer-s-big-unwind-offers-glimpse-into-complex-credit-bets?srnd=homepage-uk>)
Sean Egan-Jones says that his eponymous rating agency (which has big market share in private credit, but which is viewed with suspicion by investors like Blue Owl and Apollo) is “the Tesla of credit ratings”, referring to the investments they’ve made in technology. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/26739054-0455-449b-9566-97fb4986088d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The choice for mathematicians always used to be whether to cash in with a finance job, or to stay in academia and hope to solve problems like the Riemann Conjecture. Between the Anthropic IPO and his recently published AI-assisted proof, Levent Alpöge must be having a pretty good year all round. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/riemann-hypothesis-anthropic-math-levent-alpoge-75351bcb?st=9JjycY&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink>)
XTX Markets has opened a data centre in Finland, but Alex Gerko is already warning that further development is going to be held back by the increasing difficulty of getting planning permission to build any more. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/gerko-s-xtx-opens-finnish-data-center-warns-on-permit-delays>)
“I saw a photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs and I thought ‘oh well, that could prove interesting’”. John Malkovich reminisces about the time when he lost “pretty much everything I’d ever made” from the first few decades of his Hollywood career in the biggest fraud of the 00s. (NY Post <https://nypost.com/2026/11/24/business/john-malkovich-recalls-losing-fortune-in-bernie-madoffs-ponzi-scheme/>)
Brands like Nike and Pixar employ professional archivists and historians to turn their company’s past into interesting and valuable stories. Some banks also do this, while others might reasonably prefer to forget. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-24/from-nike-to-pixar-how-companies-mine-their-history-for-profit?srnd=homepage-uk>)

item.title: "I am an MD in an investment bank. I am exhausted from weekend children's parties"
item.description:
I am a managing director at a US investment bank. I work 90-hour weeks. And then I spend my weekends watching my four-year-old hug a life-size Pikachu and Bluey.
The prep-school birthday party circuit, is the hardest deal I work all year.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The invitations arrive on 400gsm card with gold foil edging and a wax seal. The most recent was for a five year old's birthday. I’ve signed off on nine-figure financings with less ceremony.
People think the hard part of this job is the hours. It isn’t. It's the pressure to participate in a social milieu full of wealthy people who don't seem to work nearly as much.
Personally, I’ve made my peace with the 1am risk off calls, the Sunday-night “quick call” that’s never quick, and the 6:10 to Frankfurt so often that the BA crew know how I take my coffee. I grew up in South London, went to the local comp, and got into banking through the kind of hunger you only get from watching how the 99% live daily. My wife works similar hours at a private equity firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>
Last Saturday’s party opened with Pikachu. Not a teenager in a yellow onesie, but a proper licensed character appearance, with a Charmander thrown in for good measure. Someone had clearly booked the two of them months ago through a man who knows a man. Sixteen five and four year olds cried with joy. One dad beside me filmed the whole thing like he was at Glastonbury. The magician, apparently a semi-finalist on a TV talent show, made a child’s shoe disappear and then, in fairness, made it reappear. There was a chocolate fountain taller than my daughter, a bubble artist, a face painter with a waiting list, and a cake shaped like the birthday girl’s pony. The pony was there too.
For the adults there was a sushi chef and a Ruinart bar. I had a water because I had a 10am. In Amsterdam. And because I’d been up since 5am that morning to clear my inbox and do some life admin.
This is the bit nobody tells you about the private school circuit. You don’t just pay the fees, you pay with your weekends. There’s a party almost every Saturday and Sunday, and each one quietly ratchets up the baseline. Two years ago a bouncy castle was a triumph. Now a bouncy castle is what you hire for the siblings’ area.
My daughter is four. She doesn’t know what money is but she expects a Frozen theme and a real life Elsa.
I didn’t have the heart to tell her that like Pikachu, Elsa for my purpose is a scarce asset with a premium booking fee and no availability until spring. The kind of thing my parents would have said to me, not that I had the heart to demand a birthday cake let alone a themed party and a human size cartoon character.
The other parents are benign, mostly. That’s what makes it worse. Nobody is showing off, exactly. This is just normal for them. One dad with the serenity of someone whose trust fund vested before he could walk, told me he “barely works now, just a few calls.” He was wearing loafers that cost more than my first car and he looked rested. I’d forgotten adults could look like that. He was there with the nanny.
There is a strange arithmetic at work. I work these hours so that she can be in that room. And being in that room means I’m standing at the back of it, counting down to Monday.
On the drive home she fell asleep holding her party bag. It had a Jellycat, a personalised water bottle and a rainbow bomber jacket. I arrived home to an empty stomach, had a whole night of work, admin, and packing ahead of me still.
Ivan Taylor is a pseudonym. The author works in leveraged finance at a US bank in London. His and Dave the entertainers name has been changed. Pikachu’s has not.

item.title: Hedge fund has two smiling new equities PMs weeks after making big cuts to its team
item.description:
Why would you want to work for hedge fund Walleye Capital? How about its data and technology platform, or its AI tools? How about its entrepreneurial culture and its CEO Will England? Or how about the fact that it has seats to fill after cutting much of its equity/long short team </news/as-hedge-fund-walleye-capital-ejects-p-ms-a-reminder-of-the-toxic-interview>earlier in November?
Writing on LinkedIn, Walleye says it's hired Matt Aleksinas from SIR Capital and Mike Scheer from Jain Global to join its equity long/short team.
The two arrivals come after Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/walleye-capital-stock-picking-head-anil-gondi-exit-2026-11>reported earlier this month the firm had cut Anil Gondi, the head of its equity long short business, along with a substantial portion of its long short team.
In a letter to investors concerning the cuts, England reportedly said: "Over the past few years, we invested considerable effort in improving the internal business, including bringing in new leadership. Those efforts did not produce the results we expected, and the opportunity cost and resources consumed have been too high relative to the return."
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/fb02c333-a439-4acd-b0b6-e50633ce863e?syn-25a6b1a6=1>reported that after slimming down its long/short equities business, Walleye returned an unspecified amount of capital to investors. Citing England's letter, the FT suggested the fund would focus on volatility, quantitative and external strategies.
That was two and a half weeks ago. Times change. Long/short businesses have been burned again </news/equities-hedge-funds-huang> this week, but Walleye is back in the flames. In Walleye's announcement of its new arrivals, Aleksinas said he was drawn by the firm's technology and data platforms and its use of AI. Scheer said he liked its "entrepreneurial culture and how Will's leadership empowers people to build."
In September 2023, England gave a frank interview to Colossus <https://colossus.com/episode/england-a-primer-on-multi-strategy-hedge-funds/> in which he said that portfolio management jobs can be "psychologically extremely toxic." </news/2023/09/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund>This was because of the market, said England.

item.title: One of Citi's highest paid traders left in London. Jane Street was being mentioned
item.description:
Where is Geoff Weber and why would he leave Citi?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Weber was Citi's head of G-10 rates trading. International Financing Review <https://www.ifre.com/people-and-markets/2517900/moves-senior-rates-trader-weber-leaves-citi>reported his disappearance earlier today, claiming that he was one of Citi's highest paid traders.
Citi declined to comment for this article. Weber is still registered with the bank on Bloomberg; his departure is fresh.
It's not clear where he's going next or why he would leave this close to bonuses. There are suggestions that someone has poached him and maybe his Citi bonus wasn't worth waiting around for anyway. - IFR notes that Citi said it generated lower rates trading revenues in each quarter of the year so far.
It's conceivable that Weber has gone to the sort of electronic market making firm </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms> that has deep pockets. Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> was being suggested as a possible destination by some headhunters. However, we understand this is not correct.
Weber is the second big exit from Citi's European rates team recently. Zoeb Sachee, a Paris-based trader, left at the start of this month.

item.title: Goldman Sachs' note suggests the Huang bounce may leave equities hedge fund managers unemployed too
item.description:
When Justin Lubell, the global head of equities at Citadel spoke to <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fbYXfVtUePU> John Storey, a managing director (MD) in global equities at Morgan Stanley last month, he explained what makes a good equities portfolio manager (PM).
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The best equities PMs have intellectual conviction, said Lubell. Citadel's analysts have "become really true deep experts," in their part of the world. They can spot change early on because, "They have followed the industry for a long time. They’ve built relationships with the management teams. They know the companies, they know the pipelines. They know who’s great at R&D.”
Yesterday's market opening 30% surge in NVIDIA following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO </news/john-underwood-jensen-huang> at the apparent behest of Donald Trump <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/nvidia-s-board-was-no-match-for-trump-or-jensen-huang-s-backers> (who's even alleged to have dialled into <https://www.semafor.com/article/11/23/2026/huang-reinstatement-came-at-trumps-behest> an NVIDIA board meeting) suggests such incremental skills have become less important than before. What mattered yesterday was attention to the nuances of presidential proclamations and the $100k a month Truth Social feed. <https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/paid-early-access-to-trumps-posts-raises-insider-trading-questions>
It's too early to say how Citadel's equities business performed during the Huang bounce. Maybe it did fine. Citadel has three US equities businesses, of which Lubell runs only one and his comments applied to the job of an equities portfolio manager over the long term. But a weekend note from Goldman Sachs' prime broking desk suggests that in the short term at least, there is broad pain across equities investment strategies.
After the third consecutive week of global equities selling <https://x.com/GlobalMktObserv/status/2124879526081499590?a=ULmfNMAgaywesHUHGoQ&s=20>, Goldman reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-22/goldman-traders-see-entry-point-in-us-stocks-but-warn-of-risks>said hedge funds had been shorting US single name stocks at levels last seen in June 2022. In a "quite extended" unwind, funds had reduced exposure to global equities, said Goldman. Short sales outpaced long purchases by 1.5 to 1.
In this context, yesterday's 30% pop in NVIDIA and the sudden surge in NASDAQ-100 futures is being widely interpreted as a short squeeze rather than an enduring rally and the extent and speed of the repricing is thought to have caused pain for many funds.
"Volatility in names has been extremely high," says Michael Alfaro, CIO at Gallo Partners in New York. "This has been incredibly hard for a lot of other funds because you can very easily trip risk parameters that force you to cut positions when the very next day there's a complete rebound."
It makes the job of an equities portfolio manager harder than ever, says Alfaro. Being an equities PM is particularly hard when there are rigid risk constraints, he adds. However, while other PMs have been cutting risk, Alfaro says Gallo has been able to make the most of long term opportunities.
This may be the case elsewhere, too. Anecdotally, though, the extent of yesterday's bounce has sparked another round of pod closures across the industry as portfolio managers have been stopped out. It's been an unpredictable year, even for PMs who know everything about their sectors. This is why people like Stan Druckenmiller <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6r3D-CMJkuI>are sitting out the market.

item.title: "Lovely guys" from Barclays keep congregating in the Santander financial sponsors team
item.description:
If you're a lovely person, and a financial sponsors banker </news/financial-sponsors-bankers-2026>, you've worked at Barclays and you're looking for the next step on your journey to career nirvana, then how about Santander in London?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Santander likes people of this type. Having hired known nice man Ken McGrath </news/santander-s-latest-big-london-hire-is-a-lovely-guy-who-s-been-around> from Barclays last February, Santander has now hired good guy Carlo de Carlo from Barclays too. Together, McGrath and de Carlo will run Santander's financial sponsors business in EMEA.
Both are "lovely guys" say headhunters. McGrath appears to have hired de Carlo, they observe. De Carlo left Barclays at the end of July according to his FCA Registration. He has presumably been on gardening leave.
De Carlo's departure comes after Barclays appointed Erkin Yildiz <https://home.barclays/news/press-releases/20260/04/-barclays-appoints-erkin-yildiz-co-head-of-emea-financial-sponso/> from Jefferies as co-head of its EMEA financial sponsors group in April. Yildiz is working alongside Tom Vignon, whom Barclays promoted as co-head of EMEA financial sponsors in July 2024, shortly after de Carlo landed from Bank of America.
De Carlo didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. He spent most of his career at Bank of America, where he worked for nearly 14 years before joining Barclays in June 2024. Barclays hired De Carlo after parting company with Olga Tavolzhanskaya </news/barclays-hired-a-new-financial-sponsors-md-after-cutting-a-female-incumbent-last-month>, who then reappeared running financial sponsors banking at Natixis.
