item.title: How to get a job at Goldman Sachs - the inside track
item.description:
Everyone wants to work at Goldman Sachs. Well, not quite everyone – it hasn’t been our Ideal Employer </ideal-employer> in financial services since we started running our survey and awarding the accolade again from 2023 – but it is a very in-demand place to work. Goldman Sachs got around 360,000 applications </news/goldman-sachs-internship-acceptance-rate> to its internships last year, of which 2,600 became interns, an acceptance rate of around 0.7%.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
How do you beat the crowd? When you apply to Goldman Sachs, 140 other people also want a place at the firm? It’s not easy. For what it’s worth, applications aren't evenly distributed: there is far more competition for front-office roles such as M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> or capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> than, say, risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank> or compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance>.
Then again, maybe if you are here at all, you don’t have what it takes. “If you are wondering if your skills/knowledge are good enough,” one former London-based Goldman Sachs intern tells us about the firm, then “you are not the right person to join.” It’s hard to argue with his logic – but what does good enough really mean?
It’s something that has changed in recent years. “Whilst GS historically would favour applicants from leading UK universities such as Oxbridge, LSE, Imperial and Warwick,” says Victoria McLean, CEO of London-based CV writing firm City CV and former Goldman Sachs recruiter, “their reach now is broader with greater diversity in the schools they select from, meaning this is less of a single successful candidate profile.” Last year's new investment banking analyst class at Goldman included graduates of Nottingham, Queen Mary, and even Loughborough in the UK.
One thing hasn’t changed, however. “They [Goldman] have always looked for candidates who perform well in a demanding environment, who show resilience and initiative with a genuine intellectual curiosity,” McLean says.
Even if you're resilient and genuinely piqued intellectually, you'll need to be swift. “The thing I wish I’d known earlier is to apply early and start with spring weeks. They’re a real pipeline into internships, and that route got me my first offers,” says one former Goldman Sachs intern who received (and rejected) a return offer from the firm.
McLean agrees, suggesting that the best route in is to “apply early and understand that most seats for graduate roles are filled by interns.” But, whether you’re a student or not, what do you need to maximise your application to the firm?
The ideal Goldman CV/resume and cover letter
Any good job application starts with a strong CV/Resume (localization pending) and cover letter. Writing the ideal resume is both a work of art and a science </news/the-absolutely-perfect-investment-banking-cv>, and there’s no need to repeat anything that you probably know already.
In a nutshell: your resume should be very much tailored to your application, it should be tightly written (and, by extension, deeply relevant), and ideally, it should contain bullet points, which apparently Goldman loves. Those bullet points should show what you achieved, with numbers where you can. "In such a competitive candidate pool it is critical to show impact and quantifiable achievements in your CV," says McLean.
“Always demonstrate a genuine interest in the specific business area you are applying to and where possible, include something that sets you apart or makes you interesting,” says McLean. “This could be setting up a business, committing to volunteering, successfully trading your own portfolio or competitive team sport.”
Cover letters </news/finance/cover-letter-template-will-get-job-banking> can be a more delicate art. A lot of tech companies are discarding them, but they’re still popular in banking – and what’s more, Goldman loves them. It loves cover letters so much that they even have its own, special format </news/cover-letter-template-will-get-job-banking#:~:text=The%20Goldman%20Sachs%20cover%20letter> for them. The Goldman Sachs cover letter needs to be around 300 words long, to explain your interest in the role and firm, and your suitability. Take a few points from your CV to substantiate why exactly. This is also the best place to name-drop if you've done some networking.
Standing out with your CV/resume is as important as during your interview. Ex-Goldman banker Will McTighe said a few years ago </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-goldman-sachs> that applications to the firm are often “very generic”, on account of the impeccable academics and the similar finance-society template of every candidate. “Most people have quirks,” he said. You need to show yours.
“Demonstrate how interesting you are,” said McTighe. That means doing “something a bit crazy that people think is a bit nuts.” His own quirks include ultra-marathoning from Oxford to London, despite having never run a marathon before, as well as learning Mandarin, ski instruction, and various sports.
Being interesting might even overshadow your academic background – a former Goldman recruiter we spoke to a few years ago noted that an English Literature student wrote such a brilliant and “off the wall” cover letter that they brought him in for an interview. Why? Because he showed that he was imaginative, innovative, and interesting.
McTighe does specify, however, that not all quirks have to be physical, so feel free to consider horticulture or hydroponics or haute cuisine. What is sure, however, is that you shouldn’t hide what differentiates you. It should be as much on your resume, as a point of pride, as your academic record is.
The ideal Goldman HireVue interview
If you have an appetizing application, the next step is inevitably a HireVue interview. It’s straightforward, and we spoke to HireVue ourselves to write a guide </news/2022/10/hirevue-interview-banking> for you. Goldman’s isn’t especially different – but we do have a list of particular questions that the bank (and a few others) asks here </news/hirevue-questions-banking>.
Obviously, you should try to answer the question as best you can – as in, to answer as if you were sitting in front of the question-asker while answering it. Be professional (act like a banker, not a student </news/banking-hirevue-interviews>) and prepare well – you’ll only have around 30 seconds </news/how-long-to-answer-hirevue-interview> to “prepare” your answer to a question and 120 seconds to deliver it. If you have answers prepared (and if you’re serious about getting an investment banking job, you will have), then you’ll use those 30 seconds to glance at your notes.
Your answers will then be “scanned” by HireVue’s AI to see how good a fit you’ll be for the employer you’re interviewing with. The once-viral former nightmares of eyelash density counters and lactose intolerance probability nexuses are things of the past; your answer will be judged by a human recruiter, Goldman says <https://www.goldmansachs.com/careers/blog/goldman-sachs-video-interviewing-facts.html>, and you’ll soon-ish receive a response from the bank as to whether you were successful.
“You may only have 1-2 days to complete the HireVue so being organised pays off and reduces last minute stress,” says McLean. Hopefully, if your HireVue goes well, you’ll be invited to a proper interview in the firm’s office – also known as a Superday </news/if-a-bank-doesn-t-hire-you-after-5-interviews-you-re-in-trouble>.
The ideal Goldman Sachs Superday interview
If you’ve gotten past the HireVues and received an offer for an interview, congratulations. Mostly people get filtered out before this stage, so the cards are already in your favor. The Superday interviews might be the most critical part of the application process.
“When I was at Goldman,” McLean says, “we regularly put candidates through a grueling set of 30-minute interviews back-to-back. This is still the case for many divisions.” The best thing to do is to be prepared, as with many things in life. “Have a bank of stories ready that can be used to answer competency based questions, but also be ready to talk about what your chosen division does, not just why you want to work there,” McLean says. “Be prepared!”
You will have several interviews, and all of them will matter for your chances. “Treat every interview as equally important,” McLean suggests. “Interviewers compare notes at the end of the day, so one poor meeting can have a significant impact on the outcome. And be ready to explain ‘Why Goldman’ in a way that is unique to you.”
One tip suggested by an intern is to be open with your thought processes – it matters more than you think. “Talk through your thinking out loud,” one intern tells us. “They care about how you get there as much as the answer. Being able to avoid speaking robotically is also massive.”
Being interesting is therefore important. “Giving plain responses during interviews can always put the interviewers off, and they want to hire people who are always genuine and honest,” one says. “With other banks, it’s more like the offer is yours to lose once you’re in the interview and it’s more important to not mess up. For GS, it’s yours to earn rather than to lose,” says another.
“Competence and academia are one thing,” yet another former intern at the bank tells us, “but GS hires largely based on personality and people who are not afraid to speak up, challenge when they have suggestions and back yourself when challenged back.”
Speaking two years ago on an episode of The David Rubenstein show <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JfnPxl1ic0>, Goldman’s CEO, David Solomon, put one virtue above all others for applicants: tenacity. “One of the things we look for is people that are smart,” he says, “but [also] people that want to work hard, people that believe in excellence.” That means “people that have proven that they’ve got grit and dedication and an ability to succeed.” And that includes “being able to dust themselves off and keep going.”

item.title: How to get a job at Goldman Sachs - the inside track
item.description:
Everyone wants to work at Goldman Sachs. Well, not quite everyone – it hasn’t been our Ideal Employer </ideal-employer> in financial services since we started running our survey and awarding the accolade again from 2023 – but it is a very in-demand place to work. Goldman Sachs got around 360,000 applications </news/goldman-sachs-internship-acceptance-rate> to its internships last year, of which 2,600 became interns, an acceptance rate of around 0.7%.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
How do you beat the crowd? When you apply to Goldman Sachs, 140 other people also want a place at the firm? It’s not easy. For what it’s worth, applications aren't evenly distributed: there is far more competition for front-office roles such as M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> or capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> than, say, risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank> or compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance>.
Then again, maybe if you are here at all, you don’t have what it takes. “If you are wondering if your skills/knowledge are good enough,” one former London-based Goldman Sachs intern tells us about the firm, then “you are not the right person to join.” It’s hard to argue with his logic – but what does good enough really mean?
It’s something that has changed in recent years. “Whilst GS historically would favour applicants from leading UK universities such as Oxbridge, LSE, Imperial and Warwick,” says Victoria McLean, CEO of London-based CV writing firm City CV and former Goldman Sachs recruiter, “their reach now is broader with greater diversity in the schools they select from, meaning this is less of a single successful candidate profile.” Last year's new investment banking analyst class at Goldman included graduates of Nottingham, Queen Mary, and even Loughborough in the UK.
One thing hasn’t changed, however. “They [Goldman] have always looked for candidates who perform well in a demanding environment, who show resilience and initiative with a genuine intellectual curiosity,” McLean says.
Even if you're resilient and genuinely piqued intellectually, you'll need to be swift. “The thing I wish I’d known earlier is to apply early and start with spring weeks. They’re a real pipeline into internships, and that route got me my first offers,” says one former Goldman Sachs intern who received (and rejected) a return offer from the firm.
McLean agrees, suggesting that the best route in is to “apply early and understand that most seats for graduate roles are filled by interns.” But, whether you’re a student or not, what do you need to maximise your application to the firm?
The ideal Goldman CV/resume and cover letter
Any good job application starts with a strong CV/Resume (localization pending) and cover letter. Writing the ideal resume is both a work of art and a science </news/the-absolutely-perfect-investment-banking-cv>, and there’s no need to repeat anything that you probably know already.
In a nutshell: your resume should be very much tailored to your application, it should be tightly written (and, by extension, deeply relevant), and ideally, it should contain bullet points, which apparently Goldman loves. Those bullet points should show what you achieved, with numbers where you can. "In such a competitive candidate pool it is critical to show impact and quantifiable achievements in your CV," says McLean.
“Always demonstrate a genuine interest in the specific business area you are applying to and where possible, include something that sets you apart or makes you interesting,” says McLean. “This could be setting up a business, committing to volunteering, successfully trading your own portfolio or competitive team sport.”
Cover letters </news/finance/cover-letter-template-will-get-job-banking> can be a more delicate art. A lot of tech companies are discarding them, but they’re still popular in banking – and what’s more, Goldman loves them. It loves cover letters so much that they even have its own, special format </news/cover-letter-template-will-get-job-banking#:~:text=The%20Goldman%20Sachs%20cover%20letter> for them. The Goldman Sachs cover letter needs to be around 300 words long, to explain your interest in the role and firm, and your suitability. Take a few points from your CV to substantiate why exactly. This is also the best place to name-drop if you've done some networking.
Standing out with your CV/resume is as important as during your interview. Ex-Goldman banker Will McTighe said a few years ago </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-goldman-sachs> that applications to the firm are often “very generic”, on account of the impeccable academics and the similar finance-society template of every candidate. “Most people have quirks,” he said. You need to show yours.
“Demonstrate how interesting you are,” said McTighe. That means doing “something a bit crazy that people think is a bit nuts.” His own quirks include ultra-marathoning from Oxford to London, despite having never run a marathon before, as well as learning Mandarin, ski instruction, and various sports.
Being interesting might even overshadow your academic background – a former Goldman recruiter we spoke to a few years ago noted that an English Literature student wrote such a brilliant and “off the wall” cover letter that they brought him in for an interview. Why? Because he showed that he was imaginative, innovative, and interesting.
McTighe does specify, however, that not all quirks have to be physical, so feel free to consider horticulture or hydroponics or haute cuisine. What is sure, however, is that you shouldn’t hide what differentiates you. It should be as much on your resume, as a point of pride, as your academic record is.

If you have an appetizing application, the next step is inevitably a HireVue interview. It’s straightforward, and we spoke to HireVue ourselves to write a guide </news/2022/10/hirevue-interview-banking> for you. Goldman’s isn’t especially different – but we do have a list of particular questions that the bank (and a few others) asks here </news/hirevue-questions-banking>.
Obviously, you should try to answer the question as best you can – as in, to answer as if you were sitting in front of the question-asker while answering it. Be professional (act like a banker, not a student </news/banking-hirevue-interviews>) and prepare well – you’ll only have around 30 seconds </news/how-long-to-answer-hirevue-interview> to “prepare” your answer to a question and 120 seconds to deliver it. Your answers will then be “scanned” by HireVue’s AI to see how good a fit you’ll be for the employer you’re interviewing with. The once-viral former nightmares of eyelash density counters and lactose intolerance probability nexuses are things of the past; your answer will be judged by a human recruiter, Goldman says <https://www.goldmansachs.com/careers/blog/goldman-sachs-video-interviewing-facts.html>, and you’ll soon-ish receive a response from the bank as to whether you were successful.

item.title: High-frequency traders who quit for Anthropic might be sitting on $60m+ in stock ahead of its IPO
item.description:
It's the week of Anthropic </news/anthropic-pay-vs-banking>'s IPO, which means that the AI lab </news/openai-culture>'s 5,000+ employees are about to see just how much their stock compensation is actually worth. It looks likely that Anthropic will go public with a valuation of $1.5tn <https://www.ft.com/content/314e17df-e7af-4814-b208-70a0557cb452?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, which will make multimillionaires even of employees who joined just last year... on paper, at least.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
How much did HFT </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> traders make at Anthropic?
AI labs made a significant push to hire talent from the quantitative finance </news/quant-jobs-finance> space in 2025. Sam Altman </news/sam-altman-goldman-sachs-intern-openai> publicly encouraged traders with "existential dread" <https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/1948320775586377988> to join OpenAI by attending a party organized by the firm. Anthropic hosted similar events; at one, it pitched an Anthropic career to 150 quant researchers at a rooftop bar in Manhattan. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-08-08/open-ai-perplexity-make-pitch-to-recruit-quant-traders-from-banks>Given that this push only happened last year, have they missed the boat on a major payout?
Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-talent-openai-wall-street-quant-trading-firms-2025-7> reported last July that compensation offers from AI labs for HFT quants </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> ranged from $1.5m to $3m, including stock. Around the time of this push, Anthropic was valued at $61.5bn. If we assume these quants joined the lab on packages of this size (and that they earned average cash compensation) it would give those hires an adjusted compensation of ~$29m to ~$65m. Considering even partners at Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>'s UK entity earned an estimated $55m per head last year </news/jane-street-pay>, that's not a bad haul.
Anthropic increased its valuation to $183bn just a few months after these reports, however. If stock pay was offered closer to that valuation, the quants will have received roughly $10m to $22m instead.
What is average stock pay at Anthropic?
We've analysed compensation data for 45 Anthropic engineers filed on Levels.fyi <https://levels.fyi/> between 2023 and 2026, looking at both cash and stock compensation, adjusting the stock pay to estimate its current value based on the publicly reported valuation of Anthropic at the date each datapoint was filed. On average, the employees were paid $8.2m in adjusted stock per year, but the earlier employees, naturally, were sitting on much more. The four Anthropic engineers who reported compensation in 2023 received over $27m in adjusted stock per head. The median adjusted stock payout for a single year was $4.8m.
If an Anthropic engineer worked at the firm from 2023 to today, receiving the average amount of stock in each year, they would be sitting on just over $60m.
The biggest single-year stock payout went to a San Francisco-based machine learning engineer who worked at Anthropic in 2023. They were paid $158.8k in stock that year, which would be worth $54.9m today. That engineer reported zero years of experience, suggesting they were a graduate hire. If they continued working at Anthropic beyond 2023, their overall adjusted compensation package may well have exceeded $100m.
There are some big caveats to this data. For one, the valuations Anthropic has reported were often relative to its fundraising efforts; it may have offered stock pay at a different valuation to employees, especially if they were hired a few months removed from that fundraising event.
The structure of stock compensation also varies. Anthropic's SEC filing says that ~61% of outstanding employee stock is options, which employees will have to pay cash to exercise; the remaining stock is in the form of RSUs (restricted stock units). Each type of stock takes four years to vest. A 2023 hire may have vested all of the stock earned that year, but might be waiting longer for their stock pay in subsequent years to vest too.
There's also a lockup period for staff, a common IPO practice where pre-IPO shareholders have to wait a certain period of time to sell their stock. This is usually six months, at which point Anthropic's valuation could be completely different. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-unusual-setup-for-employees-sell-stock-post-ipo-2026-11> reported this week that Anthropic employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of their stock at launch, then a further 35% after its first quarterly report. After that, employees who want to sell stock need to create a '10b5-1 plan' where they specify a stock sale at a specific price and volume at least 30 days in advance of it happening.

item.title: High-frequency traders who quit for Anthropic might be sitting on $60m+ in stock ahead of its IPO
item.description:
It's the week of Anthropic </news/anthropic-pay-vs-banking>'s IPO, which means that the AI lab </news/openai-culture>'s 5,000+ employees are about to see just how much their stock compensation is actually worth. It looks likely that Anthropic will go public with a valuation of $1.5tn <https://www.ft.com/content/314e17df-e7af-4814-b208-70a0557cb452?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, which will make multimillionaires even of employees who joined just last year... on paper, at least.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
How much did HFT </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> traders make at Anthropic?
AI labs made a significant push to hire talent from the quantitative finance </news/quant-jobs-finance> space in 2025. Sam Altman </news/sam-altman-goldman-sachs-intern-openai> publicly encouraged traders with "existential dread" <https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/1948320775586377988> to join OpenAI by attending a party organized by the firm. Anthropic hosted similar events; at one, it pitched an Anthropic career to 150 quant researchers at a rooftop bar in Manhattan. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-08-08/open-ai-perplexity-make-pitch-to-recruit-quant-traders-from-banks>Given that this push only happened last year, have they missed the boat on a major payout?
Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-talent-openai-wall-street-quant-trading-firms-2025-7> reported last July that compensation offers from AI labs for HFT quants </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> ranged from $1.5m to $3m, including stock. Around the time of this push, Anthropic was valued at $61.5bn. If we assume these quants joined the lab on packages of this size (and that they earned average cash compensation) it would give those hires an adjusted compensation of ~$29m to ~$65m. Considering even partners at Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>'s UK entity earned an estimated $55m per head last year </news/jane-street-pay>, that's not a bad haul.
Anthropic increased its valuation to $183bn just a few months after these reports, however. If stock pay was offered closer to that valuation, the quants will have received roughly $10m to $22m instead.
What is average stock pay at Anthropic?
We've analysed compensation data for 45 Anthropic engineers filed on Levels.fyi <https://levels.fyi/> between 2023 and 2026, looking at both cash and stock compensation, adjusting the stock pay to estimate its current value based on the publicly reported valuation of Anthropic at the date each datapoint was filed. On average, the employees were paid $8.2m in adjusted stock per year, but the earlier employees, naturally, were sitting on much more. The four Anthropic engineers who reported compensation in 2023 received over $27m in adjusted stock per head. The median adjusted stock payout for a single year was $4.8m.
If an Anthropic engineer worked at the firm from 2023 to today, receiving the average amount of stock in each year, they would be sitting on just over $60m.
The biggest single-year stock payout went to a San Francisco-based machine learning engineer who worked at Anthropic in 2023. They were paid $158.8k in stock that year, which would be worth $54.9m today. That engineer reported zero years of experience, suggesting they were a graduate hire. If they continued working at Anthropic beyond 2023, their overall adjusted compensation package may well have exceeded $100m.
There are some big caveats to this data. For one, the valuations Anthropic has reported were often relative to its fundraising efforts; it may have offered stock pay at a different valuation to employees, especially if they were hired a few months removed from that fundraising event.
The structure of stock compensation also varies. Anthropic's SEC filing says that ~61% of outstanding employee stock is options, which employees will have to pay cash to exercise; the remaining stock is in the form of RSUs (restricted stock units). Each type of stock takes four years to vest. A 2023 hire may have vested all of the stock earned that year, but might be waiting longer for their stock pay in subsequent years to vest too.
There's also a lockup period for staff, a common IPO practice where pre-IPO shareholders have to wait a certain period of time to sell their stock. This is usually six months, at which point Anthropic's valuation could be completely different. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-unusual-setup-for-employees-sell-stock-post-ipo-2026-11> reported this week that Anthropic employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of their stock at launch, then a further 35% after its first quarterly report. After that, employees who want to sell stock need to create a '10b5-1 plan' where they specify a stock sale at a specific price and volume at least 30 days in advance of it happening.

item.title: Barclays appears to have put a brilliant female hedge fund saleswoman at risk
item.description:
As we have said, </news/barclays-has-a-strong-incentive-to-cut-its-5-000-jobs-before-next-year> Barclays is cutting 200 jobs in its investment bank </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> this week. Among those at risk in London is thought to be a hedge fund saleswoman and a maths prodigy.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Barclays isn't commenting, but multiple sources say that the bank has put Charmaine Reason at risk in its London hedge fund sales team. Reason herself didn't respond to a request to comment.
Reason's alleged removal seems to have surprised colleagues who say she was talented and ambitious. She has a first class degree from Cambridge University.
Reason is a homegrown Barclays talent. She joined the bank as an operations analyst 16 years ago and became an assistant to the sales team before moving into sales herself. She was promoted to managing director (MD) in 2023.
Barclays' London macro sales team is home to various talents. They include Puni Rajah, </news/punitha-raja-barclays>the much-feted macro sales director who has "exploded" and whose year has become large. Rajah is widely expected to make MD in the next round of promotions. Reason's boss in hedge fund sales is thought to have been Rumit Sawjani, who's been at Barclays for nearly 20 years.
News or Reason's exit follows that of Adam Glossop </news/a-legendary-trader-left-barclays-and-people-are-sad>, a talented trader on the treasury team whose departure has caused some lamentation.

item.title: You will find Rokos Capital Management's former CTO at Symmetry Investments with his predecessor
item.description:
Yesterday, we said that Amit Sudharshan </news/now-the-cto-appears-to-have-left-hedge-fund-rokos-capital-management>no longer appeared to be the chief technology officer (CTO) at Rokos Capital Management in London. We suggested that he'd maybe gone to Greece. He hasn't. He's gone to Symmetry Investments. He has a friend there.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Sudharshan is now the London-based CTO at Symmetry instead according to his LinkedIn profile. In his absence, Rokos has an acting CTO in the form of Steve Horne, who's been there for 13 years and was previously the deputy CTO.
Rokos might want to make Horne its official new CTO soon, or maybe he will leave for Symmetry too. Sudharshan is not the only ex-Rokos CTO at the rival fund. Dan Azzopardi who was Sudharshan's predecessor is at Symmetry too, having joined in 2024 after a stint at Balyasny.
What does Symmetry have that Rokos doesn't? We don't know but would appreciate comments on the subject. Symmetry didn't respond to a request for elaboration.

item.title: This is what you need on your CV for a Jane Street internship
item.description:
Secretive electronic trading </news/a-new-bulge-bracket-of-electronic-trading-firms-is-coming-for-banking-jobs> firm Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> paid </news/jane-street-s-1-4bn-pay-is-less-communist-than-2005-goldman-sachs>$2.7m per head to its full-time employees last year. Its internships </news/electronic-trading-summer-internship-pay-2025>are similarly lucrative; intern classes of previous years have earned $64k over an 11-week period </news/2023/08/jane-street-intern-pay>, and salaries have only risen since then </news/jane-street-intern-pay>. Job listings for Jane Street's internships don't ask for specific experiences, financial services knowledge or specific university subjects. Instead, Jane Street says it is "more interested in how you think and learn than what you currently know." But how true is that, really?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We've analysed professional profiles of 159 separate students, primarily in the US, who either interned </news/internship-investment-bank> at Jane Street this year or have announced that they are interning next year. We've looked at what they're studying, where they're studying it, and what job experience they have prior to joining the firm. It has a few preferences, but Jane Street - which didn't comment for this article - seems to stay true to its principles.
What are Jane Street's target universities?
Jane Street is thought to do extensive campus recruiting </news/jane-street-entry-level-pay?_gl=1*1u74t1d*_up*MQ..*_ga*NjYzNTE5MTYuMTc0OTczNDYzNg..*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NDk3MzQ2MzYkbzEkZzAkdDE3NDk3MzQ2MzYkajYwJGwwJGg4MDIwODM3NDk.>across a list of target universities and will primarily hire its intern class from those schools. The list might be larger than you think; the 159 interns we looked at came from a total of 49 different universities.
MIT is the most popular school for Jane Street full-time staff </news/the-20-universities-jane-street-loves-most-for-its-quants-and-engineers>and alumni, but ranked third for internships. The most common university among interns was the University of Cambridge, a historic funnel of talent </news/2021/11/jane-street-jobs> into Jane Street's London office. The University of Waterloo </news/best-school-for-quant-developer-jobs>, which runs a co-op program that requires students to participate in internships to graduate, is a big source of Jane Street's engineering interns.
There are many more universities not accounted for in this list that Jane Street will hire from. The firm's website said that, in 2025, interns joined from "103 different colleges and universities." This year it hired from "over one hundred." <https://www.janestreet.com/culture/street-view/a-summer-of-learning-by-doing/> Other strong schools that Jane Street hires from are the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), </news/the-elite-graduates-earning-insane-salaries-in-electronic-trading> which have produced graduates on compensation packages of $500k. </news/jane-street-student-salaries>
How does this compare to Jane Street's competitors? In 2026, Citadel Securities and sister hedge fund Citadel accepted over 350 interns from 90+ global universities. <https://fortune.com/2026/06/11/115k-young-people-applied-citadel-internships-350-made-cut-acceptance-rate-0-36/>
What subject should I study to get a Jane Street internship?
Far and away the most popular subjects among these incoming Jane Street interns were mathematics and computer science. 84% of Jane Street's interns studied one (or both) of those subjects. Only one other subject, economics, was studied by more than 10 people.
This is expected of top players in the space. Roughly 90% of Citadel and Citadel Securities' 2026 class <https://www.citadelsecurities.com/careers/career-perspectives/ken-griffins-talent-machine-is-getting-bigger/>studied a technical subject; the remaining 10% studied finance or economics.
Young electronic trading firms </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> like Jane Street are thought to prefer younger undergraduates </news/prop-trading-firms-won-t-touch-ph-d-quants-try-banking-instead> to PhDs </news/do-you-need-a-phd-for-a-quant-job-in-finance>, and this intern sample overwhelmingly reflects that. Roughly 90% of them were undergraduate students, with just four out of 159 studying a PhD.
Note, however, that Jane Street staff have previously said the modules you study </news/jane-street-employees-reveal-what-degrees-matter-when-applying-for-quant-jobs?_gl=1*1u74t1d*_up*MQ..*_ga*NjYzNTE5MTYuMTc0OTczNDYzNg..*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NDk3MzQ2MzYkbzEkZzAkdDE3NDk3MzQ2MzYkajYwJGwwJGg4MDIwODM3NDk.> can matter more than your broader degree. Choose wisely.
What internships do I need to get into Jane Street?
It's the work experience profile of Jane Street interns where things get really interesting. The vast majority have internships, some having as many as seven, but they're across an expansive range of companies and industries. Jane Street's interns had an average of 2.2 internships before joining the firm.
The most popular company, curiously enough, was Jane Street itself; 15 of the 159 interns returned for their second internship with the firm. In multiple of these cases, students interned initially as a software engineer before returning as a quant trader.
The next most popular firms for Jane Street interns were all tech firms: Amazon, Google and Databricks. The most popular financial services firms for Jane Street's overall intern class were Citadel and Optiver, although several of its quant trading interns worked at IMC.
This, again, depends heavily on what function you want to work in. Strategy and product interns are more likely to have prior experience in investment banking. One worked in M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma>for Evercore while another worked for JPMorgan. Some quant traders had investment banking experience too; one New York trader worked on M&A for Rothschild, then worked in Goldman Sachs' sales and trading division and at Citadel Securities before landing at Jane Street. Waterloo's co-op program also inflates the number of internships among Jane Street's engineering interns.
What else will get me a job at Jane Street?
Most prospective Jane Street interns reading this will have already chosen their schools and subjects. You might have missed the window to get internship experience too, but there are several other things you can do to stand out when applying to Jane Street.
One of the most common is tutoring; 22 interns had tutoring jobs alongside their studies, commonly through global tutoring company Mathnasium. Some interns also tutored at Jane Street's own Academy of Math and Programming. ~19% of trading interns tutored in some capacity.
Roughly 15% of interns also attended a spring week or other educational event run by a trading firm. Once again, Jane Street's own events, such as its first-year trading and technology program (FTTP) were most common, followed by events held by Optiver and IMC. Spring week attendees that we've spoken to said that these events have helped them get internships </news/how-important-are-spring-weeks-and-insight-events-when-applying-for-quant-trading-internships> and even full-time roles. One student was able to secure a trading internship with no prior experience after finishing in the top 15 of IMC's annual trading tournament, Prosperity. </news/lone-jane-street-hong-kong-intern-is-the-frontrunner-in-a-global-trading-competition>
Research projects were also common. Several interns were researchers within their university's AI labs; CSAIL </news/jane-street-s-top-interns-in-2025-have-this-college-ai-lab-in-common> at MIT is a particularly renowned lab that several Jane Street employees have previously worked in, but only one intern in the dataset worked there.
Women were particularly underrepresented, making up less than 10% of the sample; several of them previously attended 'women's winternships' at trading firms like HRT.
There are also more unconventional approaches to get Jane Street's attention. Several quant trading interns traded independently on sports/prediction markets </news/traders-earning-1m-on-kalshi-are-offered-double-or-nothing-to-join-trading-firms> prior to interning at Jane Street, one of whom also had a sneaker reselling business on the side. Other students were members of their university's quant societies or investment societies.
One student studying a statistics master's at Oxford was able to get a Jane Street internship with no prior experience except as a member of the McDonald's </news/2022/05/100-hour-weeks> crew. He must have had a very impressive interview.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Self-absorbed finance bros accused of 3am parties. JPMorgan’s Millennial invisible woman is suddenly very outstanding
item.description:
City dwellers in the world’s financial capitals have never been very keen on the spectacle of bankers enjoying themselves. As a profession, banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>combines high-energy personalities, a demographic bias toward young men, and a lot of spare income to spend on intoxicants. All these things make its twentysomething employees something of an acquired taste for neighbours and nightlife patrons; some of the best clubs <https://www.reuters.com/article/business/bankers-out-of-favour-at-exclusive-london-club-idUSTRE7272YL/> used to famously ban them entirely.
It seems that in Manhattan, a crew of “finance bros” <https://nypost.com/2026/11/16/us-news/finance-bros-torturing-nyc-residents-with-wild-chelsea-rooftop-parties-featuring-dozens-of-revelers/> are carrying on the tradition and/or giving the rest of us a bad name. An apartment building on W 20th Street in Chelsea has got a little roof terrace, and it’s being used for “out-of-control drinking, bumping amplified music and screams”, according to neighbours, who report being woken up at 3am. As well as packing the terrace to a dangerous-looking level of overcrowding, apparently the bros have also taken to hitting Whiffle balls off the roof into the streets below. Neighbours are declaring themselves "exasperated" and are saying things like, “The people are selfish and self-absorbed." It does sound pretty hellish to live near.
Except … if the party house is really rocking “throughout the day and long into the night”, when are the bros doing their finance? There doesn’t seem to be any actual evidence in the news reports that any of the party guests are investment bankers, and market conditions so far this year in New York have been quite busy. Most analysts and associates </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>will have solid alibis for the times when they’re accused of playing shirtless rooftop ball games, because they’ve been working on pitch decks.
This is actually a long standing cultural phenomenon. People outside the investment banking industry don’t really understand it, and media portrayals in series like “Industry” tend to give the impression that the kind of misbehaviour you might see once or twice in your career happens every day. All the general public really know about bankers is that they are well paid. And so everything which is done in public by young men with a lot of money gets blamed on bankers.
Which is slightly irritating, because it means that whenever you go to a party, or on a date, you need to spend a bit of time convincing people that you’re not like their mental stereotype. But when compared to genuinely unpopular industries, like tech, it’s not so bad. If the worst people think about bankers is that they’re not always considerate when they’re letting their hair down, that’s obviously better than thinking we might be about to create a doomsday machine and destroy the planet. It’s not so long ago that people’s dislike of the investment banking industry was motivating them to break windows rather than just moaning to the New York Post.
Elsewhere, Jamie Dimon has described Bregje de Best <https://www.ft.com/content/cc080db6-46c1-49fb-a3d5-2680b3360b6d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, the new JPMorgan CFO, as “an extraordinary leader” who “has a deep understanding of how our company operates as well as extensive client-facing experience”. Other commentators have describe her … in exactly the same way, because outside the facts set out in the JP Morgan press release <https://www.jpmorganchase.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/jpmorganchase-announces-bregje-de-best-will-succeed-jeremy-barnum-as-cfo> announcing her promotion and Jeremy Barnum’s move to a Vice-Chairman role, there’s very little information about her in the public record.
This is partly because her career hasn’t been the kind that generates a thick file of press clippings. Bregje de Best has worked at JPMorgan for 20 years, which means effectively her entire career (she’s 43 years old). She’s had plenty of front office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> roles, but they seem to have mainly been in the highly specialised field of corporate equity derivatives and she spent five years in Hong Kong. Most recently, she was co-head of global corporate banking and (for the last year) CFO of the Corporate and Investment Bank.
In other words, she’s someone who has been highly regarded internally for a while, and who is now being placed into the front rank where she’ll be responsible for the quarterly earnings calls and managing the $1.5 trillion balance sheet. She is also the first Millennial <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennials>, using the strict definition of someone born between 1981 and 1996, to be appointed to a top-three C-Suite job at a major investment bank. (Sharon Yeshaya <https://www.bloomberg.com/profile/person/5786031> at Morgan Stanley is at the young end of Generation X). And so her sudden rise to prominence will have an entire new generation of bankers feeling old.
Meanwhile …
With a few well-known exceptions, bullies in the modern banking industry tend to operate by making unreasonable work demands and psychologically undermining their victims, rather than just shouting insults at them in meetings. It seems that the corporate culture at Nvidia (including a few guest appearances by Huang family nepos) might have been a bit more “old school”. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/business/put-downs-parties-and-a-royal-family-the-culture-inside-jensen-huangs-nvidia-6a872194?mod=mhp>)
“To be clear, this was a business decision, not a performance one”. Priya Kodeeswaran of Katamaran Capital wants investors to understand why he’s closing the fund down. The former Millennium pod manager raised $500m and was up 7.3% for the year to September, but even this might not represent critical mass in the current cost environment. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/former-man-group-money-managers-hedge-fund-shuts-operations-be476fb7>)
The political machinations behind the appointment of a chief economist for the ECB aren’t quite the same as the story of a top level investment banking job move, but they have a certain family resemblance. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/d83f2a71-aea1-4654-a89a-84ad203f6646?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
In a recent TV interview, Bill Ackman of Pershing Square didn’t look his usual youthful self. He’s gone onto social media to explain that he’s been out of sorts with a tennis injury and the lighting was unflattering. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/bill-ackman-explains-grizzled-tv-appearance-after-back-injury-2026-11>)
Tech companies are increasingly discouraging their employees from having those informal chats and serendipitous water-cooler conversations because they aren’t visible to the AI agents. Not clear yet if this means that everyone is going to have to work from home again, as these were often cited as reasons to come back to the office. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/9df59321-a7a0-4ed7-b02f-60cfc5fdcb2e?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
If you have $100,000 to spare, then rather than buying an expensive handbag, you can buy a share in an investment fund that owns lots of expensive handbags. (Finews <https://www.finews.com/news/english-news/74518-luxury-stocks-trading-used-luxury-goods-dana-auslander-blackstone-manager-fund-hermes-handbags>)

item.title: Barclays has a very strong incentive to cut its 5,000 jobs before 2027
item.description:
Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs </news/barclays-ai-job-cuts>. It is cutting 4,000 of them before Christmas and it is cutting 200 of them in the investment bank, with more cuts starting today. </news/barclays-cut-some-jobs-in-new-york-yesterday-it-s-probably-cutting-in-london-next-week>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
200 is not a large number, particularly when it is spread globally, and insiders at Barclays tell us there has been little sign of the casualties. "There's nothing worth mentioning," says one New York trader who earlier feared his office pass might not work. "A few juniors, that's all."
Barclays isn't commenting on the cuts, but in London there are suggestions that this week's small cuts in the investment bank are for people at director level and above. There are also suggestions that the cuts this week are focused on non-unionized staff and that union members were put at risk in a round of larger cuts in October, when the job losses were first announced.
Barclays hasn't confirmed that this is the case, but there is a logic to cutting as quickly as possible in the UK.
From January 2027, the UK's current £118k cap on compensation for unfair dismissal is being lifted. </news/unlimited-compensation-for-unfair-dismissal-bankers-uk>A government restriction saying that unfair dismissal can only be claimed after two years with an employer is being shortened by 75%. In less than two months, therefore, Barclays employees who deem that they were dismissed unfairly or without due procedure will be able to sue the bank for uncapped sums - even if they only joined seven months' previously.
Last year, Barclays said <https://home.barclays/content/dam/home-barclays/documents/investor-relations/reports-and-events/annual-reports/2025/Country-Snapshot-2025.pdf> it employed around 44,500 people in the UK, versus around 31,000 in India and 11,000 in the US. When the bank is cutting 5,000 staff, therefore, the UK is likely to be in the firing line.
It might be supposed that Barclays' unionised staff will be most aware of the new laws and most likely to complain. We asked Unite to comment for this article, but no one there responded.
People at Barclays' investment bank are less likely to belong to a union, but the UK government has also mandated that unions now have a right to request access to workplaces. Each week, unions can then <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/gmb-workers-rights-union-membership-hbpzft8hw> provide employees with an item of union information which has to be distributed by the employer, and the employer can't monitor who engages with it. This only came into force at the end of October.
If AI-related job cuts come for bankers and traders at Barclays, they too may heed the call of Unite. For the moment, no one seems unduly bothered. Barclays' European macro business was called out for poor performance </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time> in the bank's recently filed third quarter results, but insiders say the job cuts so far have barely registered. Today was star salesman Puni Rajah's birthday </news/punitha-raja-barclays>, and the focus was all on him and a client event he'd organised in London.
Further cuts are expected tomorrow and Thursday.

item.title: Inside Point72: "The transition from analyst to portfolio manager is really, really hard"
item.description:
It's always a tough time to be an analyst in a hedge fund </news/analyst-hedge-fund>, but recent times have been particularly harsh. Claude is pretty special at analysis work and many hedge funds aren't having a good year. </news/hedge-fund-performance-2026>Beneath the poor top level performance at big multistrategy funds </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-hiring>is a world of pain involving the closure of entire pods, including portfolio managers (PMs) and the analysts who were supporting them - even if the analysts weren't entirely to blame.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Point72 is doing better than many other funds. Although it was down 2.3% in October's fixed income turmoil, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/rokos-joins-biggest-hedge-funds-losing-money-in-october-turmoil?srnd=undefined> reported that Point72 generated 8.4% after fees in the year to September. This might be because of investment mix. But in equities, at least, it might also be because Point72 invests heavily in nurturing the analysts who inform its investment decisions.
“The transition from analyst to PM is really, really hard,” says Reid Murphy, head of business development for Europe at Point72. Going straight from analysis to portfolio management is a bit like flying a plane that you're simultaneously building, says Murphy. You may crash.
Helpfully, then, Point72 runs an analyst-to-portfolio manager training program called LaunchPoint. It nurtures investment staff until they can run their own strategies. 55% of the equities portfolio managers at the firm started in LaunchPoint, says Murphy. Many arrive from banks where they worked in equity research or on investment banking sector teams. Some come from private equity. Some come from left field areas like scientific research.
Getting onto the programme is a challenge in itself. Up to 20 interviews are possible. There are modelling tests and case studies. There are interviews with multiple PMs. "We’ve found that the people who give us the best reads on who will be successful are the people currently doing the job,” says Murphy.
LaunchPoint applicants who stand out show "qualitative skills, judgement and critical thinking," says Murphy. You need to go and investigating what you're researching instead of just looking at a screen. You need an edge.
If you make it onto the LaunchPoint programme and through to becoming an an actual equities PM, you'll need to be an expert in the particular sector you're opining on. But you'll also need to be an "idea generator." You will need to "come up with trading ideas on both the long and short side." And you will need to show that your ideas can scale: "Can you put meaningful capital behind the ideas you’re generating?”
This is all harder than it seems. "You can know names and have ideas, but what if you put meaningful capital behind them? You need to generate ideas independently, not just via a modelling template,” Murphy tells us. “There’s no set pathway. It’s not like a bank, where you go from level to level."
You will also require the P word. Passion. As analysts across the industry have recently discovered to their detriment, working for a hedge fund is not easy. “This job is a grind," Murphy says. "It’s not like on TV where you’re masters of the universe. You’re in day in, day out, trying to find the minutiae of what a company said one month versus another."
Passion for a big bonus won't carry you through, though. "You need passion for the job that goes beyond the monetary rewards. If you’re coming for the money, the job will wear you down in the periods when you don’t make money," says Murphy.
It helps, too, if you stay in your seat. The hedge fund industry is full of people switching jobs for guarantees and paid non-competes. Rivals are always trying to poach Point72's portfolio managers, says Murphy, but 70% of the firm's equity PMs who came through LaunchPoint over the last five years are still there. “Jumping around from seat to seat is destructive," he says. "What matters is longevity.”
Remember that in the year to come, whichever fund you work for.

item.title: Prop trading firms are warming to PhDs as Susquehanna launches new fellowship
item.description:
Prop trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>have not been renowned for their love of PhDs </news/do-you-need-a-phd-for-a-quant-job-in-finance> in previous years. Recruiters have said </news/prop-trading-firms-won-t-touch-ph-d-quants-try-banking-instead> that these firms like to mold young talent around their culture, but that PhDs can be overly academic or stubborn. As the major market makers grow their headcount into the thousands, this is changing, and major trading firms are going out of their way to make sure PhDs feel loved.
Click here to fill out the 2026 eFinancialCareers Bonus Expectations Survey 💸 <https://www.smartsurvey.co.uk/t/E26GDA/>
Susquehanna is launching a new global PhD fellowship, through which the trading firm will provide unrestricted gifts to the advisors of several PhD students. In the US, this gift is $200k for a two-year period. Fellows also recieve a senior research mentor and the option of attending a summer program at the firm. Susquehanna has also hired several senior PhD academics over the past year, including Bjarne Stroustrup, </news/a-high-frequency-trading-firm-just-hired-bjarne-stroustrup-creator-of-c?_gl=1*1ui43jy*_up*MQ..*_ga*NTY0Mjg0NjI2LjE3OTQ5MjE0NzA.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3OTQ5MjE0NzAkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ5MjE0NzAkajYwJGwwJGgxMjIyNTAzNzg2>creator of C++, and Gabriel Dos Reis, </news/gabriel-dos-reis-susquehanna> another senior contributor to the language.
Susquehanna is one of the largest market makers by headcount and has been more overtly interested in PhDs than most. It is one of the increasingly large group of firms to run internship programs specifically for PhDs; others include Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities. The lattermost firm had 260 PhDs, ~15% of total headcount, in 2025. </news/phd-citadel-securities>
Attitudes are shifting elsewhere too. Jane Street employees said through Jane Street's own channels in 2024 </news/jane-street-employees-reveal-what-degrees-matter-when-applying-for-quant-jobs> that "the majority of researchers at Jane Street don't have PhDs," but the firm had grown its PhD headcount to 160 as of March. </news/does-jane-street-hire-phds> Jane Street has run its own postgraduate fellowship since 2023, which offers a stipend of $50k.
Hedge funds, by contrast, have always had a love for PhDs. Some funds have hired them as a means of demonstrating intellectual capacity to investors, but others like Renaissance Technologies </news/2023/09/renaissance-technologies-culture> and Capital Fund Management </news/capital-fund-management-cfm-hedge-fund> have huge contingents of PhDs.

item.title: Ex-BNP, HSBC, JPMorgan salesperson reaches an interesting new bank
item.description:
People can have very different careers in finance. Some people, such as Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick, are lifers who have spent their whole career at one bank. Others, however, change jobs every few years.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Michael Spencer joined BBVA, the Spanish bank, in London this month as a managing director (MD) and head of its global foreign exchange (FX) macro sales team. He joined the bank from broker DeepWell Liquidity Management, where he spent just a year in its global macro & derivatives sales team, specializing in Japanese and Chinese macro offerings.
Spencer joined DeepWell from HSBC, where he was last head of the bank’s FX hedge fund sales team, selling cash & derivatives in both developed and developing markets. We reported that he was cut from his role at HSBC </news/hsbc-unexpectedly-cut-some-fx-people-in-march-one-has-got-a-new-job>, which he joined from BNP Paribas.
When he joined HSBC five years ago, Specner was just a director – despite having been an MD and head of FX hedge fund sales at JPMorgan a decade previously.
BBVA, who did not respond to a request for comment, is a natural next step, either way – it has been expanding its corporate and investment bank in London. In the first nine months of 2026, the bank’s CIB revenue rose by 21% to €6.35bn, and global markets revenue specifically rose 18%. The bank credited FX as having “maintained its contribution to growth.” It has also been going after hedge fund business particularly; in October 2025 it hired Vaughn Campos <https://www.bbvacib.com/es/insights/news/bbva-cib-amplia-su-negocio-con-hedge-funds-con-una-contratacion-clave-en-nueva-york/> from HSBC to run US hedge fund coverage.

item.title: AI on the buy side: 10+ use cases per firm, but the jury's out on half of them
item.description:
One of the most common complaints levelled at firms undergoing AI transformation </news/ai-in-asset-management> is that the cost of implementing the technology doesn't always lead to any tangible benefits for the firm. That is not true of the buy side </news/buy-side-jobs-in-asia-who-s-feeling-the-effects-of-ai-the-most>... half the time, at least.
Click here to fill out the 2026 eFinancialCareers Bonus Expectations Survey 💸 <https://www.smartsurvey.co.uk/t/E26GDA/>
AI insights firm Evident has released a new index <https://evidentinsights.com/asset-management-ai-index> tracking AI implementation across 30 different asset management firms including private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firms and hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>. Across the 30 firms, a total of 320 use cases have been publicly disclosed since 2023, an average of just over 10 per firm.
Averages can be deceiving though, as those use cases are concentrated among the top nine firms, including BlackRock, Vanguard, Bridgewater and Man Group. The top nine account for 45% of use cases, implying 16 use cases on average; the remaining 21 therefore have little more than half the disclosed use cases per firm of the top nine, at an average of 8.4.
Only 178 of the 320 use cases, ~55% of the total, had measured impacts on the respective company. 50% of measurable use cases related to portfolio management and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> were recorded by the top nine firms, but more than 90% of measurable use cases for general productivity were recorded by the other 21.
What are all these firms actually doing? BlackRock, which ranked first in Evident's index, has an agentic platform called RockAI designed to allow employees to interface with various types of agents that the firm deploys. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/cio-journal/inside-blackrocks-ai-transformation-03a1e8c7> reported in April that it was first rolled out to 5,000 developers with plans to make the tool available for non-technical 'citizen developers' down the line to make tools similar to the ones made by front-office staff at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs. BlackRock also has Asimov, an agent-powered research platform used by 150 fundamental equity researchers to speed up analysis of unstructured data.
Hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, meanwhile, has a $4.5bn fund where AI is used to make investing decisions. Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/bridgewaters-flagship-macro-fund-posts-robust-double-digit-gains-this-year-2026-10-01/>reported in October that Bridgewater's AIA Macro fund was up 16.4% at the end of September in what has been a very difficult year for hedge funds. Bridgewater's flagship Pure Alpha fund was up over 18% for the same period; it is human led, but "exists in deep partnership" <https://www.bridgewater.com/aia-labs#:~:text=Transforming%20Investment%20Research,in%20AIA%20Labs.> with Bridgewater's AI lab.
You're less likely to see private equity firms at the forefront of AI: Carlyle, Blackstone and KKR rank 16th, 20th and 22nd, respectively. The report notes that Blackstone uses AI for drafting memos, and KKR uses the technology to search through documents. Carlyle, however, is one of the rare firms to report a return on investment with AI; it reported a "value creation" of $470m in its 2024 annual report after 90% of staff had begun adopting generative AI tools, although this also includes productivity gains from its broader technology transformation.

item.description:
Yesterday we informed you that a big front office cloud guy left Brevan Howard. </news/hedge-fund-brevan-howard-s-cloud-guy-is-moving-on>Today we inform you that the actual chief technology officer appears to have left Rokos Capital Management.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Amit Sudharshan was terminated as a member of Rokos Capital Management LLP last week according to a filing with companies house. He left on May 4th according to the FCA Register.
We have not spoken to Sudharshan and Rokos declined to comment. It's conceivable that he has simply left the UK and moved to Greece along with Chris Rokos himself </news/chris-rokos-departing-hedge-fund-manager-is-not-just-a-330m-tax-payer>. It's also conceivable that he has left.

item.title: A legendary trader left Barclays and people are a little bit sad
item.description:
It's the end of an era. Adam Glossop, a former managing director at Barclays who we understand was a key figure in corporate treasury trading at the firm, has left. Glossop, who didn't respond to a request to comment is understood to have departed recently. Barclays declined to say anything about his exit.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Glossop joined Barclays from BlackRock </news/2017/09/adam-glossop-barclays> in 2017. He spent 12 years as a rates portfolio manager there.
Barclays insiders say Glossop was a major figure in corporate treasury trading and that his departure marks the end of an era. Diego Megia </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>, founder of struggling hedge fund Taula Capital, worked for Barclay's treasury team for three years from 2013 and is a revered figure among the traders who worked with him. Megia is thought to have set the tone for Barclays' treasury team; Glossop perpetuated it.
The reason for Glossop's departure is not clear. Insiders say it is a shame. "There are few bank treasuries now able to take serious risk," says one. If you want to work for a risk-taking treasury team now you might want to join JPMorgan under Charlie Bristow or maybe Deutsche Bank, they vaguely suggest.
The FCA Register shows Glossop leaving Barclays' at the end of July. His notice period is thought to have ended recently. Today is the day that Barclays is expected to cut 200 jobs from its investment bank in London and New York. </news/barclays-cut-some-jobs-in-new-york-yesterday-it-s-probably-cutting-in-london-next-week>

item.title: Morning Coffee: Sleepless nights at the top of Deutsche Bank and over-hiring control staff. When Citi thinks you're special
item.description:
Christian Sewing, chief executive of Deutsche Bank, sometimes can't sleep. In 2021, he couldn't sleep because he'd cut fewer costs than planned and felt that he should have been harsher. “I could not sleep last night as I am so worried about costs,” he told then CFO James Von Moltke.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Six years later, Sewing may have had another sleepless night after the leaking of 15m files by whistleblowers which the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/df518845-ed97-4a38-8a38-7fa9d4d24003?syn-25a6b1a6=1>says show "systemic failures" on his watch.
Deutsche Bank has published a long statement <https://www.db.com/news/detail/20261117-deutsche-bank-statement-on-recent-media-reports?language_id=1>on the leak, which it says refer to matters that "date back many years." Deutsche says it is a "different, stronger and safer bank today" and that this is reflected both in the way it's viewed by regulators and by its much improved credit rating. Deutsche Bank shares nonetheless fell slightly when the market opened.
Much like Citi </news/2023/09/citi-staff-cuts>, Deutsche dealt with its historic regulatory problems by expanding its population of compliance and control staff. In the three years to 2022, the FT says the German bank increased staff in control roles by 26%. But the leak includes a 2018 email from Sewing saying "Now the pendulum swung to[o] strongly into the ‘110 per cent control’ area." Having bumped up control staff, Sewing reportedly wrote that Deutsche needed to "scale back” on “people and committees to run all kind of investigations and other stuff” while acting in a “defendable” way to avoid upsetting regulators. Citi has been cutting back on its expanded control staff </news/citi-s-2026-layoffs-have-been-more-frequent-and-widespread-than-we-thought> too, so maybe this is standard behaviour.
The Deutsche Bank leak also suggests a lack of respect for money laundering professionals at the bank. Know Your Customer (KYC) functions were reportedly known by some internally at DB (not Sewing specifically) as "Kill Your Career." This may be apt today given that KYC functions are among the first being heavily automated by AI.
The whistleblowers who provided the leaked information said in a statement read by the FT that Deutsche still needs "a complete overhaul in management and culture.” Deutsche Bank says it's "a different bank today" and that the "market, key regulators and supervisory authorities, as well as clients and other stakeholders,” all recognise this.
Some of that recognition has been nudged along by Deutsche itself. The FT notes that messages from 2019 show Deutsche's then-CFO and its head of investor relations discussing "prepped" and "planted" questions on analyst calls. Deutsche Bank told the FT the questions were at the analysts' full discretion and that it may simply have encouraged analysts with an interest in specific topics to ask things.
Separately, if Citi really likes you, it might give you a large package to stop you moving-on. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-17/gazumping-wall-street-mimics-hedge-fund-top-talent-jpmorgan-citi-barclays-bofa>says this is what Citi did for Rob Smolen, its head of equity exotics trading. Smolen was on his way to Barclays when head of equity </news/2023/11/fater-belbachir-citi> derivatives trading David Haldane </news/citi-head-of-equity-derivatives> left. Rather than lose Smolen too, Fater Belbachir, Citi's head of equities, reportedly dangled the offer of Haldane's job and (we imagine) higher pay. Smolen stayed.
Barclays' head of markets Adeel Khan </news/adeel-khan-barclays> is also known to persuade people to stay. Khan doesn't only offer favoured people lasagne and beer, but takes overnight flights to New York to lock people in, says Bloomberg. On this occasion, Belbachir appears to have been more persuasive.
Meanwhile...
Tradeweb is launching an AI-powered assistant for government bond traders. It will help clients with tasks such as identifying the best dealer to use for a bond trade and traders will be able to use it to distil large datasets and conduct pre- and post-trade analytics. “We used to have this done by data scientists” whereas “now you have an LLM doing it.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/tradeweb-is-rolling-out-ai-assistant-for-us-treasury-traders?taid=6afb669e71866900015deb79&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
If you want a private equity job now, become an expert in batteries and energy storage. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/private-equity-pours-money-into-power-storage-esg-investing?taid=6afb7f3e71866900015decdb&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Citi couldn't sell a $400m loan finance the debt of IT services company UST Global, even a rate of 4.25 to 4.5 percentage points over the benchmark rate and a discount of 98 cents on the dollar. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/citigroup-pulls-400-million-loan-for-it-provider-ust-global?taid=6afb7a8b71866900015dec81&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>

item.title: Morning Coffee: Sleepless nights at the top of Deutsche Bank and over-hiring control staff. When Citi thinks you're special
item.description:
Christian Sewing, chief executive of Deutsche Bank, sometimes can't sleep. In 2021, he couldn't sleep because he'd cut fewer costs than planned and felt that he should have been harsher. “I could not sleep last night as I am so worried about costs,” he told then CFO James Von Moltke.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Six years later, Sewing may have had another sleepless night after the leaking of 15m files by whistleblowers which the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/df518845-ed97-4a38-8a38-7fa9d4d24003?syn-25a6b1a6=1>says show "systemic failures" on his watch.
Deutsche Bank has published a long statement <https://www.db.com/news/detail/20261117-deutsche-bank-statement-on-recent-media-reports?language_id=1>on the leak, which it says refer to matters that "date back many years." Deutsche says it is a "different, stronger and safer bank today" and that this is reflected both in the way it's viewed by regulators and by its much improved credit rating. Deutsche Bank shares nonetheless fell slightly when the market opened.
Much like Citi </news/2023/09/citi-staff-cuts>, Deutsche dealt with its historic regulatory problems by expanding its population of compliance and control staff. In the three years to 2022, the FT says the German bank increased staff in control roles by 26%. But the leak includes a 2018 email from Sewing saying "Now the pendulum swung to[o] strongly into the ‘110 per cent control’ area." Having bumped up control staff, Sewing reportedly wrote that Deutsche needed to "scale back” on “people and committees to run all kind of investigations and other stuff” while acting in a “defendable” way to avoid upsetting regulators. Citi has been cutting back on its expanded control staff </news/citi-s-2026-layoffs-have-been-more-frequent-and-widespread-than-we-thought> too, so maybe this is standard behaviour.
The Deutsche Bank leak also suggests a lack of respect for money laundering professionals at the bank. Know Your Customer (KYC) functions were reportedly known by some internally at DB (not Sewing specifically) as "Kill Your Career." This may be apt today given that KYC functions are among the first being heavily automated by AI.
The whistleblowers who provided the leaked information said in a statement read by the FT that Deutsche still needs "a complete overhaul in management and culture.” Deutsche Bank says it's "a different bank today" and that the "market, key regulators and supervisory authorities, as well as clients and other stakeholders,” all recognise this.
Some of that recognition has been nudged along by Deutsche itself. The FT notes that messages from 2019 show Deutsche's then-CFO and its head of investor relations discussing "prepped" and "planted" questions on analyst calls. Deutsche Bank told the FT the questions were at the analysts' full discretion and that it may simply have encouraged analysts with an interest in specific topics to ask things.
Separately, if Citi really likes you, it might give you a large package to stop you moving-on. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-17/gazumping-wall-street-mimics-hedge-fund-top-talent-jpmorgan-citi-barclays-bofa>says this is what Citi did for Rob Smolen, its head of equity exotics trading. Smolen was on his way to Barclays when head of equity </news/2023/11/fater-belbachir-citi> derivatives trading David Haldane </news/citi-head-of-equity-derivatives> left. Rather than lose Smolen too, Fater Belbachir, Citi's head of equities, reportedly dangled the offer of Haldane's job and (we imagine) higher pay. Smolen stayed.
Barclays' head of markets Adeel Khan </news/adeel-khan-barclays> is also known to persuade people to stay. Khan doesn't only offer favoured people lasagne and beer, but takes overnight flights to New York to lock people in, says Bloomberg. On this occasion, Belbachir appears to have been more persuasive.
Meanwhile...
Tradeweb is launching an AI-powered assistant for government bond traders. It will help clients with tasks such as identifying the best dealer to use for a bond trade and traders will be able to use it to distil large datasets and conduct pre- and post-trade analytics. “We used to have this done by data scientists” whereas “now you have an LLM doing it.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/tradeweb-is-rolling-out-ai-assistant-for-us-treasury-traders?taid=6afb669e71866900015deb79&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
If you want a private equity job now, become an expert in batteries and energy storage. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/private-equity-pours-money-into-power-storage-esg-investing?taid=6afb7f3e71866900015decdb&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>

(Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/citigroup-pulls-400-million-loan-for-it-provider-ust-global?taid=6afb7a8b71866900015dec81&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>

item.title: Citadel's head of weather engineering landed at HRT and is hiring meteorologists on $300k
item.description:
As we wrote last month </news/hrt-hired-citadel-s-head-of-weather-engineering-in-chicago>, Hudson River Trading hired Deron Roche, the head of weather engineering at Citadel. Roche left Citadel in June 2025 and after a long period of gardening leave he arrived at HRT in October.
Now he's hiring there.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
HRT has opened a vacancy for a meteorologist to build its weather analytics department "from the ground up." Based in Chicago, the meteorologist will report to Roche and will hire and mentor other meteorologists as HRT grows its team. The first role is advertised with a $200k-$300k salary, plus bonuses.
HRT's enthusiasm for meteorologists is borne of HRT's enthusiasm for natural gas and power trading, an area in which Citadel is particularly strong. Roche worked for Citadel for over 20 years. His desired hire will know about tropical forecasting and hurricane responses and will be able to use this to predict changes in the demand for power.

item.title: Hedge fund Verition hired a JPMorgan head of rates trading who retired two years ago
item.description:
Verition, the multistrategy hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> has had multiple recent departures from its London fixed income team. Now another portfolio manager has gone and a major new hire has arrived.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The major new hire is Gil Holmes, a former global head of rates trading at JPMorgan. Holmes left the bank in July 2024, saying he was retiring. Now he's back. Holmes announced on LinkedIn today that he is joining Verition as the new global head of fixed income and macro.
Holmes' arrival follows the departure of Jonathan Raiff, Verition's former head of fixed income and macro in September. Raiff has gone to Schonfeld.
Raiff's exit appears to have triggered the departure of Philipp De Casan, a onetime head of euro rates trading at Nomura, who is thought to have left Verition's London business by mutual arrangement.
