item.title: Susquehanna's new head of alt data has arrived after sitting out Citadel non-compete
item.description:
If data is the new oil, alt data </news/one-of-jane-street-s-most-important-teams-is-full-of-professional-speed-daters> is the new jet fuel. Trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> and hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> alike need data from unconventional sources to generate alpha signals, and the people working on that data are in high-demand. Algorithmic trading firm Susquehanna just appointed a new head of alt data, but might have been waiting a long time to finally bring him in.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Nico Smuts joined Susquehanna </news/gabriel-dos-reis-susquehanna>this month as its head of alt data, based in New York. He spent the last 15 months sitting out a non-compete, but spent four years prior to that at hedge fund Citadel. There, he was based in London and ran a data science function focused on international equities trading strategies.
Smuts also has a penchant for robotics. Prior to joining Citadel </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel>, he worked in Imperial College London's Robot Intelligence lab with a focus on teaching its in-house robot, Robot De Niro, to play fetch. <https://robot-intelligence-lab.gitlab.io/fezzik-docs/>This process was reliant on image recognition software, which can be useful when analysing image-based alt data such as the archetypal example of alt data: satellite footage of a Walmart parking lot. While at Imperial, Smuts also researched social media data as a source of alpha by analyzing over a million Telegram messages to develop crypto trading strategies according to a podcast <https://muckrack.com/podcast/the-alternative-data-podcast/episodes/8870209-the-nico-smuts-episode/> in May.
Citadel's alt data specialists seem to be coveted. Last month, Balyasny hired Halla Yang </news/balyasny-hired-the-former-head-of-citadel-s-data-strategies-group>, who previously headed Citadel's data strategies group, to work as a quant researcher.
Susquehanna is continuing to grow its alt data team; it has an open listing for an alt data engineer on its systematic delta one trading desk. Examples of alternative data given by the firm include "credit card panels, web-scraped product prices [and] call transcripts."
Citadel and Susquehanna declined to comment.

item.title: "Hypocritical managing directors are cutting juniors in banks. Beware!"
item.description:
I am a junior on a trading desk </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> at a top European bank. The bank I work for is going through a cost-cutting round. Some of the most junior people are among the casualties.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Last week, two people were cut who had only joined this bank one and two years ago respectively.
It seems completely hypocritical. The executive committee sent an email a few weeks ago saying that they are building a workforce for the future and putting "internal talent first". Their actions suggest otherwise.
Both of the juniors let go were cut without a performance plan or attempt to find them an alternative role on another desk. It's not the first time this has happened - a junior was cut under similar circumstances last year too.
Who made the decision? We think it was the managing directors (MDs) </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> and HR in the head office. The cuts seem unnecessary because there's been high attrition on our regional desk this year. We also think they were simply intended to instil fear into everyone left behind and to make us grateful for any bonus we may yet receive. Two first-year female analysts have only just started and now they are going to have to pick up the work of the people let go.
It seems a huge shame. Investment bank </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>jobs are increasingly about cost cutting and consolidation and are less secure than ever. This is not an easy industry to work in as a recent graduate. People I know are already mentally preparing to move back in with their parents.
This is my advice for new joiners:
1. If a bank promotes its "great place to work" credentials, ask exactly what that means for career management, in particular when there are gaps between your perception of your output and that of others in the bank.
2. Before taking an offer from a desk investigate how they treated grads from previous years - if they were harsh in managing those colleagues' careers, expect they will do the same to you.
3. Your job is always at risk, even if you perceive yourself as DEI protected - the bank can find other DEI candidates to fill that role.
4. Do not expect the bank to manage your career; you are obliged to manage it yourself.
5. Establish early where the power lies within the setting. Sycophancy towards those in power can be critical to your survival. But remember that the people with this power can change very quickly - banks are brutal shape-shifting worlds!
6. When making career choices, most candidates consider non-client-facing roles less important, but as a junior fighting for survival, your perception in those teams can still impact your career.
7. Do not believe banks when they come to hiring events and make it sound like everyone cares about you and your career. They don't! This is a hard industry and it sucks to be a junior at bank nowadays. Beware!
Patrick Griffith is a pseudonym

item.title: Prop trading firms have sales and trading teams too: this is what they do at Jane Street
item.description:
The appeal of working in a prop trading firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> is that you're not managing money on behalf of clients and have more license to take risks. Despite this, several major trading firms have 'sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>' divisions, more commonly associated with investment banking. One member of Jane Street's </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> sales and trading desk appeared on the firm's Signals and Threads <https://signalsandthreads.com/trading-at-the-speed-of-chat/> podcast to reveal what they actually do.
Click here to fill out the 2026 eFinancialCareers Bonus Expectations Survey 💸 <https://www.smartsurvey.co.uk/t/E26GDA/>
Jane Street splits its traders into two types: 'prop traders' and 'sales traders.' Chloe Casale, a desk developer for sales trading, said that the key difference for the latter is that you're trading with someone who knows they're trading with Jane Street whereas prop traders operate "anonymously on exchange." Sales traders build relationships with institutional clients like "pension fund[s and] big wealth management firm[s]" and organize trades when they request them. Casale said these firms go to Jane Street when they have "very, very large trades, trades that maybe just don’t make sense to actually execute on the exchange because you’re not going to be able to get the best price."
This is commonly known as a 'block trade.' The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/a2dcd05d-2bcd-40a4-adc6-cbbff016222f?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported in September that Jane Street is one of the top three block trade buyers in Asia. </news/as-jane-street-and-other-prop-trading-firms-expand-in-asia-these-are-the-new-faces-and-new-teams>
The pricing for these trades is still done by Jane Street's prop traders, who will then also have to gradually unwind that position in the market once the block trade completes. They will have priced the trade in a way that allows them to profit from this unwinding, but Jane Street partner Ron Minsky said the firm receives "some extra fee implicit in the prices."
What do Jane Street sales and trading people do?
Traders in banks have lamented the death of voice trading; </news/credit-trading-jobs-ruined> it seems like those jobs have actually migrated to Jane Street instead. Casale said that many of Jane Street's client trades originate over chat, such as via the Bloomberg terminal, or over the phone.
Once a trade has been requested, sales traders feed this into Jane Street's systems so that the prop traders can provide a price, which the sales trader then verifies before relaying to the client. Casale said that Jane Street is "at least trying to get quotes into our system within less than 20 seconds," but, for some clients, it also aims for "less than five." Clients often go to several other firms for a price; Casale said that, if you take 45 seconds to verify the price when the client is expecting a five second response, Jane Street "might lose that trade" to another firm that provided a quicker quote. Client trading, therefore, is about balancing speed and accuracy: Casale said "we are racing in a way with some other brokers and we want to win on price."
Client trading has become potentially more lucrative (and difficult) thanks to AI. </news/jane-street-employees-all-have-an-ai-twin> Casale said that trades with standardized formatting were automated even before the rise of LLMs, but that desk devs have begun building "specialized prompt[s]" to extract data from these messages and turn them into "standardized [requests] for our traders to look at." Casale said, however, that these prompts do not work 100% of the time; this creates a risky problem where sales traders become "so used to being correct" that they are "constantly... hitting the yes button." The edge cases where trade requests are improperly parsed can be costly to fix and harmful to Jane Street's reputation if they aren't prevented. Sales traders, therefore, need similar eagle-eyes and reflexes </news/jane-street-s-traders-on-1-4m-have-fighter-pilot-eyes-high-pain-thresholds> to the prop traders themselves.
Who does Jane Street hire as sales traders?
Much like the roles themselves have migrated from banking to prop trading, so too have the sales traders. Among the most senior sales and trading staff at the firm are several banking alumni. Brieuc Louchard <https://www.etfstream.com/articles/jane-street-recruits-axa-etf-capital-markets-head-as-sales-trader> joined the division last November; he spent seven years at SocGen working on ETF sales, but was most recently head of ETF capital markets for investment management firm AXA. Ameni Takouri, another SocGen alum, spent five years as a sales trader for Jane Street before becoming its director of Middle East sales and business development.
Jane Street hires salespeople from other financial institutions too. Slawomir Rzeszotko, head of institutional sales and trading <https://fixedincome.wbresearch.com/speakers/slawomir-rzeszotko>for Europe and Asia, was the head of Vanguard's investment products specialists team before joining Jane Street. This year he was inducted into Jane Street's UK partnership, which pays an estimated average of $55m per head. </news/jane-street-pay>
Jane Street grows its own sales and trading talent too. A listing for a sales and trading internship </news/this-is-what-it-takes-to-get-a-64k-jane-street-internship>in London says the firm is looking for "proactive, reliable and courteous" people that are also "highly analytical." While Jane Street's trading and engineering staff predominantly study math or computer science, economics graduates are much more common in the sales and trading team based on LinkedIn data.

item.title: Hedge fund Brevan Howard's big cloud guy is moving on
item.description:
Hedge fund Brevan Howard has had various departures </news/another-senior-technologist-quietly-left-hedge-fund-brevan-howard> from its technology team in the past few years. It has also made some large hires.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The latest departure, which is understood to have come about via a resignation last week, is that of Chris Knowles, who was Brevan's front office platform lead. In this role, he says (on LinkedIn) that he was tasked with producing a "refined AWS based platform for strategic quant dev and portfolio manager projects."
Knowles didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Brevan Howard declined to comment.
Knowles joined Brevan in March 2024 and therefore predated the arrival of CTO Mike Sanders in September the same year. Before Sanders joined, Brevan's technology function is thought to have expanded dramatically. Last year, around seven senior people left </news/hedge-fund-brevan-howard-parted-with-company-with-7-senior-technologists>.
It's not clear who will replace Knowles. Prior to Brevan Howard, only around two and a half years of his 22 year career appear to have been spent in financial services tech.

item.title: Without emails, junior traders had a horrible experience of forgotten processes last Friday
item.description:
When we wrote about Outlook being down </news/outlook-outage-banking>last Friday and about bankers being able to work, we assumed that traders were ok because they are equipped with Bloomberg.
That may have been wishful thinking. In the absence of modern electronic communications chaperoned by Outlook, it seems that some things reverted to the fax machine. Junior traders were instructed to use the arcane technology. It was a shock.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"The Microsoft outage really hit hard," says one 20-something trader in Hong Kong. "Brokers started faxing in their trade confos and I had to manage them. I had to double and triple check all the option expiry dates."
Such things were standard fare for juniors in the past. Kevin Rodgers, the former global head of FX trading at Deutsche Bank, says it used to be the norm for customers to send orders by fax, for trade confos (confirmations) to be sent by fax and for traders to send risk reports to other offices by fax too. Another trading veteran says telex machines were also deployed in days of yore.
Faxing came with problems. Rodgers says faxes sent by clients allowed orders to be filled at prices advantageous to traders and were a "bad move." They also included typos that could result in trades being placed wrongly. Checking for such errors was highly tedious. Juniors cut their teeth on such activities. Michael Sherwood, </news/2016/11/michael-sherwood-goldman-sachs> the former head of Goldman Sachs International, began his career manning a fax machine.
Contemporary juniors had been spared these nightmares. - Until last Friday. Some more complex trades appear to have halted altogether in the Outlook chaos. "Structured trades were paused because no one wanted to fax OTC settlement terms," says the junior we spoke to.

item.title: Macro traders who want a nice safe banking job again could always try Deutsche Bank
item.description:
If you're a macro trader </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> ejected from a hedge fund, </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> how about working for Deutsche Bank? Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/how-deutsche-bank-plans-to-rebuild-its-trading-business-in-the-us?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261116&utm_campaign=author_23851719> has a big article about how great Deutsche Bank's macro trading business is now. It also names many of the traders once from the likes of Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Barclays, Goldman Sachs who are now thriving there.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As we noted last year, there are over 20 people earning in excess of €6m ($7m) at Deutsche Bank globally, plus three people at the German bank earning over €10m. Several are likely to be among the names included in Bloomberg's encomium for Deutsche's fixed income trading business.
The high earners at DB almost certainly include 62-year-old Ram Nayak who's been at DB since 2009. Nayak runs the markets business and who is thought to be one of the highest paid </news/deutsche-bank-s-london-fixed-income-traders-wonder-who-got-the-18m> people outside the executive committee. They very likely include Kemal Askar, who joined from JPMorgan in 2015 and who runs the rates business. They very likely include Alok Modi, </news/alok-modi-deutsche-bank>the popular head of European rates who joined from Morgan Stanley in 2020. They probably also include Chris Leonard, who runs US rates and who joined from Barclays in 2021.
Equipped with this team, Bloomberg says Deutsche has added more than €1bn in annual revenue to its rates business since 2019. By the end of this year, Bloomberg says Deutsche is also likely to have increased compensation across the investment bank by 39% versus seven years ago. The implication is that much of that higher pay has been diverted to the expanded fixed income - and macro - trading business.
While Barclays has reportedly been depriving </news/mark-wade> its macro traders of capital in order to fuel its US equities business, Deutsche has been allowing its traders to make big bets. Bloomberg says Kemal Askar is encouraging traders to go "elephant hunting" for deals like "rate lock" swaps that can bring in tens of millions of euros a year.
If it sounds like a pitch to join Deutsche Bank's macro trading team, maybe it is. Maybe it's a pitch to rejoin in the style of Martial Collet-Billon, who ran away from DB to Brevan Howard for 17 months and returned in September? Maybe it's intended to get the attention of Josh Hooker </news/leaving-bluecrest-macro>, the former head of STIR trading at the German bank, whose DB team made €500m in 2022, but who nonetheless left for BlueCrest in 2023, only to leave Mike Platt's place last month? Maybe even George Toynbee, </news/deutsche-bank-s-kindest-sharpest-30-year-old-trader-left-for-a-hedge-fund>the talented young trader who left DB and joined LMR in August just before some of the most difficult markets in a generation, will take note?
None of Deutsche Bank's macro feats would seemingly be possible without the efforts of Sam Wisnia </news/2018/03/sam-wisnia-leaving-deutsche-bank>, the former Goldman Sachs partner who spent four years there before leaving for failed hedge fund Eisler Capital in 2018 </news/sam-wisnia-eisler-capital-why-people-dont-fit>. Wisnia developed Deutsche Bank's Kannon risk pricing platform </news/2022/05/eisler-capital-quant-jobs> before plucking his team of loyal strats to work with him at Eisler instead.
“Kannon has definitely taken our technology to a place where it allows us to scale very, very meaningfully,” Nayak told Bloomberg. Wisnia is now supplying his risk and pricing system to hedge fund Verition, seemingly attempting the same thing there. Verition reportedly generated </news/hedge-fund-performance-2026>returns of 0% after fees in the year to September. It seems that Wisnia's magic has yet to take effect.

item.title: Standard Chartered hired a new MD from UBS to build tools for its traders
item.description:
The process of building tools for the front office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> of an investment bank </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> used to be uniform; quant strats </news/strats-jobs-investment-banks>or a similarly technical person would build prototypes, and the most valuable products would then be passed on to engineering </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> to flesh out. Today, that process is changing dramatically in some banks, but the tech staff building the polished final products are still in demand.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Standard Chartered, for example, just hired London-based David Turner as an MD and global head of front office risk and trader tools technology within its markets division. He spent the last 26 years at UBS in a variety of technical roles; he was a technical lead for trade and capture lifecycle in the bank's equity derivatives business, and also spent a year and a half as an integration lead during the Credit Suisse merger. </news/ubs-has-only-scratched-the-surface-of-credit-suisse-s-legacy-technology>
Turner will focus on building out tools for traders; in other banks, this task has been complicated by a swathe of prototypes made by the traders themselves. Goldman Sachs has banned Claude Code </news/ben-atlas?_gl=1*vgapwl*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTk2OTUwMzAwNi4xNzk0ODI4NDg3*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3OTQ4Mjg0ODYkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ4Mjg0ODYkajYwJGwwJGgxMjE3OTQ5Nzk3#:~:text=Separately%20bankers%20and,and%20create%20content.>for its front office staff after they reportedly used it to build hundreds of individual prototypes. JPMorgan has taken the opposite approach, rolling the platform out to more non-technical employees; one JPMorgan developer told us </news/goldman-sachs-vibe-coding>that unchecked citizen development leads to "a load of slop" and places excess responsibility on the engineering teams who need to turn these tools into compliance-friendly products.
What's Standard Chartered's approach? The firm declined to comment, but it seems to be on the conservative side. Last summer it launched 'AI Factory' a centralized platform designed to increase the bank's oversight of AI tools being created, and stop duplicate tools from being made. John Sharatt, global head of infrastructure at Standard Chartered, said at an internal roundtable in September that the bank is focusing on deploying tools securely and economically. <https://thedigitalbanker.com/standard-chartered-lays-the-groundwork-for-enterprise-ai-with-data-cloud-and-talent/#:~:text=For%20John%20Sharratt,across%20multiple%20jurisdictions.>
Standard Chartered and UBS declined to comment.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Inside the life of the ruined 34-year-old finance billionaire. When you resign but everyone loves you
item.description:
It is the week of the Anthropic IPO. On Thursday, Anthropic - which as Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-15/anthropic-s-ipo-makes-dario-amodei-the-new-face-of-the-ai-boom>notes, will not be cashflow positive until 2030 and which has $900bn of spending commitments - will seek to raise up to $90.4bn at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Anthropic's founders will achieve individual fortunes of $13bn. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/anthropic-s-seven-founders-are-worth-more-than-13-billion-each?taid=6adf97821579270001ce0d28&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>Anthropic's bankers will achieve nearly $400m in fees. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/anthropic-s-seven-founders-are-worth-more-than-13-billion-each?taid=6adf97821579270001ce0d28&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>But someone will be left out of the party.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
That someone is Sam Bankman-Fried, who the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/0ef40ac9-6d01-428f-98c8-a52bf5b9a787?syn-25a6b1a6=1>notes invested $500m in Anthropic in 2021 in early stage funding round when he was aged just 29. After this week's IPO, that stake - made by Alameda Research Ventures, the investment arm of Bankman-Fried's crypto company, but 90% owned by Bankman-Fried himself - would have been worth more than $50bn.
Bankman-Fried is benefitting from none of it. Even though his early investment reportedly helped Anthropic scale-up, hire researchers and train models, he is bankrupt. Less than a year after he made the investment, his halo shattered, he was accused and convicted of fraud and money laundering, and then he was imprisoned. Bankruptcy officials sold Bankman-Fried's Anthropic stake for $1.3bn in 2024 and referred to it as "vapourware." He has been ordered to repay $11bn and unless something changes he won't get out of prison until he's 50, at least.
The Times <https://www.thetimes.com/us/news-today/article/sam-bankman-fried-prison-sentence-appeal-sd3pt9rxv> spoke to Bankman-Fried (SBF) in prison. Once lauded by Sequoia Capital as a “highly mathletic” super-intelligence at the centre of the tech universe, SBF knew nothing of Jensen Huang's woes. "It all sort of blurs together," he told the journalist. "Even the distinction between days and weeks and months melts down when you’re in prison with nothing to do.”
Silicon Valley moguls who practice dopamine fasts could try prison instead. "It's a form of sensory deprivation, almost," said SBF of his new life. There's no outlet for his "pent up mental energy." Days are spent, "reading, sleeping, punctuated with, like, rice and beans periodically." Boredon is "the major prison emotion." Bankman-Fried has reportedly written a diary <https://www.forbes.com/sites/digital-assets/2024/12/06/sam-bankman-fried-is-shopping-his-prison-diary--heres-a-peek-inside/> bemoaning the lack of decent pillows and trading muffins with fellow inmates who are high and have the munchies.
Bankman-Fried does not want to spend 25-years in prison. His conviction rested on his failure to segregate cash from his FTX crypto trading platform from Alameda Research Ventures and for investing customers' money as if it were his own. He says there were mitigating circumstances: FTX's terms of service said that customers' assets could be pooled and borrowed by the likes of Alameda and they would have been worth something if people hung on; the judge said this was just "idle communication."
While SBF floats along in incarceration, his lawyer parents are adamant that a terrible wrong has been done. “The prosecution’s misconduct in Sam’s case was extreme," his mother told the Times.
For his part, Sam Bankman-Fried seems stoical about his lost $50bn. He is mostly frustrated. "It was incredibly frustrating. Seeing it happen in real time and being powerless to say or do anything about it,” he says of the sale of his investments two years ago. He feels frustration, too, at "not being able to do anything for the world from in here. Not being able to be useful.”
“It is unbearable for me to be thinking about what has been done to this idealistic, selfless young man" says his mother. "The chasm between who Sam is and how he has been portrayed to the world is so vast I don’t know where to begin."
Separately, people are already saying some fine things about ex-NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after multiple affairs, one of which may have been with a 'Chinese spy."
Writing on both X <https://x.com/F5Adon/status/2121647023275545075?s=20> and LinkedIn, colleagues of Huang are relating stories of his deep kindness and well-honed management technique. They say it's not true that he's a faux-humble man surrounded by guffawing sycophants as described by the New York Times. <https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/opinion/jensen-huang-nvidia.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share>He doesn't have a short temper; he just gives real feedback to people who can take it.
The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/45383d86-33c4-4d99-86e5-5e058d3567c1?shareType=nongift&syn-25a6b1a6=1>says investors want Huang back. Huang was NVIDIA's only CEO for three decades and Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-12/nvidia-faced-pressure-to-boost-its-ai-backstop-before-huang-exit?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261112&utm_campaign=author_22980254> notes that he made the company into the "Central Bank of AI" by taking equity stakes in other firms and providing lending backstops across the ecosystem. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” one friend of Huang said.
Scott Bessent is not so sure. The US Treasury Secretary wants Huang gone and a new external CEO hired-in. "If Nvidia “were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the [Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency] would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed,” Bessent declared. <https://www.ft.com/content/24edbb84-7520-4ef0-a57c-30359e12ccc5?syn-25a6b1a6=1>Last month, Huang said <https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share>he'd stay at NVIDIA for 20 years.
Meanwhile...
DCM bankers will be next in line to make money from Anthropic. After it raises up to $100bn, Anthropic will leverage that up in the bond market. (NetInterest) <https://www.netinterest.co/p/a-bankers-guide-to-anthropic?utm_source=substack&publication_id=43559&post_id=224785956&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=8g1t6v&triedRedirect=true>
Anthropic's IPO has drawn orders for close to seven times the shares available. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-15/anthropic-s-ipo-makes-dario-amodei-the-new-face-of-the-ai-boom?taid=6afa025e718669000140b3db&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Deutsche Bank's fixed income business is thriving and it is down to the expansionary plans of Ram Nayak and all the people he's hired. It's expected to make almost €10 billion in revenues ($11.2 billion) this year, almost double the amount it made in 2019. America is a focus. So is growing the commodities business. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/how-deutsche-bank-plans-to-rebuild-its-trading-business-in-the-us?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261116&utm_campaign=author_23851719>
Barclays is cutting </news/barclays-cut-some-jobs-in-new-york-yesterday-it-s-probably-cutting-in-london-next-week> 200 jobs in the investment bank from Tuesday. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-13/barclays-to-cut-about-200-jobs-across-its-investment-bank?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261113&utm_campaign=author_21061455>
IG Group is cutting offices in France, Spain and Italy along with 50 jobs. It says “We have refreshed our organizational model to ensure IG is best placed to serve customers. This includes consolidating our European presence into a smaller number of larger hubs.”(Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-13/ig-group-is-said-to-close-offices-in-france-spain-and-italy?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261113&utm_campaign=author_3407732>
KPMG is adding to its UK deal team and wants to poach from Big Four rivals. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/kpmg-uk-hiring-big-four-pjzk8hqbx>
Anne Boden from Starling Bank is doing something new. “I’m building a bank that’s going to be built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents.” (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/starling-bank-anne-boden-ai-rival-lockwood-lhpv0nz5n>
Deloitte will no longer cover GLP-1 medication for weight-loss purposes through its medical plans. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/deloitte-benefits-cuts-glp-1-coverage-healthcare-costs-rise-2026-11>

item.title: The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 6: Small Pleasures
item.description:
Redundancy changes your routine, obviously. What I had not expected was how deeply it changes the way you live, and who you live it with.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
One of my former colleagues, whom I now consider a friend (remember, I have very few friends but plenty of acquaintances), was made redundant at the same time as me. I only found out a month later, when he got in touch and learned that I had been let go too. He was a developer in IT, and what redundancy did to him was frightening.
First came the money. He cut his expenses drastically, but in the end he could not afford to keep his Docklands flat. Last week I helped him move out. It was genuinely sad to watch him pack. He realised that his closest friends were, in fact, his parents, a statement I wholeheartedly agree with. He has moved back in with them. He is 38.
When we worked together, he was always telling me to live a little. I always answered that I needed to save for a rainy day. As he taped up the last box, he looked around the empty living room and said, “You were right about the rainy day.” I would rather have been wrong.
I also watched his slow descent into despair. At one point he felt suicidal, because application after application went nowhere. We did not give each other advice. We simply listened, without judgement, because we are all different. The one piece of advice I did pass on was to claim JSA. He refused, and still does.
I had always believed that being a developer was synonymous with a guaranteed job. I even encouraged my son to consider that path. My friend showed me how wrong I was, especially these days.
His story ran in parallel with mine, and it made me look hard at my own. As summer approached, it became clear that I would have no job to go to on 1 September. There are definitely fewer job adverts towards the end of June. Two more months of low self-esteem and shame lay ahead, and I began to hate my flat. It felt like a prison. I had told myself I was alone but not lonely. Watching my friend, I began to see how thin that line is.
So, one day, I decided I could not stay in any longer. My new office would be the local coffee chain in Canary Wharf. After all, it had a buzz, an internet connection and a supermarket nearby where I could pick up my free morning coffee. Believe it or not, I was excited. Small pleasures: a place with people in it, and a reason to leave the flat. It was not a job, but it was a start.

item.title: Bobby Jain on hedge fund Jain Global now: "Small town feel, big town resources"
item.description:
Bobby Jain, founder of hedge fund Jain Global, has done another podcast. </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience> It's well over an hour long and involves Bobby talking to Bloomberg journalist Nishant Kumar <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/audio/2026-11-13/special-bobby-jain-on-why-he-chose-millennium-again-podcast-mweuixg3>about his thoughts, of which he has many.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Jain Global agreed to manage money exclusively for Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium>in April and has been doing so since September. Talking to Kumar, Bobby said Jain is "a separate business [to Millennium], with a common investor base." There are information barriers between the two firms, he added.
Jain Global is hiring. Bobby said the fund has hired 20 portfolio managers since the deal with Millennium took place. He's spending a lot of time growing the platform, he said. The Millennium deal has facilitated this.
But why would you join Jain Global now, instead of - say - Millennium, whose money Jain Global is exclusively managing anyway </news/townie-wells>? Bobby said Jain Global has a special culture. "The message of small town feel big town resources is resonating," he elaborated.
At some firms the "product is autonomy," said Bobby. Jain Global can do autonomy. But it can also offer a "collaborative environment." People want to "feel that their partners or bosses are in the trenches with them." They want to see that all resources are being leveraged.
This is the small town vibe. Jain Global's 'big town resources' are coming from Millennium, where Bobby himself worked for seven years before going it alone. He says the recent move to manage money exclusively for Millennium came after a dinner with some former Millennium colleagues. "I think it’s fair to say that Millennium didn’t realise the breadth of activities that we had and the return on deployed capital…," he said. When he mentioned that he was planning to raise more money for the "second phase of our development," Jain said Millennium wanted in. Jain Global generated gross returns on called capital of 41% in its first two years of operation. </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-costs>
Millennium's resources include its big town AI investments. Bobby said he'd been able to build Jain Global's own technology infrastructure relatively quickly using AI. But gaining access to things like compute, data, and the system and expertise to make the most of AI is a different matter. This could take up to five years, said Jain. For this reason, he thinks AI will drive consolidation across the hedge fund industry as a whole.
Millennium's AI is "powerful," said Bobby. When he saw just how powerful, he said he could see how it would catapult Jain Global's own development into the future. This seems to have been a major reason for the Millennium deal from Bobby's perspective.
Now that Bobby Jain is able to spend more time being a CIO than a CEO, he said he's particularly focused on "talent acceleration." The best portfolio managers don't just like picking stocks and attending investor days but know know how to construct portfolios and how to deal with drawdowns, said Jain. "Izzy likes to say 'Everyone can buy, not everyone can sell',” Bobby recalled.
At a mature hedge fund, Jain said 20% of the investors make 80% of the money. Jain Global is a neophyte. There, 20% of the investors made 53% of the money last year. This is because Jain Global is young. "I didn't have the conviction to give the best people more capital," said Bobby. As time passes, people at Jain Global will develop a track record and this will change.
Bobby Jain is in his mid-50s. When he did his last major podcast in February </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience>, he said that his parents taught him that life goes in cycles: "They taught us from the age of 5 to 20, focus on education, 20 to 35, focus on career, 35 to 50, focus on family, 50 to 65 on service, 65 to 80 on philanthropy, 80 to 95 on spiritualism." In the latest podcast, he implied he might work for another 20 years.

item.title: Barclays cut some jobs in New York yesterday. It's probably cutting in London next week too
item.description:
Last month, Barclays says it would be cutting 5,000 jobs </news/barclays-ai-job-cuts> that might be automated by AI and that 4,000 would go before year-end. Yesterday, some of those cuts came to the investment bank in New York. Next week, we understand that they are also coming to the investment bank in London.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Barclays declined to comment for this article. Multiple insiders at the bank in New York told us that cuts have been going down. Some of those that have occurred so far are understood to have impacted recently hired juniors. Next week's cuts, which are expected from Tuesday, are expected to impact more senior staff globally.
It's not unusual for banks to cut jobs in the fourth quarter, but it is unfortunate as individuals are often cut before bonuses are allocated. The coming cuts at Barclays are thought to be spread across the investment bank and not to be focused on any one business area. One junior banker said they are standard for this time of year.

item.title: A third of quants are giving themselves an extra workday. Voluntarily
item.description:
Are you a quant </news/quant-jobs-finance>? Or are you trying to be one? Beware the long hours. Not in the office necessarily: our 2026 Compensation & Lifestyle Report </news/best-lifestyle-finance> found that quants only work around 48 hours per week, less than some middle-office professionals. Beware the hours you’ll need to spend at home.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
The CQF Institute – which awards the Certificate in Quantitative Finance (CQF) – found that <https://www.cqf.com/76-quant-finance-professionals-say-skills-gap-widening-heres-how-stay-ahead> more than 30% of industry quants spend at least 21 hours a month upskilling. With four weeks per month, that comes to around 5 hours per week. Another 21% of quants work at least 11 hours a month on upskilling, meaning that more than half of quants spend at least 2 or 3 hours a week improving their skills.
Even if a quant is not spending swathes of their free time to upskill, they know that they probably should. CQF Institute found that 84% of quants believe continuous reskilling is “mandatory”, and 41% of quants reskill completely through self-study. Many of them also do this work outside of work hours, too.
What are they learning? Well, a little bit of everything. 75% of quants surveyed by CQF thought that the skills they need were not taught at university, with the most lacking skills by far being advanced machine learning and agentic AI “systems”, followed at some distance by production-level model deployment.
It’s natural that quants are so focused on understanding and upskilling in AI. 74% of them, according to CQF, expect their role to be transformed “completely” or in a major way by the technology. Just 1% of quants expect minor changes in their role. Curiously however, around 29% of quants say they use AI only once a month or less.
Things might change in the near future. AI’s acceleration has caught up now, more or less, with the bleeding edge of mathematics. One quant, a former Tower Research trader, told us last month </news/the-quant-traders-that-left-for-fintech-don-t-want-to-stop-trading#:~:text=He%27s%20not%20alone,well%20as%20Astra.%22> that GPT-6 Astra was particularly fantastic. Other finance experts – from Jump Trading, IMC, and Balyasny – said the same about the recently-released Claude Mythos/Fable 5.2 <https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2>.
Frontier AI models being so good at quantitative work might be a worry for quants. When we speak to a quant working for hedge fund Citadel earlier this year </news/citadel-quant-day-in-the-life>, much of his time was occupied with developing and exploring signals in the market – essentially, super fine-tuned pattern recognition to gauge movement in the pattern. That’s the sort of thing that AI is intrinsically good at.

item.title: Bankers struck by Outlook outage: "I am paralysed" and "Perfect excuse not to do any work"
item.description:
Microsoft is having some problems. Outlook is down, taking email and calendars with it, and much of Teams is also affected. The company says <https://x.com/MSFT365Status> it is working to mitigate the impact but that so far, its efforts have been unsuccessful.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The outage is causing chaos for bankers who use Outlook to email clients. It is also causing chaos for bankers who use Outlook calendars on Teams to schedule meetings.
The South China Morning Post <https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-finance/article/3374291/microsoft-outlook-outage-disrupts-workers-hong-kongs-financial-sector>reported problems at banks in Asia overnight. Now those problems have come to London.
"I am paralysed" says one senior debt capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> banker who uses Outlook to email clients. "Everyone and everything is on Outlook. We rely upon it for the exchange of documents. Teams is not the same and in any case, it's down too."
Another managing director in M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> says the outage is a "big problem" and "a logistical nightmare". - "We can't send or receive emails," he says. "It is the perfect excuse not to do any work today."
Many people in financial services are working from home as it's Friday, adding to the dislocation. "A few people are in the office but it's no better there," says another M&A MD.
People in sales and trading roles are less heavily impacted and can use Bloomberg chat. People in banking say they are being instructed not to use "unauthorised communication channels," so Gmail is out. "Compliance comes first!" says one MD who says he's trying to send documents via Teams instead.
"It's messy," says another M&A MD, adding that people were having to pick up the phone. "Lots of people are having issues with calls," he says of Teams meetings. Calling on Teams still works for some people but it's not possible to schedule new meetings or to email clients. "I am just dialling into already scheduled meetings and hoping people are there."
One buyside professional told us he loves the quiet of the outage. One banker said the PAs are having a great time because they no longer have to arrange meetings and manage diaries.
As long as it's only a day all will be fine, says the DCM banker. He's planning to spend the rest of the day meeting clients in coffee shops instead.
The cause of the outage isn't clear. There are unconfirmed suggestions that it might be related to Microsoft's own automated health-check system, which may have started killing healthy servers. Many are noting that Microsoft is laying off 60,000 workers who might have avoided the problem or known how to fix it.
"We are living in some weird times," says one banker.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Ex-banker's apparent willingness to tolerate wife's affair was a catalyst. “This is a tougher environment than Covid and the global financial crisis”
item.description:
It's clear who is to blame for NVIDIA's immediate woes: Jensen Huang. Before resigning yesterday, <https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-announces-ceo-transition> Huang was reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-13/inside-jensen-huang-s-final-hours-as-the-ceo-of-nvidia?cmpid=111326_morningemea&utm_campaign=morningemea&utm_medium=email&utm_source=newsletter&utm_term=261113&utm_content=11378> going about describing himself as a "piece of sh*t," and saying "whatever" and "I don't care."
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Huang does indeed appear to have some sh*tty behaviours. Aside from the affairs, the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/tech/jensen-huang-colette-kress-nvidia-ceo-eb289097?st=nDSYtf&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email> is reporting that Huang had a line in belittling women during meetings. It claims that he specifically belittled Collette Kress, the CFO now replacing him as CEO. Last August, Huang is said to have called Kress a "reporting CFO", not someone able to drive strategy, and to have interrupted a presentation she was making to accuse her of being "a deer in the headlights."
With NVIDIA's share price down 27% over the past month and NVIDIA's board scrabbling to contain the situation, Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, <https://www.wsj.com/tech/the-chinese-woman-at-the-center-of-a-spy-probe-after-an-affair-with-jensen-huang-7bb406d2?mod=WSJ_home_mediumtopper_pos_3>has been the catalyst for revelations about Huang's conduct. So has his alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, NVIDIA's vice president of healthcare and maybe with another NVIDIA employee too. <https://www.reuters.com/technology/former-nvidia-ceo-huang-had-relationship-with-second-employee-sources-say-2026-11-12/>
At least one of the affairs might not have happened, though, had the husband of the woman involved not allegedly been semi-complicit.
The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/a-mystery-businessman-introduced-jensen-huang-to-his-paramourher-husband-1ec3b581?mod=hp_5storieswithpix_pos_2>is suggesting that Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, knew about Huang's affair with his wife because he introduced them. Wei would half-jokingly refer to his wife as being Jensen Huang's personal assistant, says the WSJ. However, the WSJ was unable to confirm this with Wei himself.
Kang Wei has a financial services background. Before jumping on the data centre bandwagon with his attractive wife, he worked in private equity in Shanghai. Before he worked in private equity in Shanghai, he was reportedly <https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/international/us/who-is-kang-wei-the-chinese-fund-executive-reported-to-be-alice-huangs-husband-and-now-under-police-investigation-in-shanghai/articleshow/135740485.cms?utm_source=contentofinterest&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=cppst>a private banker at HSBC and worked for CITIC Securities. The WSJ suggests Kang and Alice were networking together and 'capitalizing on whatever connections were at hand.' Jensen Huang at NVIDA appears to have been one such opportunity.
This is one way to get ahead. Others working in financial services may be sympathetic - the Wall Street Discriminates <https://wallstreetdiscriminates.com/?s=affair> site is full of female complaints about workplace affairs, including affairs in which women use their influence for personal gain. One senior hedge fund manager wrote on LinkedIn that, "He [Huang] can have any woman and he knows it. Even if his wife dumps him, there will be a long queue of women. He simply got caught because of US surveillance."
Nvidia's issues could be far deeper than its philandering ex-CEO. Michael Burry, who has long been shorting the chipmaker, notes that <https://michaeljburry.substack.com/p/say-it-aint-so-nvidia-on-fire-read?utm_source=substack&publication_id=6819723&post_id=224704486&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoxMjQ4ODg0LCJwb3N0X2lkIjoyMjQ3MDQ0ODYsImlhdCI6MTc5NDU1MjU2NSwiZXhwIjoxNzk3MTQ0NTY1LCJpc3MiOiJwdWItNjgxOTcyMyIsInN1YiI6InBvc3QtcmVhY3Rpb24ifQ.FxzDHFMdKQpR6MFOeXhQYAOOhDiHcAiacfzDqlTFD6k&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>the WSJ says Jensen Huang called the meeting in August because of a 'ballooning problem:' 'Nvidia was in talks to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips.'
Having affairs, including with a woman in an apparently open marriage, may turn out to be immaterial compared to what eventually transpires.
Separately, these are complicated times. They may even be the most complicated times yet.
Speaking to Bloomberg, <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-13/treasury-yield-surge-shatters-hopes-worst-of-bond-rout-is-over?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261113&utm_campaign=author_21122136> one macro fund manager said: “This is a tougher environment than during the Covid pandemic and the global financial crisis.” Unpredictability is the issue: "It’s about rolling supply shocks and wild rates volatility. We still have to be on alert for higher yields all the way till year end.”
Many portfolio managers have already found themselves on the wrong side of recent volatility. Funds are still hiring though, including at very senior levels. </news/point72-hired-a-major-macro-pm-from-millennium-in-london-and-all-is-well>
Meanwhile...
Citadel macro PM Kevin Storey left in 2022 to found a healthcare company. Now he's returned. (X) <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2120965276271538291/photo/1>
IMC trading plans to double its headcount in Hong Kong. “Once we started hiring, we found strong people across options, ETFs and futures, alongside systematic equities. So Hong Kong now hires for all of them.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-12/quant-trading-firm-imc-plans-to-double-staff-in-hong-kong>
Adrian Bracher left UBS and joined RBC Capital Markets as global head of macro and spread products structuring. (Fi-Desk) <https://www.fi-desk.com/bracher-joins-rbc-cm/>
Marex hired three directors for its cash equities business in Paris. (The Trade News) <https://www.thetradenews.com/marex-adds-trio-of-directors-to-paris-cash-equities-sales-trading-team/>
Scott Bessent is now living on a miltary base after threats to his life connected to Iran. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/politics/national-security/bessent-moved-to-military-base-after-threats-linked-to-iran-95cfced1?utm_campaign=mrf-twitter-WSJ&utm_source=twitter&utm_medium=social&mrfcid=202611126af5fd4ea029f850eaeba9ec>
Christopher Woolcott owned shares in Touchstone Exploration and he wanted them to higher so he concocted a fake bid for it using AI. He even met Paul Baay, the Touchstone chief executive, at a central London hotel, when he pretended to be a representative of the fake bidder and adopted an American accent. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/fraudster-avoids-jail-over-fake-154m-takeover-bid-mzbx6gj95>
UBS banker: "The moment to step away has arrived...The circumstances surrounding that transition were not entirely of my choosing, but what I do with the opportunity now before me is increasingly mine to determine." (Sean Cochran) <https://www.seancochrannorthstar.com/articles/knowing-when-to-step-away?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=ns001_knowing_when_to_step_away>

item.title: Tower Research hired a sales trader from a struggling rival for its fixed income push
item.description:
Major electronic trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> like Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>and Hudson River Trading </news/the-coffee-run-the-kind-trading-firm-paying-1m-to-graduates-and-100m-to-its-top-people>have been celebrating record trading revenues </news/jane-street-employees> in recent years, but not all trading firms have had such a great time. Publicly traded market maker Flow Traders has seen its stock price fall ~10% this year due to lacklustre results, including an 84% decrease in profit <https://uk.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/flow-traders-q3-2026-slides-profit-drops-84-amid-lower-volatility-93CH-4940504>from Q2 to Q3. Several senior salespeople left the firm before this year's woes, one of whom has just emerged at a competitor.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Asad Zanjani has been hired by New York-based Tower Research Capital as its head of institutional sales trading supporting its recent push into fixed income trading. He was most recently Flow Traders' Americas head of institutional sales and trading, but left the firm at the start of December according to his FINRA profile.
Fixed income is an area of keen interest for Tower Research; the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/ac9b1a01-16fb-43e0-9e6d-1bb5037d180c?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported in June that it was quoting prices in over 500 fixed-income ETFs, up from just 30 nine months prior.
Zanjani spent eight years with Flow Traders, but only held his most recent role for six months. It was previously held by Brett Sussman </news/optiver-s-hiring-spree-includes-a-head-of-ai-from-apple-and-a-jp-morgan-trader> who departed in June 2025 and emerged at Optiver in May.
Flow Traders' US sales team may be just fine without Zanjani and Sussman. Co-chief trading officer Alex Kieft said during the firm's Q3 earnings update that year-to-date net trading income was up 45%, bolstered by an increase to the firm's trading capital.
Tower Research declined to comment.

item.title: Boutique bank Evercore has a pair of new MDs. They’re rather interesting
item.description:
Being a managing director </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> (MD) in an investment bank is about as high as most banker could dream of reaching. And it is good, yes, but there is one thing better, if you’re a banker. Being an MD at not just an investment bank, but a boutique </news/boutique-investment-banks> investment bank. Like Evercore.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Noah Pottash joined Evercore in New York this week as an MD. He joined the boutique from Goldman Sachs in the city, where he spent almost a decade – four as an associate and six as a VP – and he was an auditor, of all things, at Deloitte before that.
Nicole Coffey joined Evercore as an MD too, in Washington DC. She joined the firm from Baird, the mid-market bank </news/2023/02/middle-market-banking-jobs>, with whom she spent nine years in the city. Coffey was already an MD at Baird before she left; clearly, Evercore considers some banks’ MDs to be equivalent to others’ VPs.
Becoming an MD at most banks is a major achievement. It’s the point at which your compensation, especially your bonus, explodes, because the bank is expecting you to bring in and manage clients. At Evercore, however, it’s a bit of a misdirection – the bank’s “real” MDs are its Senior Managing Directors, which fulfil much of the same role as other bank’s non-Senior MDs. Evercore still has VPs, however, making the MD title there more comparable to something like a director at other banks. Evercore did not respond to a request for comment on this article.
It’s a good time to join Evercore regardless of your title, however. The firm’s Q3 results </news/evercore-q3-2026> showed that its revenues are up by 38% in the first nine months of 2026 vs the same period in 2025, and it is on track to pay over $1.2m per head – on average. Senior managing director or not, it’s a very pretty penny.

item.title: The weird universities that will get you a hedge fund job in Abu Dhabi
item.description:
What’s the best university for a career in finance? It’s a subject of much debate. You could consult the list of UK target and semi-target universities </news/target-universities-finance-uk>, for example. Well, they can all move aside, because there might only be one real ranking in town: the UAE Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research’s list of universities whose graduates are eligible for the Abu Dhabi Golden Visa.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
The Abu Dhabi Golden Visa is a self-sponsored scheme by which productive and/or rich members of society can move to the UAE and enjoy its sweet, sweet culture and climate (and tax rate). You can get it through a few paths, such as investment in property, or by being the right kind of graduate.
What is the right kind of graduate? Well, it’s one who has graduated from a bachelor’s degree within the last two years, has a GPA of 3.5 out of 4.0 (or equivalent), and has attended one of 100 universities on a list published by the UAE itself. We’ve reproduced the list in full below.
It’s weird. For some reason, the Emirati government double-counted the University of Warwick in the UK and the University of Washington in the US. So there are actually only 98 universities on the list, although it’s unclear if the two UoWs were double counted because they were better perceived by the UAE. Probably not.
The other weird thing is that the list is a relatively straight copy of QS’ 2022 Rankings <https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings/2022?tab=indicators>, but with some changes; Duke University in the US was removed, TU Munich in Germany was removed, and Paris-Saclay was removed (the original Top 100 was actually a Top 101 due to ties). It’s unclear why these three universities were removed.
Some quirks were more sad than anything else. No universities from the Middle East were on the list. Or universities in India, despite the strength of its IIMs/IITs historically. Or Africa. More than half of the universities were in just three Anglophone countries: the USA (27 of them), the UK (17 of them), and Australia (7 of them).
Some of the choices, being based on QS’ rankings, are also odd. In the UK at least, Sheffield, Leeds, and Southampton are on the list, and none of these are target universities, but Nottingham, Bath, and Exeter are not on the list, and all of these are all semi-target universities </news/target-universities-finance-uk>. In the US, all of the Ivy leagues are represented except Dartmouth. In Europe, there is no Bocconi, St Gallen, or HEC. All three are very much top tier universities.
Luckily, if you’ve attended a university off the list, you can still get a job in Abu Dhabi. Brevan Howard has built its Abu Dhabi office up to 150 people, and Rokos Capital Management secured a full licence there this year, among others. As far as we know, neither of them base their campus recruitment on QS’ rankings.

item.title: The cautionary tale of the hedge fund quant and the $30m he does not have
item.description:
As we reported yesterday </news/cubist-hedge-fund-contract>, there is some beef between Cubist, the quant </news/biggest-quant-hedge-funds>trading arm of hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Point72, and Xin Jin, a former research lead there. Cubist says Jin used AI tools to steal its source code for eventual use at a rival. Jin says he did not.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Yesterday, Jin filed <https://civilinquiry.jud.ct.gov/CaseDetail/PublicCaseDetail.aspx?DocketNo=FSTCV266084763S> his own affidavit and 'memo in opposition' to Cubist's claims. There, Jin categorically denies that he ever "misused Cubist's Confidential Information, used AI tools to take or misuse it, or "exfiltrated" any of the AI output."
Jin says his use of Cubist's AI tools was for his work at Cubist. The accompanying memo says his job at the fund ‘included monitoring and improving model performance, combining existing models, and generating new ideas for research and conducting that research, all of which required him to understand every model the team used or was developing.’ In his affidavit, Jin says reading, reviewing and improving the team’s code and research "was my job.”
Jin also claims that many of the 4,117 individual queries that Cubist says he used to extract information via Claude Code and Codex were written by AI agents and that to the extent that he "repeatedly" deleted prompt history and output folders, this was simply him deleting AI hallucinations or responses that weren't useful, rather than him attempting to conceal anything.
Cubist's own complaint accused Jin of "data mining and synthesizing other people’s work at Cubist in order to refine it and use it at a rival.”
Most notably, Jin wants the $30m that he says Cubist owes him for compensation and investments made during the time that he worked there. He says that more than $20m of this is in the form of shares that he was "required to purchase" with his bonuses. Jin claims that Cubist seems to be treating this money as forfeited because it fired him for cause. He was fired two days after disclosing that he had accepted another job.
A spokesperson for Cubist said: "The claims in this filing are without merit. We brought this action to protect confidential information, and we will respond in the appropriate legal forum."

item.description:
As we have noted, it has been a painful time </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> to be a macro portfolio manager at a fund in London. James Whittingham from Millennium has one too. It's understood that he has left Millennium and is on his way to Point72 where he will run a large new macro pod.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Whittingham spent six years at Millennium after 14 years at Goldman Sachs, where he was a managing director in STIR trading in London. At Goldman, it's thought that he managed Stanley Sheriff, </news/star-ex-goldman-sachs-trader-retires-aged-33-following-eight-year-hedge-fund-career> the 33-year-old portfolio manager who recently left Balyasny.

Whittingham's move suggests ongoing demand for major macro PMs in London, even after a difficult year. It may also suggest the possibility of starting somewhere else with a clean slate and large guarantee after a seasonal rest.

item.title: Portfolio managers are safe from AI. Analysts are not
item.description:
AI is all the rage. And while Anthropic is gearing up its IPO for next week, the asset managers </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-asset-management> who will debate the firm’s place in client portfolios are quietly stressing about their own role in the industry, courtesy of the new technologies displacing them.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
A recent report from the Alternative Investment Management Association (AIMA) – a trade organization that acts a bit like CFA Institute for the buy-side – found unwavering confidence from the industry’s portfolio managers, an substantially less from its analysts.
74% of buy-side professionals polled by AIMA thought that portfolio managers were the profession least likely to be impacted by generative AI. Amusingly, none of them at all thought that portfolio management was the most exposed profession. On an unrelated note, JPMorgan built AI agents that beat 60/40 portfolios earlier this year, Bloomberg reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-09/jpmorgan-builds-ai-agents-that-beat-60-40-portfolio-in-backtests>.
The least safe, or perhaps the most pessimistically viewd about their role in the world, were professionals working administrative tasks. That’s hardly a surprise, as banks are pretty open about how AI can replace them. Really, it’s a slight surprise that 9% of them think they are the safest people in the industry.
Close behind administrative professionals however, and much more strangely, was investment analysts. “If Gen AI assumes more junior analytical work,” AIMA’s report asked, “firms may need new ways to give future portfolio managers the experience through which investment judgement has traditionally developed.”
It’s a reasonable proposition, although it is one that has been put forward before. Jeremy Leung, a T. Rowe Price AI solutions manager and former UBS portfolio manager, wrote in March 2026 <https://aimightbewrong.substack.com/p/ai-future-of-asset-management> that the time analysts spend “reading hundreds of filings, updating endless models, listening to management teams quarter after quarter” was disappearing. AI was changing that and making the role more “barbell-shaped”, with a “smaller number of genuinely high-leverage analysts at one end, and a more standardised, system-mediated research function at the other.” Analysts, perhaps ye need not fret.
In the middle of AIMA’s survey were technology </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank>, compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance>, and legal professionals. Curiously, despite being relatively split on AI’s impact in the report, these are generally considered as the professions most at risk of AI displacement.

item.title: Kalshi is offering $10k a month for 70+ hour weeks... playing GTA VI
item.description:
Kalshi </news/prediction-markets-jobs-kalshi-polymarket?_gl=1*13ifjcn*_up*MQ..*_ga*Nzk1OTc3MTc2LjE3OTQ0ODI5NDg.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3OTQ0ODI5NDgkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ0ODI5NDgkajYwJGwwJGg1MjYxMjk5OTM.> is no stranger to gimmicks when hiring. Last Christmas, it was hiring for a marketing executive with a salary range of $50k to $8m. </news/tarek-mansour-kalshi-sam-bankman-fried-ftx> It's back again this year with a role so unusual that it had to preface the listing with the fact that it's a "real job": the prediction markets </news/traders-earning-1m-on-kalshi-are-offered-double-or-nothing-to-join-trading-firms?_gl=1*13ifjcn*_up*MQ..*_ga*Nzk1OTc3MTc2LjE3OTQ0ODI5NDg.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3OTQ0ODI5NDgkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ0ODI5NDgkajYwJGwwJGg1MjYxMjk5OTM.> firm is offering up to $10k a month for one person to play GTA VI.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Kalshi wants a 'GTA VI Researcher' with over three years of video game streaming experience, preferably with a finance or economics degree. </news/best-qualifications-for-banking-jobs> They will be streaming the game from its launch at midnight next Thursday, focusing specifically on the in-game economy of its fictional US state, Leonida. The role is on a contract basis and pays equivalent to a salary of $100k to $120k.
The researcher will release weekly reports on this while also studying the real-world economic effects of the GTA VI launch. There has been fearmongering from some analysts that the launch could cost the US economy $1bn due to the volume of people taking days off to play it at launch.
In addition to the $10k monthly pay, the researcher will get a $15k "streaming bonus," a 100-inch TV and $75 daily for food deliveries. While it says you're expected to take the overall project at your own pace, you will be expected to have an "eagerness to play 10+ hours per day during the launch push," not including the additional work on the reports.
This might seem like overspending (and it might be), but open GTA VI-related markets have a total volume of over $12m on Kalshi. Kalshi relies on highly liquid markets like these and sports </news/quants-sports-betting> to help fund the 'truth machine' markets it uses to distance itself from traditional gambling companies. </news/22-year-old-goldman-alum-at-kalshi-branded-the-coffee-boy-by-gaming-exec-feuding-with-the-ceo> Kalshi enlists 'designated market makers,' including major trading firms, which receive incentives like lower transaction fees in their usual trading activity in exchange for making markets in smaller, illiquid areas. The firm has had an ongoing legal battle with several state governments in the US to exempt prediction markets from state gambling laws (and the associated fees and taxes).

item.title: Hedge fund Balyasny is amassing new people to keep a handle on its international business
item.description:
It's a difficult year for many hedge funds and this includes Balyasny Asset Management, which was down 2.7% after fees </news/hedge-fund-performance-2026>in the year to September and then another 3.4% (before fees) in October.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Balyasny's bad year comes after Balyasny's big hiring. Last year, it added 157 investment staff globally and 371 people in total. Its most recently filed ADV form reveals 192 London staff in investment advisory functions and 60 and 61 in Hong Kong and Singapore respectively.
As Balyasny grows internationally, it's putting guardrails in place. As we noted </news/goldman-sachs-people-are-leaving-and-declaring-that-it-s-all-been-incredible> earlier this week, it's hired Risa Lederhandler from Goldman Sachs as its first ever COO for Europe. Bloomberg <https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/balyasny-hires-goldman-partner-lederhandler-for-new-top-role> reported Lederhandler's hiring in May, but it seems she has only just arrived. She will sit on Balyasny's management committee.
Lederhandler is not Balyasny's only management hire. The fund has also hired Andrew Tsai from PDT Partners as CEO of its international business. This also appears to be a new role, and will also be based in London. Tsai has also just arrived.
And in Hong Kong, Balyasny is understood to have a new Asia COO starting next week in the form of Aleem Jivraj, the former COO for global markets at Nomura.
Balyasny declined to comment for this article. The new hires reflect the need for greater structure as Balyasny increases headcount. In what has been a challenging year for the firm so far, they may also reflect a desire for greater scrutiny of costs.

item.title: Doing an aptitude test? Trust your instincts, unless you’re an accountant
item.description:
Do you have an aptitude test coming up? It’s very possible. They’re not super common for senior hires (although some banks, such as UBS, do do them), but they’re very common for student hires. What do you do when one shows up in your inbox?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
If you’re like most people, you’re probably rushing them. It’s understandable; they feel like threading a needle. They’re a pain, they’re meant to test your intellectual instinct anyway, they have a low pass threshold… So why not just rush it, even if you get a slightly lower score than usual?
Well, about that. You might not get a lower score than usual. Research from Practice Aptitude Tests <https://www.practiceaptitudetests.com/> – which hosts a number of practice packs – found that, across some 3.8 million aptitude test sittings, the slowest test takers don’t always get the best scores.
If you have a mechanical, inductive, or deductive reasoning test for example, it can benefit you significantly to do the test quickly. Practice Aptitude Tests says that the score gap between the fastest and slowest test takers (quartiles, not maxima/minima) was between 20 and 25 points in favour of the faster test takers. The Watson Glaser test, which is popular with law students, also favoured quick respondents.
Not all tests favoured quick takers. Numerical reasoning and financial reasoning, for example, were completed with higher scores by slower test takers than quick ones. And if you want to be a police officer, accountant, or correctional officer, it also helps to take your time doing the test.
Banks use a mix of these tests on student applicants. Morgan Stanley, UBS, and Nomura </news/graduate-banking-job-cheating> are known to set numerical and verbal reasoning tests, and Morgan Stanley's </news/2021/09/psychometric-tests-morgan-stanley> also cover deductive and logical reasoning. You'll likely get both kinds in one go. Take your time on the numbers, and don't stress over pattern recognition. Others skip the tests altogether - JPMorgan used to have </news/2019/08/jpmorgan-pymetrics> games for students to play, for example.
And if you think your future career in finance is competitive, you might be surprised. According to Practice Aptitude Tests <https://www.practiceaptitudetests.com/aptitude-test-score-report/>, the most difficult tests – the ones with the lowest average scores – included nursing, air traffic, firefighting, and law. Fine company.
