item.title: Morning Coffee: A 31-year-old trader ignored by finance recruiters is the new sensation. Switzerland is the new Dubai for bankers
item.description:
If you’re trying to break into the world of hedge fund trading, but you don’t go to a “target school”, then you’re going to have a difficult time. Only a small number of the biggest funds have a graduate program, and they tend to almost exclusively recruit from the top ranked universities. The rest of the industry usually hires more experienced people to be portfolio managers and traders, and it gets them by poaching from the sell side or from other funds; in other words, the route still has to run through an elite school. If you’re a finance major at a small Christian college, like Christian Lamarco <https://www.wsj.com/business/nvidia-short-seller-culper-jensen-huang-0e0cec38?mod=mhp>, you need to get creative.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Even that doesn’t necessarily work. Lamarco thought he might be able to show that he was the equal of Ivy League graduates by entering a national stock-picking contest and coming second. But it seems Wall Street kept passing him over; he eventually got a job at an (unnamed) long-short equity fund in Chicago and stayed there for two years. Then he decided that he needed to make his own luck, and founded Culper Research, a short-selling operation.
Lamarco seems to have done quite well in that tricky investment style – he won an award from Activist Insight in 2025. He achieved an active and vocal community of haters on Reddit <https://poliscio.com/some-research-into-short-seller-culper-research/>, a badge of honour for any short seller, and he had two employees. But nothing had really caught fire until back in May, when Lamarco published a short-seller report on Nvidia, talking about the company having a “China problem” and speculating about an “uncomfortably close” relationship between the CEO and an executive at one of its customers.
That speculation appears to have been pretty close to the mark <https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgel338xql3o>, and Nvidia stock has fallen from over $220 to around $180 (so far; the news came out yesterday that the board is investigating another affair <https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-affair.html> as well). Culper’s research has gone viral, and he has spent the last week avoiding social media and turning down TV interview requests.
So does this mean that he will now be heading for the big leagues? Probably not. Hedge fund recruiters may now see him as “one that got away”, but Culper is established in his own fund and arguably doesn’t need the validation of a big multistrategy firm behind him.
Short selling is also an approach that doesn’t necessarily work well in an institutional environment, as most of the targets are much smaller than Nvidia, meaning that it’s hard to deploy capital. The research involved requires a lot of time and effort, and the subjects of reports often get litigious. Although the returns can be good and are largely uncorrelated to the market, they are lumpy and volatile. It’s a lot easier to manage this kind of business if you’re your own boss. So Christian Lamarco will probably just wait out his brief period of fame, and then go back to lucrative anonymity.
Elsewhere, the Alps have always had an appeal to tourists from the Gulf states. Interlaken in Switzerland <https://worldcrunch.com/food-travel/interlaken-the-new-swiss-mecca-for-rich-muslim-tourists/> and Zell-am-See in Austria <https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/gallery/2015/jul/20/zell-am-see-austrian-village-muslim-holiday-hotspot-in-pictures> have marketed their crystal lakes and lush pastures as a welcome change of scene from the desert. Now it seems that the mountain paradises are attempting to appeal to bankers too <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-11/headhunter-pitches-switzerland-to-mideast-bankers-eager-to-leave?srnd=homepage-americas>.
If you are based in Dubai and have $500m or more of client assets under management, a Swiss recruitment firm is saying that “You and your esteemed customers” are invited to “take full advantage of the world-famous Swiss Private Banking paradigm that provides both safety and professional excellence even during extremely challenging times”. This is a somewhat euphemistic reference to the geopolitical risk situation. And although it seems that most bankers and hedge fund managers are largely unfazed </news/dubai-hedge-fund-managers-are-unphased-by-the-war-the-uae-could-come-out-very-strongly-from-this>, Jürg Knecht at headhunters Oprandi & Partner is betting that some of them, possibly those with young families, might consider relocating to a country with nicer neighbours.
Anyone making the move may find that the income tax rate is significantly greater than zero (even in famously low-tax cantons like Zug <https://nomadcapitalist.com/finance/switzerlands-canton-of-zug-tax-rates/>), and the nightlife is not quite as lively. But the skiing is obviously a lot better, and the luxury shopping opportunities are about the same. And you don’t have to worry so much about living next door to an influencer.
Meanwhile …
After scaling back in Hong Kong over the last three years, Nomura is apparently now holding internal discussions about beginning to hire again and build back its equity capital markets franchise. The company is not commenting, but its reduced presence has probably hurt Nomura in Asian league tables given the strength of the Hong Kong IPO market. (Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/nomura-weighs-rebuilding-its-hong-kong-equity-capital-markets-business-sources-2026-11-11/>)
Squarepoint Capital has its roots in quant trading, but a couple of years ago it set up a metal trading subsidiary and now it’s trying to make long term deals for part of the output of a tin mining company in the Democratic Republic of Congo. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-11/metals-trader-backed-by-quants-in-talks-to-secure-congo-tin-deal?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261111&utm_campaign=author_22490032>)
Hamza Lemssouguer is showing the steely nerve that makes a good trader; despite the problems at Arini Capital, he has exchanged contracts on a $40m Georgian town house on Belgrave Square. This is separate from the other premium property deal he made to move Arini’s head office into expensive new premises in Mayfair; he must be quite bullish on London real estate. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/1c44cb5e-68ff-4396-a906-0bb6161e02d6?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Rob Pulford will be retiring from Goldman Sachs, after nearly 20 years at the bank during which he reached the position of co-head of the global financial and strategic investors’ group. He moved to a vice-chairman role last year. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/goldman-sachs-financial-sponsors-dealmaker-rob-pulford-to-retire-72f42120?mod=topic_news>)
“We asked ourselves, ‘Do we need other humans? Won’t they just slow us down?’”. It is now possible to launch an entire company without any employees, as long as you don’t mind sounding a bit weird. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/d338594b-ca66-418a-9884-8f562a175fed?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
You might think that your work email inbox is mostly garbage and the Teams or Slack chat even worse, but AI companies regard it all as potentially valuable training data. The mind boggles at what an AI trained on bankers’ WhatsApp groups and Bloomberg chats might be like. (WIRED <https://www.wired.com/story/ai-companies-really-really-want-to-buy-your-work-files-and-emails/>)

item.title: The 32 hedge funds currently thriving by Ken Griffin's measure. The 32 currently not
item.description:
Four months ago, Ken Griffin explained </news/ken-griffin-hedge-fund> what he thinks it takes for hedge funds to attract money from investors.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Speaking to Goldman Sachs, the Citadel CEO and founder said that for the money to "flow in" the equilibrium return must be 4% plus the risk free cost of capital.
This year, many funds are not achieving that.
If this risk free cost of capital is determined as the rate paid on three month Treasury bills, Griffin's current hedge fund hurdle rate is around 8.2%. Based on figures from Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/rokos-joins-biggest-hedge-funds-losing-money-in-october-turmoil?srnd=undefined>, the chart below shows which funds had generated year-to-date returns minus fees that were above this in the year to September, and which funds had not.
Based on Griffin's implied 8.2% hurdle, Citadel's Wellington fund will be among those favoured by investors for its performance through to September. So will DE Shaw and Point72. But other multistrategy hedge funds, including Millennium, Schonfeld, ExodusPoint, Verition, Brevan Howard, Balyasny and Walleye, will not be.
The chart below also includes single strategy hedge funds like Rokos (macro), Marshall Wace (equities), Arini (credit) and Taula (macro). They too are all below the Griffin threshold.
After October's macro fund meltdown </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up>relating to French bonds, after the pain in credit funds as risk premiums rise </news/european-high-yield>, and after last Thursday's nightmare in which Barry Ritholtz <https://ritholtz.com/2026/11/thoughts-on-the-selloff/> says there was a "huge, leveraged growth unwind by the major multi-strategy hedge funds," which found themselves caught in a "crowded, systematic, long-leveraged growth equity trade," annualised returns may yet get far worse.
What does this mean for portfolio managers, analysts and others who might want to work for the funds in red? In the short term, not much. Griffin said the risk free rate plus 4% is the long run equilibrium point. Funds typically have investors' money locked in and will have an opportunity to redeem themselves with improved returns in the future.
At multistrategy firms, four to five year lock-ups are common. Millennium, for example, raised $3.7bn for a share class with a five-year lock-up in 2019, and is moving other investors onto those terms. Arini, which was down 33% to September has funds locked in for an average of two years according to Rupak Ghose. <https://rupakghose.substack.com/p/arini-in-the-headlines>"The fund has the structural duration of capital to see these investments through to their catalysts,” said Arini founder Hamza Lemssouguer last year.
In the long term, though, persistent low performance will become problematic.
This year's poor performance is leading some to question how it is that so many multistrategy funds - which are supposed to make uncorrelated bets and so be immune to market turbulence - have lost money. Bloomberg journalist Nishant Kumar <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/audio/2026-11-11/odd-lots-the-perfect-storm-that-clobbered-hedge-funds-podcast>has suggested it was the result of crowded trades. Ritholtz reported it was "forced liquidations" as 108 separate pods were closed and unwound, resulting in the forced selling of leveraged bets after individual pods' risk limits were breached.
In theory, individual portfolio managers sitting in independent "pods" at multistrategy funds are autonomous entities. In reality, the fund as a whole will likely operate within tighter risk limits when it's been burned. Either way, the poor performance through to September puts pressure on funds to perform better in the final months of the year and into 2027.
If you want an easier ride, you might want to join a fund in green above the Griffin hurdle.

item.title: Point72 hired this quant on $400k. He says it’s withholding $30m+
item.description:
If you are a quant thinking of joining Cubist, the quant </news/biggest-quant-hedge-funds>trading arm of hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Point72, or you are a quant or portfolio manager currently at Point72, you might want to pay attention to the unfolding court case <https://civilinquiry.jud.ct.gov/CaseDetail/PublicCaseDetail.aspx?DocketNo=FSTCV266084763S>involving Xin Jin and Cubist Systematic Strategies.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Jin joined Point72 in 2019. He was recruited as a research analyst reporting to Lei Xu, head of Cubist's KEPL multi-asset systematic trading team which specialises in medium-frequency statistical arbitrage.
Jin's 2019 offer letter, included in court documents filed against Jin <https://assets.bwbx.io/documents/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/rPlWGJPfoefA/v0>by Point72, shows that he received a salary of $175k, a $50k signing bonus and a minimum $175k bonus in his first year. The signing bonus was repayable if he left voluntarily or was terminated for cause during the first year. The $175k bonus was payable in early 2021 as long as he was still working there. Anything above that was discretionary.
Jin only left Cubist/Point72 in 2026. On September 16th, he told the firm he'd accepted an offer from a rival firm. Two days later, Cubist fired him for cause, claiming that he had used AI tools to copy its source code.
Jin has yet to file his affidavit for the case, but his lawyer told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/point72-claims-fired-quant-analyst-used-ai-tools-to-steal-code>the accusations are without merit. In an initial filing, Jin said he'd been working with Cubist for three months "at his own expense" and through counsel on a forensic "preservation and return process in which Cubist itself participated." As part of this process, Jin said "every relevant device and account has been forensically imaged and is preserved." He claims that Cubist had proposed mediation, but suddenly filed the case against him.
Most notably, after seven years with the fund, Jin says Cubist owes him over $30m "in investments and compensation wrongfully withheld." Cubist declined to comment on what this comprises. Jin's lawyer declined to comment for this article. It is thought that some of that sum may relate to money that Jin had coinvested in Point72's own funds. If so, this looks like a cautionary tale for hedge fund employees everywhere who have reinvested with their employers.
For its part, Cubist says Jin conducted 4,117 queries across 2,416 sessions with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex between February 28 and May 31, 2026, and that nearly half were outside normal working hours or at weekends. It details over 60 prompts on 8 different days which were issued by Jin and which it says were aimed at cataloguing and extracting a colleague's research. It's not clear whether these prompts were directly made by Jin himself or by sub-agents working on his behalf.
Point72's filing says: “As now confirmed by the contents of his personal devices, Jin plainly was data mining and synthesizing other people’s work at Cubist in order to refine it and use it at a rival.” It claims that Jin prompted Claude Code to distil information he'd extracted into "textbook-style chapters for portability, including an eighteen-month '"study plan" for recreating them," which is says Jin planned to study during his gardening leave. The fund says it monitors employees AI prompts and their outputs.
Jin is expected to make a full filing later today explaining why he disagrees with Cubist's claims.
Jin's new role is not due to begin until June 2028, after his non-compete expires. He is having some time out. It might be more fun if he had $30m in the bank.

item.title: Goldman Sachs' most bizarre interview question is going viral again
item.description:
There are hundreds of questions you can expect in a Goldman Sachs interview </news/goldman-sachs-interview-questions>. Some, like 'Why Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs>?' are easy enough to anticipate. Some are much more bizarre.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
An interview question asked by the bank to its quants </news/quant-jobs-finance> has recently gone viral on X <https://x.com/MercuriusFilius/status/2120154542037704770>. The question (which we were first to report on in 2024 </news/the-unusual-riddle-goldman-sachs-might-ask-you-in-a-quant-job-interview>) reads as follows:
"In a room there are 253 lions and one steak. The steak is poisoned, so that if a Lion eats the steak, it will fall asleep. While asleep, the other lions will treat it the same as they would treat the steak. If another lion eats the poisoned lion, it too will fall asleep. Each lion behaves perfectly rationally. Do any of the lions eat the steak?"
The quant we spoke to who was asked this question said that a lion will eat the steak because there is an odd number of lions overall. A single lion would eat the steak with no repercussions whereas, if there were two lions, neither would eat the steak for fear of being eaten themselves. If there were three lions, one would eat the steak knowing the logic of two lions would apply to the remaining lions after it did so. This logic continues eternally, meaning that a lion will always eat the steak on an odd number, but avoid it on an even.
Several responses <https://x.com/richabbs1/status/2120424140888764430?a=wLHIWJyhPEX3QfD8znE&s=20> came to the same conclusion, but these questions are obtuse by design and encourage interpretation. Several people noted that, while the lions behave perfectly rationally, they may not have perfect information. While the phrasing of the question sometimes notes that the lions are aware of the poison, it did not in this instance. The lions also may not know the total number of lions in the room, thus may not be able to tell whether the total is odd or even.
Robert Yang, a former MIT professor, </news/jane-street-target-universities> said "what's actually interesting is to see how many holes someone can poke about the assumptions." Alongside questioning whether the lions have perfect information, Yang questioned the utility of the steak versus the utility of eating a lion and asked whether the lions could communicate with each other.
obvious answer is that no lion eats when there's an even number of lions, and 1 lion eats when odd number but what's actually interesting is to see how many holes someone can poke about the assumptions rational lion for n lion with 1 poisoned food (steak or a sleeping lion) n=1, eat & sleep soundly n=2, no one eats. if you eat, then you are food in n=1 n=3, one eats, then we back to n=2 no one eats ... game theory lion - lions are rational, but is this shared knowledge? - can lions talk to each other? - is this a repeatable game? will there be steak tomorrow? economics lion - what is the utility of the steak? is it juicy? - what is the utility of eating a lion? it's gross, no? bio lion - how long does it take for the lion to fall asleep? is it long enough for it to run home? philosophy lion - what's the essence of a poisonous steak? if a lion takes just a bite, does it fall asleep? quantum lion - who's observing the result and can lion eat the observer instead? corporate lion - does the management want the lion to eat? i can make it happen either way founder lion - the biggest lion will just eat all other lions first and then eat the steak
— Robert Yang (@GuangyuRobert) November 11, 2026 <https://x.com/GuangyuRobert/status/2120401293181329845?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw>
Many responses (presumably from non-quants) questioned what the point is of asking such an absurd question. These types of brainteaser are also common in algorithmic trading firms </news/electronic-trading-interviews> and are designed to see whether you can make decisions under pressure while explaining your reasoning. The process is usually more important than the result.
Do you think the traditional answer to this question is right or wrong? Let us know in the comments.

item.title: Anthropic hired Goldman Sachs' ex-chief security architect from Google
item.description:
Generally, when technical talent moves from financial services to an AI lab, </news/the-difference-between-working-as-a-quant-in-finance-and-as-a-researcher-in-an-ai-lab> it's quants </news/quant-jobs-finance>and engineers </news/highest-paying-tech-jobs-london>from trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> making the switch. Hires from banking are much more rare, but David LaBianca is the exception that proves the rule. After 12 years at Goldman Sachs, then six at Google, he is now headed to Anthropic. </news/anthropic-s-product-team-is-led-by-ex-bankers-and-traders-this-is-who-it-s-hiring>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
LaBianca joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff working on security engineering. At Google he was a senior director of security engineering. At Goldman Sachs, he was an MD as well as the bank's chief cybersecurity architect according to a profile for cybersecurity conference RSAC. LaBianca was also a technical fellow at Goldman, a title bestowed upon the bank's most technically capable VPs, MDs and partners. Miruna Stratan, a Goldman Sachs partner, told Business Insider in 2024 that tech fellows have been "at the centre of all the major business transformations through technology since the program began."
Anthropic seems the natural choice for LaBianca, given the lab's historic focus on AI safety. Cybersecurity was one of the first things mentioned by Anthropic this week when it released its new models, Mythos and Fable 5.2. <https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2>Fable has been built with "strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse," while the underlying model behind both Mythos and Fable underwent "extensive prerelease safety testing."
LaBianca will presumably get the chance to earn some Anthropic stock as part of his package. Unlike other finance professionals who left for the firm years ago, he may not have to wait too long for it to pay out. Anthropic has officially submitted documents to the SEC this week to start the process of its initial public offering at a valuation of up to $1.4tn <https://www.ft.com/content/26fd23df-830e-481b-a3bc-19bcab48c5f6>. Bankers told the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/68bcba57-0575-44ee-80f4-2e5ea23a431e?syn-25a6b1a6=1>a day after the filing that the valuation could rise again to $1.5tn due to excess demand. Considering Anthropic was valued closer to $18bn in 2024 <https://techcrunch.com/2024/05/13/anthropic-is-expanding-to-europe-and-raising-more-money/>, Anthropic's other employees will presumably deem the longer wait worth it.
The traffic between finance and AI isn't entirely one way. Another Google employee within its AI lab, Deepmind, </news/balyasny-ai-hiring-google-deepmind> recently left for a hedge fund; Nataniel Ruiz, a PhD computer scientist and Deepmind researcher has joined Citadel's equity quantitative research team. His historic focus has been on generative photo and video models, suggesting he might try to use AI to get quantitative insights from alternative video data.
Anthropic, Google and Citadel declined to comment.

item.title: Bank of America’s newest FIG banker came courtesy of Barclays
item.description:
Banks have been doing great this year – both traders and bankers have enjoyed bumper years. But it’s not just big banks that are hot, and non-bank lenders are growing too, even if the financing they need is a bit different.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
David MacGown joined Bank of America this month as Head of Americas Specialty Finance, based in New York. He joined the firm from Barclays, where he spent five years, and was also head of Americas specialty finance. He was at Credit Suisse before that - a few years ahead of the curve of all his colleagues that joined the British bank </news/2023/01/credit-suisse-clawbacks-job-cuts> when the Swiss one collapsed back in 2021.
Specialty finance is a type of asset-backed financing – pooling together car loans, credit card debt, equipment leases and the like and lending against them. MacGown’s background is in the financial institutions group (FIG) of banking, and while this usually means working with banks, specialty finance usually goes to non-bank lenders. Bank of America did not respond to a request for comment.
Specialty finance is doing reasonably well. A market update from Houlihan Lokey earlier this year <https://cdn.hl.com/pdf/2026/spring-2026-specialty-finance-market-update.pdf> noted that M&A transaction value in specialty finance was $59.5bn across 2025, and transaction value was up by 22% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. If that trend holds throughout 2026, transaction value should reach $73bn, although transaction count is set to decline.

item.title: Reports of hiring freezes at top banks are circulating
item.description:
Are you planning to sign a contract for a new job at a leading bank before Christmas? Good luck if so. There are suggestions that some banks are getting cold feet.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, one junior trader said he received a verbal offer to join a leading bank in New York, but that the offer was suddenly paused. The bank promised to resume discussions in the New Year. Hiring has been frozen, he said.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The bank concerned denied that it has a hiring freeze in place. It's conceivable that it only impacts a particular team. Multiple headhunters working on sales and trading mandates told us that they haven't encountered hiring freezes this year.
And yet hiring freezes are not unusual. Particularly among banks thinking of cutting jobs in the fourth quarter, of which there are many </news/only-goldman-sachs-jp-morgan-morgan-stanley-and-nomura-didn-t-mention-cost-cuts-in-q4> in 2026.
"Banks are still hiring on a case by case basis," says one London credit headhunter. "However, the usual end of year restrictions are being placed on offers and additional headcount." This is standard from mid-October, he says. "The hiring window gets shorter as people prepare for next year. The business may have a policy in place not to offer any guarantees if the intended joiner will only arrive in 2027 anyway."

item.title: How technical interviews for the most elite $850k quant finance jobs are changing
item.description:
Interviewing for a technical job </news/electronic-trading-interviews> in financial services used to involve hours of practicing LeetCode </news/goldman-sachs-interview-questions-software-engineer> questions but, in a post-AI world, how necessary is it to actually code in interviews? It depends on where you want to work.
For most corporate roles, AI has been banned in the interview process in recent years, but that has been changing. HackerRank has rolled out Chakra, </news/citi-analyst-program> an agentic AI interviewing system, which had reportedly conducted over 500,000 interviews during testing across companies like Capgemini and Snowflake as of October. This system permits the applicant to use AI as part of coding processes, and assesses how they interact with the tools. HackerRank CEO Vivek Ravisankar told TechCrunch <https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/05/hackerranks-ai-interviewer-offers-a-glimpse-into-what-job-interviews-could-become/?utm_medium=organic_social&utm_source=TWITTER> that "anybody can produce an artifact" but that interviews now need to assess why and how an applicant builds that artifact.
Chakra is not widespread in finance yet; Ravisankar told us that financial services firms are in the "early stages" of adopting Chakra, but "adoption is very strong in adding an AI assistant for their candidates and evaluating AI fluency."
For many hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> and prop trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>, where graduates can earn up to $1m, </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street> AI still seems to be taboo. One student currently interviewing for quant </news/quant-jobs-finance> roles across hedge funds and trading firms told us that interviews progress to on-sites much faster than they did in the past and that he has "never been allowed to use AI" during them "to prevent cheating."
Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> seems to be the exception: it released a blog post <https://blog.janestreet.com/software-engineering-interviews-are-changing-a-little/> this month describing how it "started trialling some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates" in this summer's recruitment cycle for which LLMs were permitted. The focus in these interviews is less on coding and more on "software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code." Usage of LLMs is also assessed.
Other than this new round, which was not used for each on-site, Jane Street said its interviews "haven’t changed." The focus is still on talking through a problem with an interviewer, and AI is usually not permitted. When we analyzed the type of LeetCode questions financial services firms ask </news/leetcode-questions-for-banks-hedge-funds-trading-firms>, we found that electronic trading firms asked a much higher proportion of easy questions than hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> and even banks. </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank>
Other firms may not be too far behind. Citadel Securities chief people officer Alex DiLeonardo told Fortune in August that judgement when using AI tools is a quality that employers "will increasingly look for as they recruit new talent." At a Semafor conference in April, DiLeonardo said that the firm looks at "AI skill" during campus hiring and looks at the "intrinsic capabilities that make [candidates] well suited to leverage AI tools." He did not say whether Citadel Securities had changed its interview process, however.
One way that other trading firms assess candidates are take-home assignments </news/fintech-engineers-beg-for-leetcode-over-time-consuming-alternative> which are more complex than standard coding problems. The student said these are more common, and that the approach to AI is more relaxed compared to on-sites. "If you can explain the code and take ownership," you can do well in these projects. If you can't, you won't. It's also increasingly common for trading firms to develop interactive games as part of the interview process to test candidates' decision making under pressure. The student said that, if you know someone who has played these games and can describe how they work, it's easy to reverse-engineer them using AI as part of your prep; some people have already done this and released their games for free online, like ex-commodities trading intern Deacon Larson, who released Crude Desk </news/the-video-game-that-will-prove-you-deserve-a-job-in-commodities-trading> last month.

item.title: Nomura's head of crypto derivatives trading swaps Dubai for a prop trading firm in Singapore
item.description:
As we have reported in the past, trading jobs in Dubai can be short-lived. </news/hedge-funds-dubai-abu-dhabi> Recent geopolitical conflicts </news/dubai-hedge-fund-managers-are-unphased-by-the-war-the-uae-could-come-out-very-strongly-from-this> between the UAE and Iran have only intensified this, but that's not the only reason people are leaving the city. One senior trader </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> in the crypto </news/2021/08/crypto-jobs> arm of a bank is leaving for a big new opportunity: to run a new crypto desk for a proprietary trading firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
John Kim has joined Chicago-based firm DV Trading in its Singapore office as the head of a new discretionary crypto trading team. He was most recently head of derivatives trading for Laser Digital, the digital asset arm of Japanese bank Nomura. His new team will operate through DV Chain, the firm's dedicated crypto arm, which was founded in 2016 but has historically focused on market making rather than discretionary strategies.
Kim only joined Laser in October 2025, but spent three years before that as head of derivatives trading for crypto investment bank Galaxy Digital. He was hired alongside two other traders in his team. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-10-06/nomura-crypto-unit-poaches-three-of-galaxy-s-derivatives-traders> Kim's hiring plans are unknown, but Luca Invernizzi, one of the other two hires, spoke publicly to CoinDesk <https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2026/10/18/bitcoin-s-usd100-000-year-end-hope-divides-analysts-as-inflation-clouds-outlook> last month as a Laser Digital representative, suggesting he won't be following Kim out the door again.
DV Trading, meanwhile, has grown its headcount to over 600 employees. CEO Jared Vegosen has been described as a "super smart and nice guy" in a 2016 Chicago Business <https://www.chicagobusiness.com/recognitions/40-under-40/2016/jared-vegosen/> profile; Vegosen himself started his career as a tech recruiter and real estate agent before getting into trading and told Chicago Business that "being smart was always cool in my life."

item.title: Morning Coffee: Nice, safe, high paying finance jobs have a little puke. The complicated bank chief with the deluxe private jet
item.description:
The good thing about buy-side jobs is that they tend to pay well. The bad thing is that your performance is usually very easy to measure, quite public, and often hard to make excuses for. So you don’t necessarily have much job security – there are plenty of managers at multi-strategy hedge funds who get massive bonuses one year, then have a few bad months, lose 7.5% and get cut.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
So the holy grail of investment careers is to find an employer that pays close to Wall Street, but which doesn’t have Wall Street’s aggressive nature. Historically, a good place to look for these kind of jobs has been in public sector pension funds </news/canadian-pension-plan-pay>, which don’t have to worry about fund redemptions and which often bid salaries and bonuses surprisingly high in an attempt to be “competitive” for talent.
All good things come to an end, though, and it seems that after years of reporting “a challenging environment for stock picking” and “unexpected changes in China”, the Canadian Pension Plan Investment Board <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/canada-s-top-pension-merges-active-equities-arm-lays-off-dozens?taid=6af3374ec6e521000183a1b8&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter> has finally lost patience with its active equities unit. Frank Ieraci, the head of the team, will be leaving and it will be merged with the capital markets unit. The big new department will be run by a woman, Heather Tobin.
However, this isn’t necessarily the end of the road. The active equities team employed 120 people, but the reorganisation is only going to involve “dozens” of layoffs. It seems that most of the staff will just move over to the new “Active Public Markets” department. So it looks like the risk / reward tradeoff has still turned out to be pretty good. And it’s a career strategy that might reproduce internationally – Stichting Pensioenfunds ABP <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-09/europe-s-biggest-pensions-manager-ends-active-equities-strategy?srnd=homepage-europe> has also closed down its active equities strategy, but this has only resulted in 40 redundancies out of a staff of more than a thousand.
Another favoured kind of employer for people who value job security has always been the head offices of big national-champion insurance companies. The French finance professionals at AXA <https://www.lesechos.fr/finance-marches/banque-assurances/assurance-axa-supprime-150-emplois-au-sein-de-son-siege-mondial-2262084?utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=cm_x&utm_source=Twitter#Echobox=1794325230-1> might not have been quite as well paid as their neighbours in La Defense, but they do seem to benefit from the country’s highly protected labour markets. Although Axa is cutting 12.5% of its head office staff, it’s doing so through a voluntary redundancy program rather than compulsory layoffs, and those who go are being offered financial and career support.
The forcible ejection of staff is therefore small. There isn’t really any such thing as total job security in banking – it is inherently a volatile industry. And for any one individual, your future is much more likely to be determined by what you do yourself than the place you do it at. But some employment situations are more risky than others, and it does make sense to consider this along with the potential upside.
Elsewhere, the FT has an extremely long and interesting profile of Ana Patricia Botín-Sanz de Sautuola O’Shea <https://www.ft.com/content/0eab6768-1bdb-4a6c-bf6a-2fb8d35eef03?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, better known as the executive chair of Santander. It starts from her earliest days, being taught golf by Seve Ballasteros and identified by her father, Emilio Botín, as his chosen successor to take over the family bank. And it continues to the present day, running the largest bank in Europe by market cap and flying around in a Gulfstream G700 <https://www.gulfstream.com/en/aircraft/gulfstream-g700/>, an exceptionally sweet-looking long range business jet with a list price of nearly $80m.
It’s certainly been quite a journey, and by no means necessarily an easy one. Emilio Botín apparently told his executives to be much tougher on his daughter than on all the other employees, so that she wouldn’t get the nepo treatment. And as a young banker on the graduate scheme at JPMorgan, she got an assessment as “a bit overwhelming to her fellow participants”. It seems quite understandable that she doesn’t want to put her own children through the same experience; she says she will be the last Botín to run the bank.
Along the way, of course, she got quite a lot of advice from Andrea Orcel, the current CEO of Unicredit. Famously, Orcel was offered the CEO job at Santander and accepted it, before a complicated set of disagreements (which are still confusing – pay was part of the story, as was the relationship between him as CEO and Botín as chair) derailed the appointment. The FT reveals that this is still not quite settled – after a Spanish court awarded Orcel €43.4m, Santander’s appeal is likely to be judged next year. You can’t have a career like Botín’s without at least a bit of drama.
Meanwhile …
Charles Elkan, a former machine learning lead at Goldman Sachs and Alex Popa, a former PM at Capital Group, are launching “Poesis”, which intends to become a multi-strategy hedge fund fully staffed by AI agents. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/goldman-capital-group-alumni-debut-ai-run-stock-picking-fund?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261110&utm_campaign=author_1707910>)
They may be earning less than Wall Street CEOs in terms of their salary, but if the Anthropic IPO gets away at the currently expected valuation, its founders will cash out about $250m each, keep stakes worth $18bn and still have total voting control. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/finance/anthropic-founders-stakes-are-worth-18-billion-apiece-at-ipo-price-2c746365?st=fUiNw6>)
Point72 Capital is claiming that one of its quants used their internal AI tools (based on Claude and Codex) to “data mine” other employees’ code and data and transfer it to his personal devices. Xin Jin denies this and “looks forward to setting the record straight”, according to his lawyer. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/point72-claims-fired-quant-analyst-used-ai-tools-to-steal-code?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261110&utm_campaign=author_3487187>)
Greenlight Capital have won their litigation against their former analyst James Fishback, and he apparently now has to hand back all the compensation he ever received there. (David Einhorn <https://x.com/davidein/status/2120246085058691555?s=19>)
Christopher Woolcott has been sentenced for fraud and forgery after trying to create the impression of a takeover bid for a commodities company to push its share price up. He adopted an American accent to pretend to be a private equity executive, used ChatGPT to forge lawyers’ letters and created a message board account called “Junkie Monkey”. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-10/fake-private-equity-executive-convicted-over-bid-to-pump-shares>)
Michael Abraham and David Tapnack have left UBS and PwC respectively to set up Crevora Partners. Their new boutique will apparently do “old-style merchant banking”, which apparently means co-investing in their advisory clients rather than playing a lot of gold while drinking martinis. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/ex-ubs-pwc-dealmakers-return-to-old-style-merchant-banking-with-new-advisory-firm-5f76dccd>)

item.title: HKTE London Career Showcase – a welcome to global talent
item.description:
HKTE London Career Showcase – a welcome to global talent
Organised by Hong Kong Talent Engage (HKTE), the Hong Kong‧Global Talent & Career Showcase took place on October 17th and 18th at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London and was well received, drawing over 4,500 visits and 12,000 CV submissions, with several candidates having preliminary interviews on site.
The event featured more than 200 vacancies offered by over 50 leading enterprises from Hong Kong and the Chinese Mainland, attracting UK-based professionals, entrepreneurs and graduates. Participating enterprises came from industries such as banking and finance, innovation and technology, engineering and construction, and other professional services.
For professionals seeking information rather than immediate action, the showcase also featured a forum and workshops offering valuable career insights, practical career advice and interview tips. For those concerned about the culture shock or family relocation, dedicated sessions explained how these can be handled and what HKTE can assist. Attendees could also benefit from face-to-face CV consultations and professional executive headshots to help tailor their applications.
Adam Janmohamed, a British competition lawyer who has been working in Hong Kong for three years, summed up the city’s appeal in a video shown at the event—part of a new series of promotional talent videos recently produced by HKTE <https://youtu.be/oaHUMuNR_Nk?si=08CCmKs_bNIBjBsV> . He recalls that within a week he had already fallen in love with the city, citing its lifestyle and the balance between work and opportunities to connect with nature. What drew him most, however, was the opportunity to gain exposure to both the Chinese Mainland and global markets.
“Hong Kong really sits in the middle of it all. It’s the super connector across languages, time zones and markets, and the perfect base for working with international clients. You can travel easily to the Chinese Mainland and stay closely connected to opportunities across Asia. That mix has pushed my career much faster than I expected.”
As Adam puts it, it is Hong Kong’s thriving market, together with its role as a gateway to the Chinese Mainland, that many global talent like him value and are drawn to. The career opportunities available to professionals and graduates across this economically dynamic area are reflected in Hong Kong’s position in the IMD Global Talent Ranking, where it rose to fourth place globally last year, higher than any other centre in Asia.
One of the forum speakers, who also attended as an employer, was particularly impressed by the quality of London talent. Ian Choy, an Executive Director at Gammon Construction and the President of the Hong Kong Institute of Human Resources Management, noted that the candidates present ranged from graduates to PhDs and experienced professionals. He pointed out that about 10% of his company’s total staff were global talent, saying that they could “bring specialised skillsets or experiences that are in high demand in Hong Kong.” Ian’s team spoke to several highly promising PhD candidates and is considering them for AI or engineering roles—fields where the city needs to attract more talent. He added: “We received more than 100 CVs on-site alone; after collecting them, the next step is to review the CVs and contact suitable candidates when we are back in Hong Kong. We hope to welcome a new cohort of talent to Hong Kong early next year.”
From the perspective of talent, candidates such as Leo Wickert, a British university student interested in a career in auditing, valued the opportunity to meet employers face to face. He said that “you can read some information online, but when you come here, you actually get to talk to someone and learn more—that’s a big part of it. It’s very impressive … The roles here come from a range of industries, and the workshops have given me a good understanding of industry trends and deeper insight into the sector”.
This was borne out by a post-event survey, which found that nearly 90% of the attendees enhanced their understanding of Hong Kong and the Chinese Mainland, while 95% thought that they were more likely to explore job opportunities in both places.
The successful London event is part of Hong Kong’s “Go Global Together” strategy, under which HKTE brings together institutions and enterprises from Hong Kong and the Chinese Mainland to promote their strengths overseas.
Felix Chan, the Director of HKTE said that “Our support does not end with the showcase. In the coming year, HKTE will continue to visit key regions, including the Chinese Mainland, Europe, Asia Pacific, and North America to promote the development opportunities available across Hong Kong and the Chinese Mainland, introduce various talent attraction measures, and provide incoming talent and their families with comprehensive support services.”
HKTE connects Hong Kong’s opportunities with prospective talent around the world. For upcoming career fairs, events and further roles in Hong Kong, please visit the Hong Kong Talent Engage website and check back for the latest updates:
https://www.hkengage.gov.hk/en <https://www.hkengage.gov.hk/en>

item.title: A load of macro people are swapping jobs in Wall Street banks and maybe this man started it
item.description:
Macro people are falling into </news/santander-s-head-of-linear-rates-trading-in-london-is-now-living-his-best-life-at-capula> and out of </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> hedge funds. They are also cycling between banks in New York.
Headhunters point to at least eight senior macro moves between banks in recent months, most of which appear to be the result of musical chairs.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Opinions vary on who went first. Some say it was Chris McNulty, who left Deutsche Bank in September and has now arrived at Bank of America, where he is head of rates swaps.
Around the time McNulty arrived at BofA, Ammar Ahmed left the American bank to become head of rates swaps at BNP Paribas, which he officially joined in October. Michael Martini, BNP's incumbent US head of rates swaps then left BNP's US business at the end of October according to his FINRA registration. Martini didn't respond to a request to comment.
If it wasn't McNulty, some say the saga was set off by Kunal Maini, who left his job running fixed income trading at BNP Paribas for SMBC in July, starting the sequence of moves. As well as hiring Maini, SMBC hired Rutwik Parikh from BNP as its head of dollar swaps. BNP then hired Ahmed in return.
The moves followed Yassine Haddoui's exit from Verition to become BNP's head of US linear rates in August.
Zoe Liu also went from Bank of America to BMO to run US treasury trading. And Jeff Mundy just went from BMO to SMBC to do the same. Sam El Prince left Morgan Stanley in October.
"A lot has happened," said one headhunter. "It's been a round robin," said another. Whether it began with Bank of America or BNP Paribas is a moot point.

item.title: Entrepreneur with remote jobs for unemployed hedge fund quants is inundated with applications
item.description:
As we have observed </news/blackstone-pay-cut>, the new regret among quantitative portfolio managers is that they joined an electronic trading firm instead of a hedge fund when they left a bank. Jane Street and Citadel Securities are thought to be thriving. Hedge funds, not so much.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There are other options. At the peak of the last Thursday's fund chaos, Christina Qi, founder and CEO of market data platform Databento, broadcast on social media that she had 20 jobs to fill. Qi said she would like to fill them with people coming out of "pod shops."
"Our team includes alumni from Citadel, Two Sigma, Tower Research, Flow Traders, SIG, and other leading trading firms," said Qi, inviting applicants to work remotely and flexibly and to "be able to talk openly about what you do for a living."
Qi tells us that at least 2,000 applicants responded to her call. Every single one was reviewed "by hand."
The applications came mostly from hedge funds and prop shops, says Qi. They also came from fintechs, crypto firms and banks. And they came from independent traders. There are many people out there.
Qi says 2,000 applications for 20 jobs sounds like a lot but is actually "pretty average given the state of the job market these days." There may be more jobs to come. Databento intends to double its 40 person team "in the next few quarters."
Databento raised $97m <https://databento.com/blog/series-b> in series B financing in July. Qi founded the firm in 2020 after having some awkward finance internships. </news/2023/06/christina-qi-hedge-fund>The last time we spoke to her, she'd had 20,000 applications for five jobs </news/the-fintech-boss-who-received-20-000-applications-for-five-jobs-it-s-sad> so maybe things have improved for the jobseeker.

item.title: Trading firm CEO investing $1bn in AI suggests an entire class of market maker will be wiped out
item.description:
Major electronic trading </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> firms like Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> and HRT </news/the-coffee-run-the-kind-trading-firm-paying-1m-to-graduates-and-100m-to-its-top-people> have been investing billions of dollars into their AI infrastructure. The market making space is much larger than just the tier-one firms </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> though, and not everyone can afford to buy tens of thousands of GPUs. </news/quant-trading-gpus>The CEO of one trading firm investing heavily in AI infrastructure thinks that many of these trading firms are doomed to fail in the long term.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Evgeny Gaevoy, CEO of Wintermute, spoke today at the Digital Asset Summit in London about how the "middle tier" of market making "has been less and less successful" in recent years. AI is accelerating this; he said that many of the mid-tier trading firms "can't afford to participate in an arms race on the latency side </news/hft-jobs-medium-frequency-trading> and they definitely can't participate on the AI side." The largest trading firms earn tens of billions in net trading revenue, so the billions they're spending on AI are "peanuts for them in the grand scheme of things." Mid-tier firms also lack the deep market specialization of the smaller, lower-tier firms who are more likely to thrive in newer markets like equity-linked digital assets; Gaevoy said that market is becoming increasingly competitive, "especially on the latency side."
Gaevoy said that Wintermute has 160 employees... which would put it in that mid-tier space. The difference is that Wintermute has "both the capital to invest and a lot of room to grow." The firm made its name in crypto, but Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-12/wintermute-plans-1-billion-ai-investment-to-compete-on-wall-street> reported in August that Wintermute is branching out into equities, commodities and FX while investing up to $1bn into its low-latency and AI infrastructure.
The chances of new tier-one firms emerging are low. Gaevoy said "it might be possible if a bunch of small players team up to combine into something big." If you're building a new trading firm in 2026, he suggests you need to be content with your ceiling being "10/20 people making $1m a head per year."
Gaevoy also said that Wintermute is competing for a very different type of trader to the major firms; graduates working in a tier-one firm "want an established, safe [and] controlled environment. </news/what-interns-at-jane-street-actually-do-from-2022-to-now>" Wintermute is instead "targeting people who can take risks," and Gaevoy believes the $1bn investment puts the firm in a "pretty sweet spot" to be able to hire them. It's willing to pay those people a lot of money; Wintermute's most recent UK accounts via Companies House (for 2024) show that it paid 82 employees an average of ~$1m.

item.title: Blackstone and KKR are slowing down on carried interest. One firm is not
item.description:
Private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> is the promised land for many an aspiring junior financier, and even many an aspiring senior financier, too. A big part of the allure is the potential for carried interest </news/what-is-carried-interest> payments – the massive accumulating profit share of a successful deal that is split up amongst a deal team. Carried interest can comfortably reach eight figures </news/private-equity-credit-pay>.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Unfortunately, carried interest relies on something that firms cannot guarantee: the successful exiting of investments above a hurdle rate. Results from Blackstone, Apollo and KKR suggest that this did not happen equally across firms in the third quarter.
At Blackstone, pay tied to realised carried interest - locked-in income from exits, rather than just paper gains - fell 39% year on year across the whole business in Q3. At KKR it fell 35%, although this was partly because KKR now books some performance fees as fee income instead. At Apollo, however, it rose 156%.
The decline in carried interest was not matched by spending on salaries and bonuses in Q3. At Blackstone, salaries, bonuses, and share awards rose 7%. At KKR, they rose 23%. At Apollo, they rose 22%.
Carried interest is only paid when firms sell investments at a profit, so it can swing rather dramatically from quarter to quarter based upon exits. Blackstone’s realised carried interest from private equity specificially halved in Q3, while Apollo’s rose 80% overall, helped by exits from funds including Fund X, and it paid a bigger share of that to staff. Salaries and bonuses are mostly paid out of management fees, which rose at all three firms... but Apollo said its salary bill rose mainly because it had more staff.
None of the firms disclosed headcount in their Q3 figures, making a per-head comparison impossible. Each also has a different mix of private equity, private credit, insurance and other businesses under its umbrella.

item.title: Does UBS's London trading floor have a mouse problem?
item.description:
Does UBS's London trading floor have a mouse problem? This would seem to depend upon where you sit.
Various employees at UBS tell us that the office at 5 Broadgate has got a mouse issue and that it is particularly acute on the trading floor on floor two where many fixed income trading desks are housed.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"It's pretty bad," says one anonymous trader. "There are mice running across the floor...You often see them during the day. A few weeks ago I heard a scream from the row next to me where a mouse had literally run by a guy’s feet while he was sat at his desk."
UBS declined to comment. Other traders at the Swiss bank said they had not seen mice on the trading floor, although one said he had seen a mouse in the canteen. Another told us that the mouse issue has been a longstanding problem. Another said it's no big deal and that all major office buildings in London have some form of infestation.
To the extent that there is a problem, traders say it's worse on the second than on the fourth floor trading floors and that it's worse again if you're working late or during quiet periods. "Last year I worked a couple of the days between Christmas and New Year and I probably saw six mice a day," says one trader.
That same trader says mouse traps have been installed by management to resolve the problem, but they are not always emptied promptly.
"For a big European investment bank to have a trading floor full of mice I think is absurd," he said. "Even in the canteen if you go there late afternoon or evening when it’s quiet, you can see them running around."
Another senior trader at the Swiss bank says UBS is not an outlier. "It's like every bank I've worked for," he says. "You see some mice." It's because people eat at the desks, says another trader familiar with the floor. It was allegedly worse at Goldman Sachs when Goldman was in Peterborough Court.

item.title: Santander's ex-head of linear rates trading in London is living his best life at Capula
item.description:
Macro hedge funds have been having a hard time and ejecting quantities of people, </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> but they are also hiring. Greg Rickards at Santander has been hired.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Writing on LinkedIn, Rickards says he has joined British hedge fund Capula Investment Management as a portfolio manager. Rickards didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. He has spent the past 17 years at Santander and was head of linear rates trading for the bank in London since 2018.
Rickards' arrival comes after Capula parted company </news/ex-citi-trader-out-at-hedge-fund-capula-after-just-three-months> with Michele Beretta </news/capula-hedge-fund-hiring> from Citi, who was only there for three months and Andrea Casulli from Goldman, whose pod Beretta joined. The FCA Register suggests Gregory Nataf left the London entity last week and that Nimesh Mistry, a senior manager, left at the end of October.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-28/hedge-fund-capula-launches-new-strategy-in-diversification-push> reported in August that Capula had launched a diversification push after historically focusing on relative value trading across fixed income. To this end it hired Yao Hua Ooi, who built a systematic trading strategy for AQR. Last year it hired various energy traders, including John Anderson from Millennium.
It's not clear how Capula is performing in 2026. Last year, it paid an average of $630k </news/capula-hedge-fund> in London and revenues fell 19%.

item.title: Goldman Sachs people are leaving and declaring that it's all been "incredible"
item.description:
When you leave Goldman Sachs you had better be positive about your experience there. As has been widely observed, </news/2023/01/leaving-goldman-sachs> people who leave Goldman Sachs tend to talk about Goldman Sachs a lot, as if Goldman Sachs was the peak of their self-actualisation.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This might be because working for Goldman Sachs is great. Christian Alexander </news/the-ex-goldman-sachs-md-living-in-a-van-i-have-nothing-bad-to-say-about-that-place>, the ex-Goldman Sachs MD now living in a van and writing a Substack <https://substack.com/@norebates>, told us that he cried on the sidewalk when he walked away and "can't say anything bad about that place." Goldman is a caring place, said Alexander. He left in 2013, though.
More recent Goldman Sachs leavers do not seem to be shedding tears. But they are congregating on LinkedIn and using similar language to describe their time there.
"It's been an incredible 11 years," says Evan Tylenda, the former head of EMEA GS Sustain. The people at Goldman Sachs are "amazing", says Tylenda. There was cool work and there were "great conversations."
Risa Lederhandler is leaving too. She spent over two decades at Goldman Sachs and four years as a partner and was latterly global head of equities franchise operations. Her 22 years at Goldman were also "incredible." The people were also "talented and inspiring."
Both Tylenda and Lederhandler have jobs to go to. Bloomberg <https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/balyasny-hires-goldman-partner-lederhandler-for-new-top-role> reported in May that Lederhandler is becoming Balyasny's chief operating officer in Europe. Tylenda has returned to San Francisco for a new opportunity. Both declare themselves "excited."
Tylenda and Lederhandler offer a masterclass in how you must speak after leaving a job. It's not clear whether people recently cut </news/goldman-sachs-cut-some-jobs-last-week-it-s-that-time-of-year>from Goldman will be equally thrilled, but if you want former colleagues to vouch for you declarations of gratitude and excitement are mandatory.

item.title: The finance professionals scared of AI might just be using the wrong tools
item.description:
Finance is a heavily regulated industry, meaning that the newest AI tools </news/how-to-get-a-banking-ai-job>can't always be made readily available. This means that you can either be handed the most enterprise-appropriate off-the-shelf tool, or your firm can develop one in-house. The people using these tools also seem to be the biggest sceptics.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We surveyed ~2,500 current and prospective financial services professionals </news/finance-working-hours-ai> on their sentiment towards AI </news/who-is-most-afraid-of-ai-in-finance>, as well as what tools they use for work. 39% of employees using internal AI tools said they do not trust AI at all, the most of any type of tool. The rate of mistrust among ChatGPT and Claude users was 27% and 29% respectively.
When looking at each sector individually, it is also interesting to note that the sectors with the highest level of AI mistrust also had the highest percentage of respondents using internal tools.
What makes in-house tools so mediocre? One banker using exclusively internal tools said that they "hallucinate a lot... </news/goldman-sachs-new-ai-trepidation-means-big-compliance-salaries-for-now>they can improve analysis but checking the results takes up time." A UK-based risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank>professional said her internal tools frequently flag "false positives." A Hong Kong technologist said that he bypasses protocol to access external tools rather than use internal ones: "with a VPN, we can access almost anything."
Interestingly, the three sectors most doubtful of AI also reported Microsoft Copilot among their top two most-used tool, and were the only sectors to do so. 30% of Microsoft CoPilot users said they didn't trust AI; one equities trader said the tools are being "pushed to automate processes" in her organization but "it's so lacking; it's causing more problems than if a human did the work in the first place." One compliance professional said he's only allowed to use Copilot because "IT is scared" of other external tools.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Senior managing directors on $17m unhappy about their $15m pay cut. Jane Street & Citadel Securities probably thriving
item.description:
The cost of living is rising everywhere and it's not easy when your pay is also falling - even if you do still have a salary and bonus of $2m.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Senior managing directors (SMDs) on Blackstone's real estate team are experiencing the squeeze. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/real-estate/commercial/dwindling-pay-fuels-high-profile-exits-from-blackstones-marquee-real-estate-team-317f2676> says their team was once 'marquee' and that they could earn $15m in carried interest </news/what-is-carried-interest> alongside their $2m of salary and bonus. One head of business was even said to be making $30m in carried interest. Now the carried interest is no longer carrying them along.
It's a sorry tale and one that will be familiar to anyone accustomed to receiving large amounts of lightly-taxed money which stop suddenly. Many are in a similar situation. The financial services industry has become full of people living paycheck to paycheck, says Ahmed Husain </news/leaving-banking-private-equity>, a former Goldman Sachs managing director who's spent the past 12 years working with family offices. </news/family-office-jobs>
The problem in Blackstone's real estate team is the same as the problem in all the other private equity teams whose carried interest has disappeared: </news/as-carried-interest-dwindles-private-equity-professionals-want-this-instead> previous investments have not generated successful exits. The WSJ says Blackstone's team invested in data centres, life sciences, student accommodation and logistics hubs. Only the data centre investments are thriving. One student accommodation investment was sold for 70% below its purchase price. The WSJ notes that four out of 13 Blackstone real estate funds were below the threshold for paying carried interest in the firm's 2025 annual report.
Senior people have been leaving. The WSJ says they have done so for all sorts of reasons but that a dozen have gone. The global head of real estate left two months ago to spend more time with his family after saying he wanted to meditate and to get more sleep. Others are said to have left because they were weary of travel and being 'on call non-stop.' Others were eased out or retired.
Blackstone didn't respond to our request to comment on the WSJ article. It told the WSJ: "Our real-estate business has enormous continuity and tremendous talent, including 45 partners with an average tenure of 14 years at the firm.” It also said the number of MDs remains the same. As people used to earning $17m leave, maybe a new generation of senior people will learn to get by on $2m instead?
Separately, as hedge funds flounder </news/hedge-fund-losses-2026>, top electronic trading </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>firms may be doing fine.
Barry Ritholtz <https://ritholtz.com/2026/11/thoughts-on-the-selloff/> writes that while multistrategy hedge fund pods found themselves in a 'crowded, systematic, long-leveraged growth equity trade' that was unwinding last Thursday, electronic trading firms were probably doing the unwinding.
'My bet is that Citadel Securities and Jane Street were the counterparties to a massive unwind,' says Barry. 'We will find out if that suspicion is true as soon as rumors of windfall trading profits in November for those two firms begin to circulate.'
As we wrote last week, </news/hedge-fund-manager-unemployed> some junior quants are already bemoaning their decisions to join hedge funds instead of market-making firms.
Meanwhile...
Citadel Securities hired 100 people in Asia this year and now has 400 people there. 200 are in Hong Kong. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-09/citadel-securities-plots-asia-push-with-hiring-office-expansion?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261109&utm_campaign=author_19908303>
UK fund manager Nick Train said his trust has delivered its best monthly performance since 2000 as AI losers Experian, software group Sage, analytics company Relx, London Stock Exchange Group and property website Rightmove are back in fashion. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/e3a7d3b9-5391-4f2d-a12a-2b252a18b73a?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Sometimes it's easier to get $2m in funding than a job. 27-year-old Hugo Stack failed to get an entry level job in finance and now he's building a start-up called Mecone to bring perpetual futures trading to a wider investor base. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/20-somethings-are-ditching-entry-level-jobs-to-become-their-own-bosses-168d1f48?mod=hp_lead_pos8>
Hedge funds have been deleveraging and looking for cheap hedges. Systematic volatility dispersion baskets are the fashion. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-08/traders-look-to-wall-street-quant-strategies-to-hedge-next-crash?srnd=phx-markets>
Sequoia realised it didn't need a team in London after US partners like Alfred Lin and Andrew Reed were running the big European deals anyway. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-09/sequoia-quits-london-after-us-team-lands-buzzy-european-ai-deals?srnd=homepage-uk>
Alice Huang, who had an affair with Jensen Huang (no relation) once worked for HSBC. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/tech/the-chinese-woman-at-the-center-of-a-spy-probe-after-an-affair-with-jensen-huang-7bb406d2?mod=WSJ_home_mediumtopper_pos_3>
Jensen Huang's two children, daughter Madison Huang and son Spencer Huang, both work for Nvidia, as does Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/jensen-huang-apologized-to-nvidia-for-his-infidelity-his-kids-are-on-staff-190f3176?mod=WSJ_home_mediumtopper_pos_4>

item.title: If Townie Wells can leave Jain Global and choose Millennium money, could other Jain PMs do the same?
item.description:
Townie Wells is leaving Jain Global. Rumours about Wells' possible exit have been circulating ever since Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jain-global-millennium-deal-details-equity-unit-exits-2026-5>reported in May that the stock picking unit Wells ran for Jain Global had "struggled to get off to a good start" in 2026 and that at least four of its portfolio managers had left. Now, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-09/jain-s-equities-head-townie-wells-leaves-to-start-own-hedge-fund>is reporting that Wells has departed to start his own fund.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Wells didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Bloomberg said he's already in talks with Millennium for a multibillion dollar allocation. This will likely be as a separately managed account (SMA).
Wells will be in good company. Jain Global itself agreed to manage money exclusively for Millennium in April and began doing so from September.
Jain Global began life as a standalone multistrategy hedge fund run by ex-Millennium co-CIO Bobby Jain </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience>, but it generated reported returns of 0.5% in 2024, 3.7% in 2025 and 0.6% for this year through to April. Bobby returned other investors' money and agreed to manage money exclusively for Izzy Englander at Millennium, with whom he'd previously worked for six years.
Townie Wells was reportedly one of Jain Global's most profitable portfolio managers in 2025. Bloomberg says he was considering taking Millennium money and starting his own firm three years ago. After leaving Citadel, he opted to work with Bobby Jain instead. Now he's going it alone.
If Wells can now leave Jain Global and take money directly from Millennium, might other senior Jain Global PMs do the same? Jain Global had 65 portfolio managers </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-costs>in April this year and not all are likely to have this option. However, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-12-14/bobby-jain-fills-seven-cio-positions-fleshes-out-senior-staff> reported in late 2023 that Jain Global had seven strategy CIOs, of whom Wells was only one. Might the remaining other CIOs seek Millennium money directly for their own independent funds too?
Jain Global isn't commenting on the record. Nor is Millennium. Wells may simply have wanted more independence; Bloomberg says Bobby Jain stepped in to help run the equities business earlier this year. It’s conceivable that backing Wells’ own fund would be a way for Millennium to keep him as an investment partner, rather than losing him to another fund. A person close to Jain suggested Wells' move was a good outcome for the parties involved.
It's not clear what kind of risk limits Millennium is imposing on its money at Jain Global. However, Millennium has a reputation for imposing strict rules on drawdowns, with portfolio managers who lose 7.5% or more said to be cut without discussion. One senior equities PM who's running his own fund suggests that Wells may simply have decided that he'd be better off alone: "He probably has superior economics and much more autonomy now," he says. "Before he was an employee on a payout. Now he's a principal."
Millennium has been amassing a senior equities team in-house. Goldman Sachs partner Erdit Hoxha <https://www.ft.com/content/6554d91e-c2b7-4510-9db7-2ac4bd62469e?syn-25a6b1a6=1> left Goldman for Millennium in February. Drew Gillanders </news/drew-gillanders-millennium>left Citadel for Millennium in October. Pasi Tolmunen is on his way there from Aito Capital. Jack Ingles is joining from Point72. All are thought to have been out of the market on non-competes during the recent ructions. </news/as-hedge-fund-walleye-capital-ejects-p-ms-a-reminder-of-the-toxic-interview>
Jain Global has also been bolstering its equities team. </news/hedge-fund-jain-global-made-two-big-equities-hires-in-london> It hired Valentin Tataru from JPMorgan and Murat Bostan from KMB Capital (his own fund) in October. Bloomberg reported in September that Jain has been pitching itself to potential hires as a trading firm where portfolio managers collaborate with one another, whereas Millennium provides more independence and autonomy.
Jain's pitch now looks more important as a differentiator. One senior employee at a rival fund observes that Millennium could probably always have hired Jain's people itself had it wanted them. Maybe it could just offer the ones it likes funds of their own instead? Jain Global may even want that if it keeps people in the broader Millennium fold.

item.title: Female Asian bankers fear discrimination following the Jensen Huang affair
item.description:
If Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang can spark an 8% drop <https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/south-korea-says-nvidia-issues-wont-affect-contracted-gpu-supplies-2026-11-09/>in NVIDIA's share price after admitting <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/nvidia-jensen-huang-email-board-of-directors-statement.html>an affair with an attractive suspected Chinese spy <https://news.sky.com/story/tech-giant-nvidia-launches-investigation-after-reports-ceo-was-targeted-by-chinese-intelligence-13609986> many years younger than himself, what would happen if senior bank CEOs confessed something similar? What if major western banks or hedge funds were found to have employed female spies in senior roles?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As Huang's infraction percolates the markets, there are gnawing fears that financial services firms will become more hesitant about employing Chinese women in the future. "There are very few Asian women at the top of Western banks as it is," says one female managing director in Hong Kong, speaking off the record. "It's still a boys club here, especially in the markets business."
The object of Jensen Huang's affections didn't work for NVIDIA but was reportedly in Huang's orbit as a major buyer of NVIDIA chips in Asia. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-09/alice-huang-suspected-china-spy-spent-years-in-nvidia-s-orbit>reports that they were first photographed together at a conference in 2024.
Bankers and hedge fund managers have already taken to speculating who Chinese spies might be. One senior female trader said it's become an excuse for sexist jokes and that the real issue is the integrity of the NVIDIA CEO. "He's betrayed his ethics," she says, arguing that it's men and not women who should be subject to greater scrutiny.
"If this Chinese spy situation is real and serious then people will be doing a lot more due diligence before senior hiring," says the head of one financial services search firm in New York.
The female MD in Hong Kong said the affair risks triggering discrimination against all Asian women in financial services. "Americans can't differentiate between Singaporean women and Chinese nationals," she observed. Earlier this year, one young Asian woman in Singapore wrote here </news/sexism-banking-asia>that she'd been subjected to significant sexism and that her male colleagues had closed ranks against her.
NVIDIA's board said <https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/statement-from-nvidia-board-of-directors> it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," but that it is investigating suggestions that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," all the same.
